$$C_P^{\text{para}} = 38.1\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1} \quad (T > 631\,\text{K})$$

At the Curie transition itself, there is an associated latent-like enthalpy contribution of $\Delta H_C = 450\,\text{J mol}^{-1}$ (heat absorbed by the system at $T_C$).

Starting from $T_1 = 550\,\text{K}$, calculate the total molar entropy change $\Delta S$ when 2.5 mol of nickel is heated at constant pressure to $T_2 = 720\,\text{K}$.

Given: $R = 8.314\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$
L2|medium.solution:
## Step-by-step solution

**Identify the three contributions to $\Delta S$**

Heating from 550 K to 720 K crosses the Curie point at 631 K. At constant pressure, $\delta Q_\text{rev} = C_P\,\mathrm{d}T$, so:

$$\mathrm{d}S = \frac{\delta Q_\text{rev}}{T} = \frac{C_P\,\mathrm{d}T}{T}$$

The total molar entropy change splits into three pieces:

$$\Delta \underline{S} = \underbrace{\int_{550}^{631} \frac{C_P^\text{ferro}}{T}\,\mathrm{d}T}_{\text{(i) heat ferrromagnetic Ni}} + \underbrace{\frac{\Delta H_C}{T_C}}_{\text{(ii) Curie transition}} + \underbrace{\int_{631}^{720} \frac{C_P^\text{para}}{T}\,\mathrm{d}T}_{\text{(iii) heat paramagnetic Ni}}$$

---

**Piece (i) — heat ferromagnetic Ni from 550 K to 631 K**

$$\Delta \underline{S}_1 = C_P^\text{ferro}\,\ln\!\frac{631}{550} = 44.3 \times \ln\!\left(\frac{631}{550}\right)$$

$$\ln\!\frac{631}{550} = \ln(1.1473) = 0.13749$$

$$\Delta \underline{S}_1 = 44.3 \times 0.13749 = 6.091\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

---

**Piece (ii) — entropy of the Curie transition at $T_C = 631\,\text{K}$**

$$\Delta \underline{S}_2 = \frac{\Delta H_C}{T_C} = \frac{450}{631} = 0.713\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

---

**Piece (iii) — heat paramagnetic Ni from 631 K to 720 K**

$$\Delta \underline{S}_3 = C_P^\text{para}\,\ln\!\frac{720}{631} = 38.1 \times \ln\!\left(\frac{720}{631}\right)$$

$$\ln\!\frac{720}{631} = \ln(1.1410) = 0.13198$$

$$\Delta \underline{S}_3 = 38.1 \times 0.13198 = 5.028\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

---

**Total molar entropy change**

$$\Delta \underline{S} = 6.091 + 0.713 + 5.028 = 11.832\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

---

**Scale to 2.5 mol**

$$\Delta S = n \times \Delta \underline{S} = 2.5 \times 11.832 = \boxed{29.6\,\text{J K}^{-1}}$$

---

**Sanity check**

As a rough order-of-magnitude check, average $C_P \approx 41\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$, $\Delta T = 170\,\text{K}$, average $T \approx 635\,\text{K}$:

$$\Delta \underline{S} \approx \frac{41 \times 170}{635} \approx 11.0\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

Close to our computed 11.83 J mol$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$ — the difference reflects the transition contribution and the logarithmic (not linear) nature of the integral. $\checkmark$
L2|medium.final_answer: $\Delta S = 29.6\,\text{J K}^{-1}$ (for 2.5 mol of Ni heated from 550 K to 720 K at constant pressure)
common_mistakes: **Using $\Delta S = C_P \Delta T / T_{\text{avg}}$ instead of integrating $C_P/T$**: students sometimes divide by a single average temperature rather than integrating $\mathrm{d}T/T$, which yields $\ln(T_2/T_1)$. This is only a rough approximation and loses accuracy.

**Omitting the Curie transition contribution**: the transition entropy $\Delta H_C / T_C = 0.71\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$ is modest but must be included. Students who treat the $C_P$ curve as continuous across 631 K will miss this term entirely — analogous to skipping the latent heat of fusion when heating through a melting point.

**Forgetting to multiply the molar entropy change by the number of moles**: the integral gives a *molar* $\Delta S$ in J mol$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$; scaling to $n = 2.5\,\text{mol}$ is a separate step that students under exam pressure often overlook.

L2|medium.title: Entropy Change on Isothermal Compression of Nitrogen
L2|medium.statement:
A sample of 3 mol of nitrogen gas (N$_2$, diatomic ideal gas) is compressed isothermally and reversibly at 450 K from an initial pressure of 1.5 atm to a final pressure of 12 atm.

(a) Using the appropriate Maxwell relation, derive the expression for the entropy change of the gas during this isothermal compression.

(b) Calculate $\Delta S$ for the gas.

(c) What is the entropy change of the universe for this reversible process?

Given: $R = 8.314$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$.
L2|medium.solution:
## Step 1 — Derive $\Delta S$ for an isothermal process using a Maxwell relation

From the Gibbs free energy differential:
$$\mathrm{d}G = -S\,\mathrm{d}T + V\,\mathrm{d}P$$

Applying the exactness condition (Maxwell relation from $G$):
$$\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial P}\right)_{T} = -\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_{P}$$

For an ideal gas, $PV = nRT$, so at constant $P$:
$$\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_{P} = \frac{nR}{P}$$

Substituting into the Maxwell relation:
$$\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial P}\right)_{T} = -\frac{nR}{P}$$

Integrating at constant $T$ from $P_1$ to $P_2$:
$$\Delta S = \int_{P_1}^{P_2} -\frac{nR}{P}\,\mathrm{d}P = -nR\ln\frac{P_2}{P_1}$$

## Step 2 — Substitute values

$$\Delta S = -nR\ln\frac{P_2}{P_1} = -(3)(8.314)\ln\frac{12}{1.5}$$

Compute the pressure ratio:
$$\frac{P_2}{P_1} = \frac{12}{1.5} = 8$$

$$\Delta S = -(3)(8.314)\ln 8 = -(24.942)(2.0794)$$

$$\boxed{\Delta S_{\text{gas}} = -51.9 \text{ J K}^{-1}}$$

The negative sign is physically expected: compressing the gas reduces the number of accessible microstates ($\Omega$ falls), so $S = k_B \ln\Omega$ decreases.

## Step 3 — Entropy change of the universe

This is a **reversible** isothermal process. For any reversible process:
$$\mathrm{d}S_{\text{universe}} = 0$$

This means $\Delta S_{\text{surroundings}} = +51.9$ J K$^{-1}$ exactly cancels the gas's entropy decrease. The surroundings absorb the heat released by the gas during compression:
$$Q_{\text{surroundings}} = -Q_{\text{gas}} = +T\,|\Delta S_{\text{gas}}| = (450)(51.9) \approx +23{,}355 \text{ J}$$

and $\Delta S_{\text{surr}} = Q_{\text{surr}}/T = 23{,}355/450 = +51.9$ J K$^{-1}$, confirming $\Delta S_{\text{universe}} = 0$.

$$\boxed{\Delta S_{\text{universe}} = 0}$$
common_mistakes: Forgetting the negative sign in the Maxwell relation $\left(\partial S/\partial P\right)_T = -\left(\partial V/\partial T\right)_P$ and obtaining a positive $\Delta S$ for compression — which contradicts the physical expectation that compression reduces disorder.

Using $\Delta S = nC_V \ln(T_2/T_1)$ or $nC_P\ln(T_2/T_1)$, which applies to isobaric or isochoric heating, not to an isothermal pressure change; the $1/T$ temperature factor in those formulas does not apply here.

Claiming that $\Delta S_{\text{universe}} = 0$ means nothing happened — the correct interpretation is that the process is reversible, so the entropy decrease of the gas is exactly offset by the entropy increase of the surroundings that absorb the released heat.

L2|medium.title: Entropy Change on Isothermal Expansion of Argon
L2|medium.statement:
A sealed, thermally conducting piston-cylinder device contains 3 mol of argon (Ar) gas at 400 K and an initial pressure of $P_1 = 8\text{ atm}$. The gas is allowed to expand reversibly and isothermally until the pressure drops to $P_2 = 2\text{ atm}$.

(a) Calculate the entropy change $\Delta S$ of the argon gas during this process.

(b) Calculate the entropy change $\Delta S_\text{surroundings}$ during this process.

(c) State the entropy change of the universe $\Delta S_\text{universe}$ and justify your answer in terms of the Second Law.

**Given data:** $R = 8.314\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$; treat Ar as an ideal gas.
L2|medium.solution:
## Step 1 — Identify the process and the relevant formula

The process is **isothermal** ($T = 400\text{ K} = \text{constant}$) and **reversible**. For an ideal gas at constant temperature, the entropy change of the gas is found from the Maxwell relation derived in L3 (and previewed in L2):

$$\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial P}\right)_T = -\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P$$

For an ideal gas, $\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P = \frac{nR}{P}$, so:

$$\mathrm{d}S = -\frac{nR}{P}\,\mathrm{d}P \quad (\text{at constant } T)$$

Integrating from $P_1$ to $P_2$:

$$\Delta S = -nR\ln\frac{P_2}{P_1}$$

Alternatively, this follows directly from $\delta Q_\text{rev} = T\,\mathrm{d}S$ and the ideal-gas isothermal work.

## Step 2 — Compute $\Delta S_\text{gas}$ (part a)

Substitute $n = 3\text{ mol}$, $R = 8.314\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$, $P_1 = 8\text{ atm}$, $P_2 = 2\text{ atm}$:

$$\Delta S_\text{gas} = -nR\ln\frac{P_2}{P_1} = -(3)(8.314)\ln\frac{2}{8}$$

$$= -(3)(8.314)\ln(0.25)$$

$$= -(3)(8.314)(-1.3863)$$

$$= +34.59\text{ J K}^{-1}$$

$$\boxed{\Delta S_\text{gas} \approx +34.6\text{ J K}^{-1}}$$

The positive sign makes physical sense: the gas expands, occupying more volume, so there are more accessible microstates and entropy increases.

## Step 3 — Compute $\Delta S_\text{surroundings}$ (part b)

For a **reversible** process, the heat absorbed by the gas equals the heat released by the surroundings. First, find $Q$ for the gas.

For an isothermal process on an ideal gas, $\Delta U = 0$ (since $U$ depends only on $T$ for an ideal gas). Therefore the First Law gives:

$$Q = -W = +\int_{V_1}^{V_2} P\,\mathrm{d}V = nRT\ln\frac{V_2}{V_1} = nRT\ln\frac{P_1}{P_2}$$

$$Q_\text{gas} = (3)(8.314)(400)\ln\frac{8}{2} = (3)(8.314)(400)(1.3863)$$

$$Q_\text{gas} = +13{,}836\text{ J} \approx +13.84\text{ kJ}$$

The surroundings lose this amount of heat, so $Q_\text{surr} = -13{,}836\text{ J}$. The surroundings are at a constant temperature $T = 400\text{ K}$ (the process is isothermal and the cylinder is thermally conducting), so:

$$\Delta S_\text{surroundings} = \frac{Q_\text{surr}}{T} = \frac{-13{,}836}{400}$$

$$\boxed{\Delta S_\text{surroundings} \approx -34.6\text{ J K}^{-1}}$$

## Step 4 — Entropy of the universe (part c)

$$\Delta S_\text{universe} = \Delta S_\text{gas} + \Delta S_\text{surroundings} = +34.6 + (-34.6) = 0$$

$$\boxed{\Delta S_\text{universe} = 0}$$

**Justification:** The Second Law states $\mathrm{d}S_\text{universe} \geq 0$, with equality holding **only for a reversible process**. Because this expansion is specified as reversible (quasi-static, the external pressure equals the gas pressure at every instant), no entropy is generated. The entropy gained by the gas is exactly offset by the entropy lost by the surroundings. This is consistent with $\mathrm{d}S_\text{universe} = 0$.
L2|medium.final_answer: (a) $\Delta S_\text{gas} = +34.6\text{ J K}^{-1}$; (b) $\Delta S_\text{surroundings} = -34.6\text{ J K}^{-1}$; (c) $\Delta S_\text{universe} = 0$ (reversible process).
common_mistakes: **Confusing the system entropy with the universe entropy.** Students often see $\Delta S_\text{gas} > 0$ and conclude the Second Law is satisfied without checking the surroundings. The Second Law requires $\Delta S_\text{universe} \geq 0$, not $\Delta S_\text{system} \geq 0$. Here the surroundings lose exactly the same entropy the gas gains, giving $\Delta S_\text{universe} = 0$.

**Using $\Delta S = nC_V \ln(T_2/T_1)$ or $\Delta S = nC_P \ln(T_2/T_1)$.** These formulas apply when temperature changes. Here the process is isothermal ($T_2 = T_1$), so those expressions give zero — which is wrong. The correct formula for an isothermal ideal-gas process uses the pressure (or volume) ratio: $\Delta S = -nR\ln(P_2/P_1)$.

**Forgetting the sign on the surroundings' entropy.** The surroundings supply heat to the gas (since the gas absorbs $Q > 0$), so the surroundings lose heat. Students often write $\Delta S_\text{surr} = +Q/T$ instead of $-Q/T$, and incorrectly conclude $\Delta S_\text{universe} > 0$ for a reversible process.

L2|medium.title: Entropy Change on Mixing Hot and Cold Water
L2|medium.statement: Two thermally insulated containers hold water. Container 1 holds $m_1 = 0.500$ kg of water at $T_1 = 360$ K, and Container 2 holds $m_2 = 1.50$ kg of water at $T_2 = 280$ K. The two containers are placed in thermal contact inside a rigid, perfectly insulated outer vessel so that no heat is exchanged with the surroundings. The specific heat capacity of water is $c_P = 4184$ J kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$ (treat as constant). (a) Find the final equilibrium temperature $T_f$. (b) Calculate the entropy change of the hot water, $\Delta S_1$. (c) Calculate the entropy change of the cold water, $\Delta S_2$. (d) Calculate the total entropy change of the universe, $\Delta S_\text{univ}$, and state whether this process is consistent with the Second Law.
L2|medium.solution:
## Step 1 — Final Equilibrium Temperature

The outer vessel is rigid and perfectly insulated, so the system (both containers together) exchanges no heat or work with the surroundings. By the First Law, the total internal energy is conserved. Since $c_P$ is constant and the containers are at atmospheric pressure:

$$m_1 c_P (T_f - T_1) + m_2 c_P (T_f - T_2) = 0$$

Divide through by $c_P$:

$$m_1(T_f - T_1) + m_2(T_f - T_2) = 0$$

$$T_f = \frac{m_1 T_1 + m_2 T_2}{m_1 + m_2} = \frac{(0.500)(360) + (1.50)(280)}{0.500 + 1.50}$$

$$T_f = \frac{180 + 420}{2.00} = \frac{600}{2.00} = \boxed{300 \text{ K}}$$

## Step 2 — Entropy Change of the Hot Water

Water in Container 1 cools from $T_1 = 360$ K to $T_f = 300$ K at constant pressure. Because $S$ is a state function we can compute $\Delta S$ along any reversible path connecting the same endpoints. For a reversible isobaric path:

$$\Delta S_1 = \int_{T_1}^{T_f} \frac{m_1 c_P}{T}\,\mathrm{d}T = m_1 c_P \ln\frac{T_f}{T_1}$$

$$\Delta S_1 = (0.500)(4184)\ln\frac{300}{360} = 2092 \times \ln(0.8333)$$

$$\ln(0.8333) = -0.1823$$

$$\Delta S_1 = 2092 \times (-0.1823) = \boxed{-381.4 \text{ J K}^{-1}}$$

The hot water loses entropy as it cools — consistent with intuition.

## Step 3 — Entropy Change of the Cold Water

Water in Container 2 warms from $T_2 = 280$ K to $T_f = 300$ K:

$$\Delta S_2 = m_2 c_P \ln\frac{T_f}{T_2} = (1.50)(4184)\ln\frac{300}{280}$$

$$= 6276 \times \ln(1.07143)$$

$$\ln(1.07143) = 0.06899$$

$$\Delta S_2 = 6276 \times 0.06899 = \boxed{+433.1 \text{ J K}^{-1}}$$

## Step 4 — Total Entropy Change of the Universe

The outer vessel is perfectly insulated, so the surroundings are unaffected: $\Delta S_\text{surr} = 0$.

$$\Delta S_\text{univ} = \Delta S_1 + \Delta S_2 + \Delta S_\text{surr} = -381.4 + 433.1 + 0$$

$$\boxed{\Delta S_\text{univ} = +51.7 \text{ J K}^{-1}}$$

**Conclusion.** $\Delta S_\text{univ} > 0$, confirming that this irreversible mixing process is consistent with the Second Law. Heat flows spontaneously from hot to cold, generating entropy. The process cannot be reversed without external intervention — if you tried to un-mix the temperatures, you would have to do work on the system (a refrigerator), which would generate even more entropy in the surroundings.
L2|medium.final_answer: (a) $T_f = 300$ K; (b) $\Delta S_1 = -381$ J K$^{-1}$; (c) $\Delta S_2 = +433$ J K$^{-1}$; (d) $\Delta S_\text{univ} = +51.7$ J K$^{-1} > 0$ — consistent with the Second Law.
common_mistakes: **Using $\Delta S = Q/T$ with a single fixed temperature** for the liquid water rather than integrating $m c_P / T$ over the temperature range. A single temperature cannot represent a substance that is continuously changing temperature; the correct formula is $\Delta S = m c_P \ln(T_f/T_i)$.

**Assuming $\Delta S_\text{univ} = 0$ because the vessel is insulated.** Students conflate an adiabatic process with a reversible (isentropic) one. The insulation only ensures $\Delta S_\text{surr} = 0$; the irreversible heat transfer *inside* the vessel still generates entropy. Adiabatic does not imply isentropic unless the internal process is also reversible.

**Adding the magnitude of $\Delta S_1$ to $\Delta S_2$ without keeping the sign of $\Delta S_1$ negative**, giving $\Delta S_\text{univ} = 381 + 433 = 814$ J K$^{-1}$. Always carry the sign of each entropy change through the addition; only the algebraic sum gives $\Delta S_\text{univ}$.

L2|medium.title: Entropy Change on Heating Zinc Through Its Melting Point
L2|medium.statement:
Zinc is heated at constant atmospheric pressure from 500 K to 1000 K. Zinc melts at $T_m = 692.7$ K with a molar enthalpy of fusion of $\Delta H_\text{fus} = 7133$ J/mol. The molar heat capacities are:

$$C_P^\text{solid} = 25.44 + 6.86\times10^{-3}\,T \quad [\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}]$$

$$C_P^\text{liquid} = 31.38 \quad [\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}]$$

Calculate the total molar entropy change $\Delta S$ for this process.
L2|medium.solution:
The process crosses the melting point of zinc, so we cannot use a single integral from 500 K to 1000 K. We must split the calculation into **three contributions**:

1. Heating solid Zn from 500 K to 692.7 K.
2. Melting at 692.7 K (isothermal phase change).
3. Heating liquid Zn from 692.7 K to 1000 K.

---

### Step 1 — Heat solid Zn from 500 K to 692.7 K

At constant pressure, $\delta Q_\text{rev} = C_P^\text{solid}\,\mathrm{d}T$, so

$$\Delta S_1 = \int_{500}^{692.7} \frac{C_P^\text{solid}}{T}\,\mathrm{d}T = \int_{500}^{692.7} \frac{25.44 + 6.86\times10^{-3}\,T}{T}\,\mathrm{d}T$$

$$= \int_{500}^{692.7} \left(\frac{25.44}{T} + 6.86\times10^{-3}\right)\mathrm{d}T$$

$$= 25.44\,\ln\!\frac{692.7}{500} + 6.86\times10^{-3}\,(692.7 - 500)$$

$$= 25.44\times\ln(1.3854) + 6.86\times10^{-3}\times192.7$$

$$= 25.44\times0.3256 + 1.322$$

$$= 8.284 + 1.322 = 9.606\;\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

---

### Step 2 — Melting at 692.7 K

The phase change is isothermal and isobaric, so:

$$\Delta S_2 = \frac{\Delta H_\text{fus}}{T_m} = \frac{7133}{692.7} = 10.30\;\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

---

### Step 3 — Heat liquid Zn from 692.7 K to 1000 K

$C_P^\text{liquid}$ is constant, so:

$$\Delta S_3 = \int_{692.7}^{1000} \frac{C_P^\text{liquid}}{T}\,\mathrm{d}T = 31.38\,\ln\!\frac{1000}{692.7}$$

$$= 31.38\times\ln(1.4436)$$

$$= 31.38\times0.3669 = 11.51\;\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

---

### Total entropy change

$$\boxed{\Delta S = \Delta S_1 + \Delta S_2 + \Delta S_3 = 9.606 + 10.30 + 11.51 = 31.4\;\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}}$$

**Sanity check:** All three contributions are positive, as expected — heating and melting always increase entropy. The phase-change term $\Delta S_2 = 10.30$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$ is comparable to the sensible-heating terms, reinforcing the L1 lesson that phase changes cannot be neglected in energy/entropy accounting.
common_mistakes: Integrating a single $\int_{500}^{1000} C_P/T\,\mathrm{d}T$ with either the solid or the liquid $C_P$ across the entire range, ignoring the phase change at 692.7 K and the different $C_P$ values in each phase.

Forgetting to include $\Delta S_\text{fus} = \Delta H_\text{fus}/T_m$ for the melting step — students sometimes add the latent heat to the enthalpy but forget to account for it separately in the entropy calculation.

Using $\Delta S_2 = \Delta H_\text{fus}/\Delta T$ (dividing by a temperature interval) instead of dividing by the fixed transition temperature $T_m$, which is the correct formula for an isothermal phase change.

L2|medium.title: Entropy Change in Heating Copper Through Its Debye Region
L2|medium.statement:
A research group is characterising the low-temperature thermal properties of a copper heat sink. They heat $n = 2.00$ mol of pure solid copper at constant pressure from $T_1 = 200\,\text{K}$ to $T_2 = 500\,\text{K}$.

The molar heat capacity at constant pressure for solid copper over this range is well described by
$$C_P = 22.64 + 6.28 \times 10^{-3}\,T \quad [\text{J}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}]$$
where $T$ is in kelvin.

**(a)** Calculate the total entropy change $\Delta S$ of the copper over this heating process.

**(b)** Calculate the total enthalpy change $\Delta H$ of the copper over the same process.

**(c)** A student claims that the ratio $\Delta H / \Delta T$ (where $\Delta T = T_2 - T_1$) gives the same answer as $\Delta S$. Show numerically whether this claim is correct and explain why it is or is not thermodynamically valid.
L2|medium.solution:
## Step 1 — Set up the entropy integral

At constant pressure, the reversible heat exchanged per mole per kelvin is $\delta Q_\text{rev} = C_P\,\mathrm{d}T$, so the Second Law definition $\mathrm{d}S = \delta Q_\text{rev}/T$ gives the molar entropy change:
$$\Delta \underline{S} = \int_{T_1}^{T_2} \frac{C_P}{T}\,\mathrm{d}T$$

Substitute $C_P = 22.64 + 6.28\times10^{-3}\,T$:
$$\Delta \underline{S} = \int_{200}^{500} \frac{22.64 + 6.28\times10^{-3}\,T}{T}\,\mathrm{d}T = \int_{200}^{500}\left(\frac{22.64}{T} + 6.28\times10^{-3}\right)\mathrm{d}T$$

## Step 2 — Evaluate the entropy integral

$$\Delta \underline{S} = \left[22.64\,\ln T + 6.28\times10^{-3}\,T\right]_{200}^{500}$$

$$= 22.64\,(\ln 500 - \ln 200) + 6.28\times10^{-3}\,(500 - 200)$$

$$= 22.64\,\ln\!\frac{500}{200} + 6.28\times10^{-3}\times300$$

$$= 22.64\,\ln(2.500) + 1.884$$

$$= 22.64\times0.9163 + 1.884$$

$$= 20.74 + 1.884 = 22.62\;\text{J}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$$

## Step 3 — Total entropy change for $n = 2.00$ mol

$$\boxed{\Delta S = n\,\Delta\underline{S} = 2.00 \times 22.62 = 45.2\;\text{J}\,\text{K}^{-1}}$$

## Step 4 — Evaluate the enthalpy integral

At constant pressure, $\mathrm{d}H = C_P\,\mathrm{d}T$, so:
$$\Delta\underline{H} = \int_{200}^{500}\left(22.64 + 6.28\times10^{-3}\,T\right)\mathrm{d}T$$

$$= \left[22.64\,T + \frac{6.28\times10^{-3}}{2}\,T^2\right]_{200}^{500}$$

$$= 22.64\,(500-200) + 3.14\times10^{-3}\,(500^2 - 200^2)$$

$$= 22.64\times300 + 3.14\times10^{-3}\times(250{,}000 - 40{,}000)$$

$$= 6792 + 3.14\times10^{-3}\times210{,}000$$

$$= 6792 + 659.4 = 7451\;\text{J}\,\text{mol}^{-1}$$

## Step 5 — Total enthalpy change for $n = 2.00$ mol

$$\boxed{\Delta H = 2.00 \times 7451 = 14{,}902\;\text{J} \approx 14.9\;\text{kJ}}$$

## Step 6 — Test the student's claim

The student's proposed shortcut:
$$\frac{\Delta H}{\Delta T} = \frac{14{,}902\;\text{J}}{300\;\text{K}} = 49.7\;\text{J}\,\text{K}^{-1}$$

The correct answer is $\Delta S = 45.2\;\text{J}\,\text{K}^{-1}$.

These differ by about 10%, so **the claim is numerically wrong**.

**Why?** The definitions are:
$$\Delta H = \int_{T_1}^{T_2} C_P\,\mathrm{d}T \qquad \text{vs.} \qquad \Delta S = \int_{T_1}^{T_2} \frac{C_P}{T}\,\mathrm{d}T$$

The student's ratio $\Delta H/\Delta T$ equals an *average* $C_P$ over the interval, which is not the same as $\Delta S$. The entropy integral carries an extra $1/T$ weighting inside the integrand — heat absorbed at low $T$ contributes more entropy per joule than the same heat absorbed at high $T$. These two quantities are only equal in the trivial limit of infinitesimally small $\Delta T$, where both reduce to $C_P/T$.
L2|medium.final_answer: (a) $\Delta S = 45.2\;\text{J}\,\text{K}^{-1}$; (b) $\Delta H = 14.9\;\text{kJ}$; (c) the student's ratio gives $49.7\;\text{J}\,\text{K}^{-1} \neq 45.2\;\text{J}\,\text{K}^{-1}$ — the claim is wrong because the $1/T$ weighting inside the entropy integral cannot be replaced by $1/\Delta T$.
common_mistakes: Confusing the entropy integral $\int(C_P/T)\,\mathrm{d}T$ with the enthalpy integral $\int C_P\,\mathrm{d}T$ — students sometimes write $\Delta S = \Delta H / T$ using a single average temperature rather than integrating $C_P/T$ term by term.
Forgetting to multiply the per-mole result by $n = 2.00\,\text{mol}$, leaving the answer as a molar quantity in J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$ instead of the total in J K$^{-1}$.

Evaluating $\ln(500/200)$ as $\ln 500 - \ln 200 \approx 6.215 - 5.298 = 0.916$ correctly but then accidentally computing $22.64 \times 9.163$ (off by a factor of 10) instead of $22.64 \times 0.916$, giving an entropy change ten times too large.

L2|medium.title: Entropy Change on Heating Titanium Through an Allotropic Transition
L2|medium.statement:
Pure titanium undergoes an allotropic transformation from the hexagonal close-packed (HCP) $\alpha$ phase to the body-centred cubic (BCC) $\beta$ phase at $T_\text{trans} = 1155\,\text{K}$ at atmospheric pressure. The enthalpy of the $\alpha \to \beta$ transformation is $\Delta H_\text{trans} = 3{,}800\,\text{J/mol}$.

The molar heat capacities (at constant pressure, in $\text{J}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$) are:
$$C_P^{\alpha}(T) = 22.09 + 10.46 \times 10^{-3}\,T$$
$$C_P^{\beta}(T) = 24.94 \;\text{J}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1} \quad (\text{approximately constant above the transition})$$

Starting with 1 mole of $\alpha$-Ti at $T_1 = 900\,\text{K}$, the titanium is heated at constant pressure to a final temperature of $T_2 = 1300\,\text{K}$.

Calculate the total molar entropy change $\Delta S_\text{total}$ for this process.
L2|medium.solution:
## Step-by-step solution

The process must be split into **three distinct stages** because the material changes phase at 1155 K:

| Stage | Process | Temperature range |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Heat $\alpha$-Ti | $900\,\text{K} \to 1155\,\text{K}$ |
| 2 | Allotropic transition $\alpha \to \beta$ | at $1155\,\text{K}$ |
| 3 | Heat $\beta$-Ti | $1155\,\text{K} \to 1300\,\text{K}$ |

---

### Stage 1 — Heating $\alpha$-Ti from 900 K to 1155 K

At constant pressure, $\delta Q_\text{rev} = C_P^{\alpha}\,\mathrm{d}T$, so the entropy change is:
$$\Delta S_1 = \int_{900}^{1155} \frac{C_P^{\alpha}}{T}\,\mathrm{d}T = \int_{900}^{1155} \frac{22.09 + 10.46\times10^{-3}\,T}{T}\,\mathrm{d}T$$

Split the integrand:
$$\Delta S_1 = \int_{900}^{1155} \frac{22.09}{T}\,\mathrm{d}T + \int_{900}^{1155} 10.46\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{d}T$$

$$\Delta S_1 = 22.09\,\ln\!\frac{1155}{900} + 10.46\times10^{-3}\,(1155 - 900)$$

**First term:**
$$22.09 \times \ln(1.2833) = 22.09 \times 0.2493 = 5.508\;\text{J}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

**Second term:**
$$10.46\times10^{-3} \times 255 = 2.667\;\text{J}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

$$\boxed{\Delta S_1 = 5.508 + 2.667 = 8.175\;\text{J}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}}$$

---

### Stage 2 — Allotropic transition at 1155 K

The transformation occurs at a single temperature (invariant for a pure substance at fixed pressure). Using the Clausius relation for a phase change:
$$\Delta S_2 = \frac{\Delta H_\text{trans}}{T_\text{trans}} = \frac{3{,}800}{1155} = 3.290\;\text{J}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

$$\boxed{\Delta S_2 = 3.290\;\text{J}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}}$$

---

### Stage 3 — Heating $\beta$-Ti from 1155 K to 1300 K

$C_P^{\beta}$ is approximately constant, so:
$$\Delta S_3 = \int_{1155}^{1300} \frac{C_P^{\beta}}{T}\,\mathrm{d}T = 24.94\,\ln\!\frac{1300}{1155}$$

$$= 24.94 \times \ln(1.1255) = 24.94 \times 0.1183 = 2.950\;\text{J}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

$$\boxed{\Delta S_3 = 2.950\;\text{J}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}}$$

---

### Total entropy change

Because entropy is a **state function**, the total entropy change is the sum of the three contributions:
$$\Delta S_\text{total} = \Delta S_1 + \Delta S_2 + \Delta S_3$$

$$\Delta S_\text{total} = 8.175 + 3.290 + 2.950$$

$$\boxed{\Delta S_\text{total} = 14.41\;\text{J}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}}$$

---

### Sanity check

- All three contributions are **positive**, which is physically correct: heating a substance and transforming it to a higher-symmetry phase both increase the number of accessible microstates, so $S$ always increases.
- The phase-change contribution (3.29 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹) is smaller than the sensible-heating contributions, which is physically reasonable: Ti's $\alpha \to \beta$ transition has a relatively small latent heat (3.8 kJ/mol) compared to melting (~15 kJ/mol).
- The entropy integral uses $\int (C_P/T)\,\mathrm{d}T$, which differs from the enthalpy integral $\int C_P\,\mathrm{d}T$ only by the $1/T$ weighting — a key distinction from the First Law calculation.
common_mistakes: **Using $\Delta H / T$ with the wrong temperature for Stage 1 or 3.** Some students apply $\Delta S = \Delta H / T$ (valid only for isothermal phase changes) to the sensible-heating stages, for example writing $\Delta S_1 = \int C_P\,\mathrm{d}T / T_\text{average}$. The correct form for heating over a range is $\int (C_P/T)\,\mathrm{d}T$, which uses $\ln(T_2/T_1)$, not $\Delta H / T_\text{average}$.

**Omitting the allotropic transition entirely.** Students who use a single integral $\int_{900}^{1300} C_P / T\,\mathrm{d}T$ with the $\alpha$-phase $C_P$ throughout ignore both the latent heat of transformation and the change in $C_P$ above 1155 K. This underestimates $\Delta S$ and uses the wrong heat capacity in Stage 3.

**Confusing the entropy integral with the enthalpy integral.** The enthalpy change uses $\int C_P\,\mathrm{d}T$ (no $1/T$), whereas the entropy change uses $\int (C_P/T)\,\mathrm{d}T$. Forgetting the $1/T$ weighting is the single most common algebraic error on Second Law entropy calculations.

L2|medium.title: Entropy Change of Isobaric Cooling of Argon Gas
L2|medium.statement:
A rigid laboratory gas line supplies argon (Ar) gas at constant pressure. An engineer cools $n = 3.5$ mol of argon gas isobarically (at constant pressure of 1 atm) from an initial temperature of $T_1 = 600\,	ext{K}$ down to $T_2 = 200\,	ext{K}$.

Argon is a monatomic ideal gas with molar heat capacity at constant pressure $C_P = 	frac{5}{2}R$.

**(a)** Calculate the entropy change $\Delta S_	ext{gas}$ of the argon gas for this process.

**(b)** The surroundings act as a large thermal reservoir held at a constant temperature of $T_	ext{surr} = 200\,	ext{K}$. Calculate the entropy change of the surroundings, $\Delta S_	ext{surr}$.

**(c)** Calculate the total entropy change of the universe, $\Delta S_	ext{univ} = \Delta S_	ext{gas} + \Delta S_	ext{surr}$, and state whether this result is consistent with the Second Law.

**Given:** $R = 8.314\,	ext{J mol}^{-1}	ext{K}^{-1}$.
L2|medium.solution:
## Step 1 — Entropy change of the gas (Part a)

For an isobaric process on an ideal gas, the heat exchanged reversibly is $\delta Q = n C_P\,\mathrm{d}T$. The entropy change of the gas between two states is a state-function calculation, so we integrate along any reversible path connecting those states. Here the isobaric path itself is used:

$$\Delta S_\text{gas} = \int_{T_1}^{T_2} \frac{n C_P}{T}\,\mathrm{d}T = n C_P \ln\!\frac{T_2}{T_1}$$

Substituting $C_P = \tfrac{5}{2}R = \tfrac{5}{2}(8.314) = 20.785\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$:

$$\Delta S_\text{gas} = (3.5)(20.785)\ln\!\frac{200}{600}$$

$$= 72.75 \times \ln(0.3333)$$

$$= 72.75 \times (-1.0986)$$

$$\boxed{\Delta S_\text{gas} \approx -79.9\,\text{J K}^{-1}}$$

The negative sign is expected: cooling reduces the thermal motion of atoms, decreasing the number of accessible microstates and hence lowering entropy.

## Step 2 — Heat exchanged with the surroundings

At constant pressure, $Q = n C_P \Delta T$:

$$Q_\text{gas} = n C_P (T_2 - T_1) = (3.5)(20.785)(200 - 600)$$

$$= 72.75 \times (-400) = -29{,}100\,\text{J}$$

The gas releases $29{,}100\,\text{J}$ of heat to the surroundings. By conservation of energy, the surroundings absorb:

$$Q_\text{surr} = +29{,}100\,\text{J}$$

## Step 3 — Entropy change of the surroundings (Part b)

The surroundings are a large reservoir at a fixed temperature $T_\text{surr} = 200\,\text{K}$. A reservoir absorbs heat at constant temperature, so:

$$\Delta S_\text{surr} = \frac{Q_\text{surr}}{T_\text{surr}} = \frac{+29{,}100}{200}$$

$$\boxed{\Delta S_\text{surr} = +145.5\,\text{J K}^{-1}}$$

## Step 4 — Total entropy change of the universe (Part c)

$$\Delta S_\text{univ} = \Delta S_\text{gas} + \Delta S_\text{surr} = -79.9 + 145.5$$

$$\boxed{\Delta S_\text{univ} \approx +65.6\,\text{J K}^{-1} > 0}$$

**Consistency with the Second Law:** $\Delta S_\text{univ} > 0$, confirming that this process is **irreversible** and spontaneous in the forward direction. The large positive $\Delta S_\text{surr}$ outweighs the negative $\Delta S_\text{gas}$, as required.

Note that if the surroundings were held at the *same* initial temperature as the gas ($600\,\text{K}$) and the cooling occurred quasi-statically through a sequence of reservoirs, $\Delta S_\text{univ}$ would approach zero (reversible limit). The large temperature gap ($600\,\text{K}$ gas dumping heat into a $200\,\text{K}$ reservoir) is the source of irreversibility here.
L2|medium.final_answer: $\Delta S_\text{gas} \approx -79.9\,\text{J K}^{-1}$, $\Delta S_\text{surr} = +145.5\,\text{J K}^{-1}$, $\Delta S_\text{univ} \approx +65.6\,\text{J K}^{-1} > 0$ (irreversible, consistent with Second Law)
common_mistakes: Calculating $\Delta S_\text{surr}$ using the gas temperature $T_1$ or $T_2$ instead of the fixed reservoir temperature $T_\text{surr} = 200\,\text{K}$. The surroundings are a reservoir at a single fixed temperature; only that temperature appears in $\Delta S_\text{surr} = Q_\text{surr}/T_\text{surr}$.

Computing $\Delta S_\text{gas}$ as $Q/T$ using a single temperature (e.g. $Q/T_1$ or $Q/T_2$) instead of integrating $\int n C_P\,\mathrm{d}T/T = n C_P \ln(T_2/T_1)$. The gas temperature changes continuously, so the logarithmic form is required.

Assigning the wrong sign to $Q_\text{surr}$: the gas cools, so $Q_\text{gas} < 0$, and the surroundings absorb heat, so $Q_\text{surr} = -Q_\text{gas} > 0$. Forgetting this sign flip leads to a negative $\Delta S_\text{surr}$ and an incorrect (negative) $\Delta S_\text{univ}$.

L2|medium.title: Entropy Change for Adiabatic Free Expansion of a Gas
L2|medium.statement:
A rigid, thermally insulated container is divided into two equal compartments by a thin internal partition. The left compartment contains $2.5$ mol of an ideal monatomic gas (e.g. neon) at $400\,\text{K}$ and $6.0\,\text{atm}$. The right compartment is completely evacuated.

The partition is suddenly punctured and the gas expands freely to fill the entire container. The container remains thermally insulated from the surroundings throughout.

**(a)** Using the First Law, determine the final temperature $T_f$ of the gas after expansion.

**(b)** Calculate the entropy change of the gas, $\Delta S_\text{gas}$, for this process. Explain how you handle the fact that the actual process is irreversible.

**(c)** State what happens to $\Delta S_\text{surroundings}$ and hence evaluate $\Delta S_\text{universe}$. Does your result confirm the Second Law? 

Data: $R = 8.314\,\text{J}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$; for a monatomic ideal gas, $C_V = \tfrac{3}{2}R$.
L2|medium.solution:
## Step-by-step solution

### Part (a) — Final temperature

The container is **rigid** (no volume change for the *total* system) and **thermally insulated** ($Q = 0$). Under the sign convention $\Delta U = Q + W$:

$$W = -P_\text{ext}\,\Delta V = 0$$

because the gas expands into a **vacuum** — there is no opposing pressure ($P_\text{ext} = 0$), so the gas does no work against anything.

Applying the First Law to the gas as the closed system:

$$\Delta U = Q + W = 0 + 0 = 0$$

For an ideal gas, internal energy depends only on temperature:

$$\Delta U = n\,C_V\,(T_f - T_i) = 0$$

$$\Rightarrow \quad T_f = T_i = \boxed{400\,\text{K}}$$

The temperature is **unchanged** after free expansion of an ideal gas.

---

### Part (b) — Entropy change of the gas

Even though the actual process is **irreversible** (a sudden, unrestrained expansion into vacuum), entropy is a **state function**. We compute $\Delta S_\text{gas}$ by constructing any convenient **reversible path** connecting the same initial and final states.

**Identifying initial and final states:**

- Initial: $T_i = 400\,\text{K}$, volume $V_i$ (left half only).
- Final: $T_f = 400\,\text{K}$ (from part a), volume $V_f = 2V_i$ (whole container).

Since $T_i = T_f$, the reversible path is simply an **isothermal reversible expansion** at $400\,\text{K}$ from $V_i$ to $2V_i$.

**Finding the initial molar volume $V_i$:**

Using the ideal gas law for the initial state:
$$V_i = \frac{n R T_i}{P_i} = \frac{2.5 \times 8.314 \times 400}{6.0 \times 1.013 \times 10^5}$$

$$= \frac{8314}{6.078 \times 10^5} = 0.01368\,\text{m}^3$$

(This value is not actually needed — see below.)

**Entropy change for the chosen reversible isothermal path:**

For an ideal gas during a reversible isothermal process, $\mathrm{d}U = 0$, so $\delta Q_\text{rev} = -\delta W_\text{rev} = P\,\mathrm{d}V$. Then:

$$\mathrm{d}S = \frac{\delta Q_\text{rev}}{T} = \frac{P\,\mathrm{d}V}{T} = \frac{nR}{V}\,\mathrm{d}V$$

Integrating from $V_i$ to $2V_i$:

$$\Delta S_\text{gas} = \int_{V_i}^{2V_i} \frac{nR}{V}\,\mathrm{d}V = nR\ln\frac{2V_i}{V_i} = nR\ln 2$$

Substituting numbers:

$$\Delta S_\text{gas} = 2.5 \times 8.314 \times \ln 2 = 2.5 \times 8.314 \times 0.6931$$

$$\boxed{\Delta S_\text{gas} = +14.4\,\text{J}\,\text{K}^{-1}}$$

The entropy of the gas **increases** — consistent with the gas spreading into more microstates.

**Note on the irreversible path:** We could not write $\Delta S = \int \delta Q/T$ along the actual path (that integral gives zero, since $Q = 0$, which would be wrong). Instead we used a reversible path between the same endpoints. This is the standard technique: *choose any reversible path, calculate $\int \delta Q_\text{rev}/T$; the answer is the true $\Delta S$ because $S$ is a state function.*

---

### Part (c) — Entropy of surroundings and universe

The container is **thermally insulated**, so **no heat is transferred to or from the surroundings** at any stage:

$$Q_\text{surroundings} = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \Delta S_\text{surroundings} = \frac{Q_\text{surroundings}}{T_\text{surroundings}} = 0$$

Therefore:

$$\Delta S_\text{universe} = \Delta S_\text{gas} + \Delta S_\text{surroundings} = +14.4 + 0 = \boxed{+14.4\,\text{J}\,\text{K}^{-1}}$$

**Confirmation of the Second Law:** The process is spontaneous and irreversible (the gas will never spontaneously contract back into the left half), and indeed $\Delta S_\text{universe} > 0$. The entropy of the universe has increased, consistent with the Second Law. A zero value would indicate a reversible process; a negative value would be forbidden.
common_mistakes: **Computing $\Delta S$ directly from $Q/T = 0$:** Because the actual expansion is adiabatic ($Q = 0$), some students write $\Delta S = Q/T = 0$ and conclude entropy does not change. This is wrong because $\Delta S = \int \delta Q_\text{rev}/T$ requires a *reversible* path; the real path is irreversible. One must construct an equivalent reversible path (here, isothermal reversible expansion) and integrate along that path instead.

**Assuming the temperature drops during free expansion:** Students familiar with throttling (Joule-Thomson) sometimes expect cooling. However, free expansion into a vacuum does zero work ($P_\text{ext} = 0$), so $\Delta U = 0$ and $T_f = T_i$ for an ideal gas. Temperature change only arises if real-gas intermolecular forces are present.

**Treating the irreversible process as though it violates the Second Law because $\Delta S_\text{gas} > 0$ while $Q = 0$:** Some students think a positive $\Delta S_\text{gas}$ must be 'paid for' by heat flowing in. In fact, irreversible processes can increase a system's entropy with no heat exchange — the entropy is generated internally by the irreversibility itself (the spontaneous expansion). The Second Law requires only $\Delta S_\text{universe} \geq 0$, not that entropy changes are always tied to heat flows.

L2|hard.title: Entropy Change During Iron Phase Transformation with Heating
L2|hard.statement:
Iron undergoes an allotropic transformation from $\alpha$-Fe (BCC) to $\gamma$-Fe (FCC) at 910 °C (1183 K) at 1 atm pressure. The latent heat of this transformation is $\Delta H_{\alpha\to\gamma} = 900$ J/mol. A 2.5 kg sample of pure iron is heated from 300 K to 1400 K at constant pressure (1 atm). The molar heat capacities are:

$$C_P^{\alpha}(T) = 37.3 + 6.19\times10^{-3}\,T \quad [\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}], \quad 300\,\text{K} \leq T \leq 1183\,\text{K}$$

$$C_P^{\gamma}(T) = 24.9 + 8.16\times10^{-3}\,T \quad [\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}], \quad 1183\,\text{K} \leq T \leq 1400\,\text{K}$$

The molar mass of iron is 55.85 g/mol.

**(a)** Calculate the **total molar entropy change** $\Delta S_\text{total}$ (in J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$) for heating iron from 300 K to 1400 K, including the allotropic transformation at 1183 K.

**(b)** Hence calculate the **total entropy change** $\Delta S$ (in J/K) for the entire 2.5 kg sample.

**(c)** The iron is then cooled rapidly back to 300 K in an insulated quench bath (the quench bath absorbs all the heat). The quench bath contains 15 kg of water, initially at 300 K, with $C_P^{\text{water}} = 75.3$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$ and molar mass 18.01 g/mol. Assuming the final temperature of the water after quenching is 363 K (the iron cools completely to 300 K), calculate the **entropy change of the universe** $\Delta S_\text{universe}$ for the quenching step only, and state whether this process is consistent with the Second Law.
L2|hard.solution:
## Step-by-step Solution

### Part (a) — Total Molar Entropy Change from 300 K to 1400 K

The total molar entropy change is the sum of three contributions:

$$\Delta S_\text{total} = \underbrace{\int_{300}^{1183} \frac{C_P^{\alpha}}{T}\,\mathrm{d}T}_{\text{(i) heat } \alpha\text{-Fe}} + \underbrace{\frac{\Delta H_{\alpha\to\gamma}}{T_\text{trans}}}_{\text{(ii) phase change}} + \underbrace{\int_{1183}^{1400} \frac{C_P^{\gamma}}{T}\,\mathrm{d}T}_{\text{(iii) heat } \gamma\text{-Fe}}$$

This is directly analogous to the standard entropy construction from L2 §2.4:
$$\Delta S = \int_{T_1}^{T_2}\frac{C_P}{T}\,\mathrm{d}T + \frac{\Delta H_\text{trans}}{T_\text{trans}} + \int_{T_\text{trans}}^{T_3}\frac{C_P^\text{new}}{T}\,\mathrm{d}T$$

---

#### Contribution (i): Heat $\alpha$-Fe from 300 K to 1183 K

With $C_P^{\alpha} = a + bT$, $a = 37.3$, $b = 6.19\times10^{-3}$:

$$\Delta S_1 = \int_{300}^{1183}\frac{a + bT}{T}\,\mathrm{d}T = a\ln\frac{T_2}{T_1} + b(T_2 - T_1)$$

$$= 37.3\ln\frac{1183}{300} + 6.19\times10^{-3}\times(1183 - 300)$$

$$= 37.3\times\ln(3.943) + 6.19\times10^{-3}\times 883$$

$$= 37.3\times 1.3716 + 5.464$$

$$= 51.16 + 5.46 = 56.62\;\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

---

#### Contribution (ii): Allotropic transformation at 1183 K

$$\Delta S_2 = \frac{\Delta H_{\alpha\to\gamma}}{T_\text{trans}} = \frac{900}{1183} = 0.761\;\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

---

#### Contribution (iii): Heat $\gamma$-Fe from 1183 K to 1400 K

With $C_P^{\gamma} = a' + b'T$, $a' = 24.9$, $b' = 8.16\times10^{-3}$:

$$\Delta S_3 = a'\ln\frac{1400}{1183} + b'(1400 - 1183)$$

$$= 24.9\times\ln(1.1834) + 8.16\times10^{-3}\times 217$$

$$= 24.9\times 0.1682 + 1.771$$

$$= 4.188 + 1.771 = 5.959\;\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

---

#### Total molar entropy change:

$$\boxed{\Delta S_\text{total} = 56.62 + 0.761 + 5.959 \approx 63.34\;\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}}$$

---

### Part (b) — Total Entropy Change for the 2.5 kg Sample

First, calculate the number of moles in 2.5 kg:

$$n = \frac{2500\;\text{g}}{55.85\;\text{g/mol}} = 44.76\;\text{mol}$$

Then:

$$\Delta S = n \times \Delta S_\text{total} = 44.76 \times 63.34$$

$$\boxed{\Delta S = 2834\;\text{J/K} \approx 2.83\;\text{kJ/K}}$$

---

### Part (c) — Entropy Change of the Universe During Quenching

In the quench step, hot iron (at 1400 K) cools to 300 K; the heat released is absorbed by the water bath (initially 300 K, rising to 363 K).

#### Entropy change of the iron ($\Delta S_\text{Fe}$):

This is simply the **negative** of what we computed in part (a) and (b), because the iron undergoes the reverse process (cooling from 1400 K to 300 K through the same $\gamma\to\alpha$ transformation at 1183 K). Since $S$ is a state function:

$$\Delta S_\text{Fe} = -\Delta S = -2834\;\text{J/K}$$

#### Entropy change of the water ($\Delta S_\text{water}$):

Number of moles of water:
$$n_\text{water} = \frac{15{,}000\;\text{g}}{18.01\;\text{g/mol}} = 832.9\;\text{mol}$$

The water heats from 300 K to 363 K at constant pressure. Using $\delta Q_\text{rev} = C_P\,\mathrm{d}T$:

$$\Delta S_\text{water} = n_\text{water}\int_{300}^{363}\frac{C_P^\text{water}}{T}\,\mathrm{d}T = n_\text{water}\,C_P^\text{water}\ln\frac{363}{300}$$

$$= 832.9 \times 75.3 \times \ln(1.210)$$

$$= 62{,}717 \times 0.1906$$

$$= 11{,}954\;\text{J/K}$$

> Note: We integrate $C_P/T$ for the water because the water temperature changes during the process. The correct expression is $\Delta S = nC_P\ln(T_2/T_1)$ from L2 §2.4.

#### Entropy change of the universe:

$$\Delta S_\text{universe} = \Delta S_\text{Fe} + \Delta S_\text{water} = -2834 + 11{,}954$$

$$\boxed{\Delta S_\text{universe} = +9{,}120\;\text{J/K} > 0}$$

**This is consistent with the Second Law.** The process is irreversible — hot iron suddenly dumped into cold water is a classic irreversible heat transfer. The entropy of the iron decreases, but the entropy gained by the water more than compensates. The positive $\Delta S_\text{universe}$ confirms the process is spontaneous and irreversible.
L2|hard.final_answer: (a) $\Delta S_\text{total} \approx 63.34$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$; (b) $\Delta S \approx 2834$ J/K for the 2.5 kg sample; (c) $\Delta S_\text{universe} \approx +9{,}120$ J/K $> 0$, consistent with the Second Law (irreversible process).
common_mistakes: **Forgetting the allotropic transformation entropy term.** Students often integrate $C_P/T$ straight from 300 K to 1400 K using a single polynomial, omitting the $\Delta H_\text{trans}/T_\text{trans}$ term at 1183 K. This is the same error as skipping a latent heat in an enthalpy calculation — phase changes always add a discontinuous entropy contribution $\Delta H/T_\text{trans}$ that cannot be captured by the $C_P$ integral alone.

**Computing $\Delta S_\text{water}$ as $Q/T_\text{initial}$ instead of integrating.** Because the water temperature changes from 300 K to 363 K, the correct entropy change is $nC_P\ln(T_2/T_1)$, not $Q/T_\text{initial} = nC_P\Delta T/300$. Using a fixed $T$ in the denominator overestimates entropy and applies only when $T$ is constant (e.g. a phase change or an isothermal reservoir). This distinction is explicitly covered in L2 §2.4.

**Applying the Second Law to the iron alone.** The Second Law states $\Delta S_\text{universe} \geq 0$, not $\Delta S_\text{system} \geq 0$. The iron's entropy decreases during quenching ($\Delta S_\text{Fe} < 0$), which is entirely permissible. Students who check only the iron's entropy and declare a Second Law violation have forgotten that the iron is not an isolated system — the water (surroundings) must be included in the universe balance.

L2|hard.title: Entropy Change for Heating Liquid Copper Through Solidification
L2|hard.statement:
A materials engineer is studying the thermodynamics of a copper casting process. Starting from solid copper at $T_1 = 800\,\text{K}$, the copper is heated at constant pressure (1 atm) until it reaches $T_2 = 1400\,\text{K}$ in the liquid state. The melting point of copper is $T_m = 1358\,\text{K}$ and the molar enthalpy of fusion is $\Delta H_\text{fus} = 13{,}050\,\text{J/mol}$.

The molar heat capacities are:
$$C_P^\text{solid}(\text{Cu}) = 22.64 + 6.28 \times 10^{-3}\,T \;\;\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$
$$C_P^\text{liquid}(\text{Cu}) = 31.38 \;\;\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

For a sample of $n = 3.50\,\text{mol}$ of copper, calculate:

**(a)** The total molar entropy change $\Delta \underline{S}_\text{total}$ (J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$) for heating copper from 800 K to 1400 K, accounting for the phase change.

**(b)** The total entropy change $\Delta S_\text{total}$ (J/K) for the 3.50 mol sample.

**(c)** The minimum temperature $T^*$ (in K) of a heat reservoir that could supply all the heat required for this process reversibly. Treat the reservoir as transferring heat at a single fixed temperature. Use your result from part (b) and the total heat $Q_\text{total}$ absorbed by the sample.
L2|hard.solution:
## Step-by-Step Solution

### Part (a): Molar entropy change — three contributions

The path from 800 K to 1400 K crosses a phase transition at $T_m = 1358\,\text{K}$. We must split the calculation into three pieces:

$$\Delta \underline{S}_\text{total} = \underbrace{\int_{800}^{1358} \frac{C_P^\text{solid}}{T}\,\mathrm{d}T}_{\text{(i) heat solid}} + \underbrace{\frac{\Delta H_\text{fus}}{T_m}}_{\text{(ii) melt}} + \underbrace{\int_{1358}^{1400} \frac{C_P^\text{liquid}}{T}\,\mathrm{d}T}_{\text{(iii) heat liquid}}$$

---

**Piece (i) — heat solid from 800 K to 1358 K:**

With $C_P^\text{solid} = a + bT$ where $a = 22.64$ and $b = 6.28 \times 10^{-3}$:

$$\int_{800}^{1358} \frac{a + bT}{T}\,\mathrm{d}T = a\ln\frac{1358}{800} + b(1358 - 800)$$

$$= 22.64 \times \ln(1.6975) + 6.28 \times 10^{-3} \times 558$$

$$= 22.64 \times 0.5293 + 3.504$$

$$= 11.98 + 3.50 = 15.48\;\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

---

**Piece (ii) — melting at $T_m = 1358\,\text{K}$:**

$$\Delta \underline{S}_\text{fus} = \frac{\Delta H_\text{fus}}{T_m} = \frac{13{,}050}{1358} = 9.61\;\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

---

**Piece (iii) — heat liquid from 1358 K to 1400 K:**

$$\int_{1358}^{1400} \frac{31.38}{T}\,\mathrm{d}T = 31.38 \times \ln\frac{1400}{1358} = 31.38 \times \ln(1.0309)$$

$$= 31.38 \times 0.03044 = 0.955\;\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

---

**Total molar entropy change:**

$$\boxed{\Delta \underline{S}_\text{total} = 15.48 + 9.61 + 0.955 = 26.04\;\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}}$$

---

### Part (b): Total entropy change for 3.50 mol

$$\Delta S_\text{total} = n \times \Delta \underline{S}_\text{total} = 3.50 \times 26.04$$

$$\boxed{\Delta S_\text{total} = 91.1\;\text{J/K}}$$

---

### Part (c): Minimum reservoir temperature $T^*$

First compute the **total heat absorbed** by the sample $Q_\text{total} = n \times \Delta \underline{H}_\text{total}$.

**Molar enthalpy change — same three pieces (using $\int C_P\,\mathrm{d}T$ without the $1/T$):**

**(i)** Heat solid 800 → 1358 K:
$$\Delta \underline{H}_1 = a(1358 - 800) + \frac{b}{2}(1358^2 - 800^2)$$
$$= 22.64 \times 558 + \frac{6.28 \times 10^{-3}}{2}(1{,}844{,}164 - 640{,}000)$$
$$= 12{,}633 + 3.14 \times 10^{-3} \times 1{,}204{,}164$$
$$= 12{,}633 + 3{,}781 = 16{,}414\;\text{J/mol}$$

**(ii)** Melting at 1358 K:
$$\Delta \underline{H}_2 = 13{,}050\;\text{J/mol}$$

**(iii)** Heat liquid 1358 → 1400 K:
$$\Delta \underline{H}_3 = C_P^\text{liquid} \times (1400 - 1358) = 31.38 \times 42 = 1{,}318\;\text{J/mol}$$

**Total molar enthalpy:**
$$\Delta \underline{H}_\text{total} = 16{,}414 + 13{,}050 + 1{,}318 = 30{,}782\;\text{J/mol}$$

**Total heat for 3.50 mol (constant pressure, so $Q = n\,\Delta\underline{H}$):**
$$Q_\text{total} = 3.50 \times 30{,}782 = 107{,}737\;\text{J} \approx 107.7\;\text{kJ}$$

**Now find $T^*$.**

If a single reservoir at fixed temperature $T^*$ supplies all the heat $Q_\text{total}$ reversibly, its entropy change is:
$$\Delta S_\text{reservoir} = -\frac{Q_\text{total}}{T^*}$$

For the **combined process** (sample + reservoir) to be reversible, we require $\Delta S_\text{universe} = 0$:
$$\Delta S_\text{sample} + \Delta S_\text{reservoir} = 0$$
$$91.1 - \frac{107{,}737}{T^*} = 0$$

Solving:
$$T^* = \frac{Q_\text{total}}{\Delta S_\text{sample}} = \frac{107{,}737}{91.1}$$

$$\boxed{T^* \approx 1183\;\text{K}}$$

**Interpretation:** A single isothermal reservoir at $\approx 1183\,\text{K}$ would be the thermodynamic equivalent temperature — the harmonic-mean-like temperature at which the entire heat transfer could occur reversibly. Any real reservoir must be hotter than the sample's final temperature (1400 K) to actually drive heat flow; the value $T^* = 1183\,\text{K}$ confirms that if the reservoir were cooler than $\sim 1183\,\text{K}$ it could not supply this heat reversibly.
common_mistakes: **Omitting the latent-heat entropy term.** Students often compute $\int_{800}^{1400}(C_P/T)\,\mathrm{d}T$ using a single polynomial across the entire range, forgetting that copper melts at 1358 K. This misses the $\Delta H_\text{fus}/T_m = 9.61\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$ contribution and gives an entropy change that is too small.

**Confusing $\Delta S$ with $\Delta H / T$ for non-isothermal steps.** For the sensible-heating segments, the correct formula is $\int (C_P/T)\,\mathrm{d}T$, not $\Delta H / T_{\text{avg}}$. Using the latter (dividing the enthalpy change of a segment by some average temperature) is only an approximation and is not the Second Law formula. Only the isothermal phase-change step allows $\Delta S = \Delta H / T$ exactly.

**Setting $\Delta S_\text{universe} = \Delta S_\text{sample}$ in part (c).** The reservoir also changes entropy. The reversibility condition is $\Delta S_\text{universe} = \Delta S_\text{sample} + \Delta S_\text{reservoir} = 0$, giving $T^* = Q/\Delta S_\text{sample}$. Students who forget to include the reservoir entropy often set up an equation with no unknown and cannot solve for $T^*$.

L2|hard.title: Entropy Change of Iridium Heated Through a Solid–Solid Transition
L2|hard.statement:
Iridium (Ir) exists in a low-temperature FCC phase (α-Ir) below 2443 K and transforms to a BCC phase (β-Ir) above 2443 K before melting at 2719 K. A research group heats 3 mol of solid iridium at constant pressure (1 atm) from 500 K to 2600 K.

The following thermochemical data are given:

**Molar heat capacities (J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹):**
$$C_P^{\alpha}(T) = 21.5 + 8.40 \times 10^{-3}\,T \quad (\text{valid for FCC α-Ir, 298–2443 K})$$
$$C_P^{\beta}(T) = 26.8 + 2.10 \times 10^{-3}\,T \quad (\text{valid for BCC β-Ir, 2443–2719 K})$$

**Solid–solid transition at 2443 K:**
$$\Delta H_{\alpha \to \beta} = 4{,}350 \text{ J mol}^{-1}$$

Calculate the **total entropy change** $\Delta S$ (in J K⁻¹) for the 3 mol sample heated from 500 K to 2600 K at constant pressure.

Report your final answer to four significant figures.
L2|hard.solution:
## Strategy

Because $S$ is a state function, we compute $\Delta S$ along the actual constant-pressure path from 500 K to 2600 K. The path has **three segments**:

1. Heat α-Ir from 500 K → 2443 K (FCC phase)
2. α → β solid–solid transition at 2443 K (latent entropy)
3. Heat β-Ir from 2443 K → 2600 K (BCC phase)

At constant pressure, $\delta Q_\text{rev} = C_P\,\mathrm{d}T$, so $\mathrm{d}S = C_P\,\mathrm{d}T/T$.

All molar quantities are multiplied by $n = 3$ mol at the end.

---

## Segment 1 — Heat α-Ir from 500 K to 2443 K

$$\Delta S_1 = \int_{500}^{2443} \frac{C_P^\alpha}{T}\,\mathrm{d}T = \int_{500}^{2443} \left(\frac{21.5}{T} + 8.40 \times 10^{-3}\right)\mathrm{d}T$$

Integrating term by term:
$$\Delta S_1 = 21.5\,\ln\!\frac{2443}{500} + 8.40 \times 10^{-3}\,(2443 - 500)$$

**First term:**
$$21.5 \times \ln(4.886) = 21.5 \times 1.5861 = 34.10 \text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

**Second term:**
$$8.40 \times 10^{-3} \times 1943 = 16.32 \text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

$$\Delta S_1 = 34.10 + 16.32 = 50.42 \text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

---

## Segment 2 — Solid–solid transition at 2443 K

The transition occurs isothermally at $T_{\text{trans}} = 2443$ K. At constant pressure:
$$\Delta S_2 = \frac{\Delta H_{\alpha \to \beta}}{T_{\text{trans}}} = \frac{4{,}350}{2443} = 1.780 \text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

---

## Segment 3 — Heat β-Ir from 2443 K to 2600 K

$$\Delta S_3 = \int_{2443}^{2600} \frac{C_P^\beta}{T}\,\mathrm{d}T = \int_{2443}^{2600} \left(\frac{26.8}{T} + 2.10 \times 10^{-3}\right)\mathrm{d}T$$

$$\Delta S_3 = 26.8\,\ln\!\frac{2600}{2443} + 2.10 \times 10^{-3}\,(2600 - 2443)$$

**First term:**
$$26.8 \times \ln(1.06426) = 26.8 \times 0.06228 = 1.669 \text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

**Second term:**
$$2.10 \times 10^{-3} \times 157 = 0.3297 \text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

$$\Delta S_3 = 1.669 + 0.3297 = 1.999 \text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

---

## Total molar entropy change

$$\Delta S_\text{molar} = \Delta S_1 + \Delta S_2 + \Delta S_3 = 50.42 + 1.780 + 1.999 = 54.20 \text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

## Total entropy change for 3 mol

$$\boxed{\Delta S = n \times \Delta S_\text{molar} = 3 \times 54.20 = 162.6 \text{ J K}^{-1}}$$

---

## Sanity checks

- **Units:** $[\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}] \times \text{mol} = [\text{J K}^{-1}]$ ✓
- **Sign:** Heating at constant pressure always increases entropy ($\Delta S > 0$) ✓
- **Dominance:** Segment 1 (heating over a ~1943 K range) dominates; Segment 3 (only 157 K range with lower $C_P$) contributes very little — physically sensible ✓
- **Phase transition contribution:** $\Delta S_2 = 1.78$ J mol⁻¹K⁻¹ is small compared to the sensible heating terms, consistent with a solid–solid transition having a much smaller latent heat than melting or vaporisation ✓
L2|hard.final_answer: $\Delta S = 162.6$ J K$^{-1}$ (for 3 mol from 500 K to 2600 K)
common_mistakes: **Forgetting the solid–solid transition latent entropy.** Students often integrate $C_P^\alpha/T$ all the way from 500 K to 2600 K with a single polynomial, skipping the $\Delta H_{\alpha\to\beta}/T_\text{trans}$ term and the change in $C_P$ polynomial at 2443 K. This is analogous to skipping the latent heat when computing enthalpy through a phase change — entropy and enthalpy both have discontinuities at phase transitions.

**Confusing the entropy integral with the enthalpy integral.** $\Delta H = \int C_P\,\mathrm{d}T$ but $\Delta S = \int (C_P/T)\,\mathrm{d}T$. The factor of $1/T$ inside the integral is critical. Students who write $\Delta S = \Delta H / T$ using only one average temperature will get the wrong answer because $T$ varies over the integration range.

**Forgetting to multiply the molar result by $n = 3$ mol.** Since tabulated $C_P$ values are molar (J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹), the integral gives a molar entropy change. The question asks for the total entropy change of the sample, so the final step of multiplying by the number of moles is mandatory; omitting it gives an answer three times too small.

L2|hard.title: Entropy Change of Superheated Iron Vapour Condensation and Solidification
L2|hard.statement:
Iron (Fe) is produced in a high-temperature plasma reactor and must be cooled from gaseous vapour at 4000 K all the way down to a solid ingot at 300 K. The cooling occurs at constant pressure of 1 atm. Use the thermodynamic data below to calculate the **total molar entropy change of the iron** over this entire cooling process.

**Transition temperatures and latent heats (at 1 atm):**
| Transition | Temperature (K) | $\Delta H_{\text{trs}}$ (J/mol) |
|---|---|---|
| Condensation (gas → liquid) | $T_{b} = 3134$ K | $-349{,}600$ |
| Solidification (liquid → solid) | $T_{f} = 1811$ K | $-13{,}810$ |

**Molar heat capacities $C_P$ (J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$) at 1 atm:**
| Phase | $C_P$ |
|---|---|
| Gas (Fe vapour, monoatomic ideal) | $\tfrac{5}{2}R = 20.79$ |
| Liquid Fe | $46.02$ (treat as constant) |
| Solid Fe ($\alpha$-phase, below 1811 K) | $37.12 + 6.17\times10^{-3}\,T$ |

Note: Ignore any solid-state allotropic transitions of iron within the 300–1811 K range for this problem. Take $R = 8.314$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$.

Calculate $\Delta S_{\text{total}}$ (J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$) for cooling from 4000 K to 300 K.
L2|hard.solution:
## Strategy

The process involves **five sequential steps** at constant pressure. At constant $P$, $\delta Q_{\text{rev}} = C_P\,\mathrm{d}T$ for single-phase heating/cooling, and $\delta Q_{\text{rev}} = \Delta H_{\text{trs}}$ at each phase transition. The entropy change for each step is:
$$\Delta S = \int_{T_1}^{T_2} \frac{C_P}{T}\,\mathrm{d}T \quad\text{(single phase)}\qquad \text{or} \qquad \Delta S = \frac{\Delta H_{\text{trs}}}{T_{\text{trs}}}\quad\text{(phase change)}$$

Because $S$ is a **state function**, the total entropy change is independent of path — we simply sum the five contributions along our stepwise reversible path.

---

## Step 1 — Cool Fe gas from 4000 K to $T_b = 3134$ K

$$\Delta S_1 = \int_{4000}^{3134} \frac{C_P^{\text{gas}}}{T}\,\mathrm{d}T = C_P^{\text{gas}}\,\ln\!\frac{T_2}{T_1}$$

$$\Delta S_1 = 20.79 \times \ln\!\frac{3134}{4000} = 20.79 \times \ln(0.7835)$$

$$\ln(0.7835) = -0.2438$$

$$\Delta S_1 = 20.79 \times (-0.2438) = -\mathbf{5.07}\;\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

---

## Step 2 — Condensation (gas → liquid) at $T_b = 3134$ K

$$\Delta S_2 = \frac{\Delta H_{\text{cond}}}{T_b} = \frac{-349{,}600}{3134} = -\mathbf{111.55}\;\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

The large negative value is expected: condensation dramatically reduces the number of accessible microstates (gas → liquid).

---

## Step 3 — Cool liquid Fe from $T_b = 3134$ K to $T_f = 1811$ K

$$\Delta S_3 = \int_{3134}^{1811} \frac{C_P^{\text{liq}}}{T}\,\mathrm{d}T = 46.02 \times \ln\!\frac{1811}{3134}$$

$$\ln\!\frac{1811}{3134} = \ln(0.5779) = -0.5481$$

$$\Delta S_3 = 46.02 \times (-0.5481) = -\mathbf{25.23}\;\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

---

## Step 4 — Solidification (liquid → solid) at $T_f = 1811$ K

$$\Delta S_4 = \frac{\Delta H_{\text{solid}}}{T_f} = \frac{-13{,}810}{1811} = -\mathbf{7.63}\;\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

---

## Step 5 — Cool solid $\alpha$-Fe from $T_f = 1811$ K to 300 K

With $C_P^{\text{sol}} = 37.12 + 6.17\times10^{-3}\,T$:

$$\Delta S_5 = \int_{1811}^{300} \frac{37.12 + 6.17\times10^{-3}\,T}{T}\,\mathrm{d}T = \int_{1811}^{300}\!\left(\frac{37.12}{T} + 6.17\times10^{-3}\right)\mathrm{d}T$$

$$= 37.12\,\ln\!\frac{300}{1811} + 6.17\times10^{-3}\,(300 - 1811)$$

**First term:**
$$37.12 \times \ln(0.16566) = 37.12 \times (-1.7981) = -66.77\;\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

**Second term:**
$$6.17\times10^{-3} \times (-1511) = -9.33\;\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

$$\Delta S_5 = -66.77 + (-9.33) = -\mathbf{76.10}\;\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

---

## Total Entropy Change

$$\Delta S_{\text{total}} = \Delta S_1 + \Delta S_2 + \Delta S_3 + \Delta S_4 + \Delta S_5$$

$$= (-5.07) + (-111.55) + (-25.23) + (-7.63) + (-76.10)$$

$$\boxed{\Delta S_{\text{total}} = -225.58\;\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}}$$

---

## Sanity Checks

1. **Sign:** All contributions are negative — we are cooling and condensing, both of which *reduce* accessible microstates $\Omega$, so $S = k_B\ln\Omega$ must decrease. ✓
2. **Dominant term:** The condensation step ($-111.55$) contributes nearly half the total. The enormous latent heat of vaporisation of iron ($349.6$ kJ/mol) reflects how much extra volume and disorder the gas phase has — releasing that latent heat dumps a large amount of entropy into the surroundings. ✓
3. **Second Law check:** $\Delta S_{\text{total}} < 0$ for the iron system alone does **not** violate the Second Law. The surroundings absorb the heat removed from the iron; their entropy increases by at least $|\Delta S_{\text{iron}}|$, so $\Delta S_{\text{universe}} \geq 0$. ✓
common_mistakes: **Forgetting to split at each phase transition.** A student who writes a single integral $\int_{4000}^{300} C_P/T\,\mathrm{d}T$ ignores both the condensation and solidification latent heats. Since $S$ is a state function one *could* choose any path, but the direct integral only works if $C_P$ is a single continuous function — which it is not when phase changes occur. Each phase transition must be handled as a separate $\Delta H_{\text{trs}}/T_{\text{trs}}$ term.

**Confusing $\Delta S_{\text{system}} < 0$ with a Second Law violation.** The iron loses entropy when it cools and solidifies, but this only means the *surroundings* must gain at least as much entropy from the released heat. Students often incorrectly conclude the process is forbidden because $\Delta S_{\text{iron}} < 0$; the Second Law applies to the *universe* ($\Delta S_{\text{universe}} \geq 0$), not to a sub-system alone.

**Using $\Delta H_{\text{fus}}$ (melting) instead of $\Delta H_{\text{cond}}$ or $\Delta H_{\text{solid}}$ (the reverse processes).** Tabulated values are often listed for the endothermic direction (melting, vaporisation). When cooling, the process is reversed and the sign of $\Delta H$ must be flipped. Failing to flip the sign gives the wrong sign for $\Delta S$ at the phase-change steps, turning a negative contribution into a positive one.

L2|hard.title: Entropy Budget of an Irreversible Heat Transfer Between Reservoirs
L2|hard.statement:
Two large thermal reservoirs are brought into thermal contact. Reservoir H is maintained at $T_H = 1200$ K and reservoir C is maintained at $T_C = 400$ K. A quantity of heat $Q = 48{,}000$ J flows irreversibly from H to C.

(a) Calculate $\Delta S_H$, the entropy change of reservoir H.

(b) Calculate $\Delta S_C$, the entropy change of reservoir C.

(c) Calculate $\Delta S_\text{universe}$, the total entropy change of the universe. Comment on whether this is consistent with the Second Law.

(d) Calculate the **lost work** $l_w$ associated with this irreversible heat transfer, assuming the heat could instead have been used to drive a Carnot (reversible) heat engine operating between the same two reservoirs. Express $l_w$ in joules and as a fraction of $Q$.

(e) A student proposes to make the process 'less irreversible' by inserting an intermediate reservoir at $T_M = 800$ K, so that heat flows first from H ($1200$ K) to M ($800$ K), and then from M ($800$ K) to C ($400$ K), each step transferring the full $48{,}000$ J. Calculate $\Delta S_\text{universe}$ for this two-step scheme and compare it to part (c). Does the intermediate reservoir reduce the entropy generation?
L2|hard.solution:
## Step-by-step solution

### Part (a) — Entropy change of reservoir H

Reservoir H is a large thermal body held at constant temperature $T_H = 1200$ K. It **loses** $Q = 48{,}000$ J of heat, so the heat absorbed *by* H is $-Q$.

Because the reservoir is internally at uniform temperature, any heat exchange is effectively reversible for the reservoir itself:

$$\Delta S_H = \frac{-Q}{T_H} = \frac{-48{,}000}{1200} = \boxed{-40\;\text{J/K}}$$

The entropy of the hot reservoir **decreases** — it loses energy and disorder.

---

### Part (b) — Entropy change of reservoir C

Reservoir C absorbs $Q = 48{,}000$ J at constant $T_C = 400$ K:

$$\Delta S_C = \frac{+Q}{T_C} = \frac{48{,}000}{400} = \boxed{+120\;\text{J/K}}$$

The entropy of the cold reservoir **increases** by a larger amount because the same energy arriving at lower temperature represents a greater fractional increase in disorder ($1/T$ weighting).

---

### Part (c) — Total entropy change of the universe

The 'universe' here is H + C (the two reservoirs; no other system is involved):

$$\Delta S_\text{universe} = \Delta S_H + \Delta S_C = -40 + 120 = \boxed{+80\;\text{J/K}}$$

**Comment:** $\Delta S_\text{universe} > 0$, which is entirely consistent with the Second Law. Heat flowing spontaneously from a hot body to a cold body is an **irreversible** process; every such irreversible process must generate entropy in the universe. The magnitude $+80$ J/K quantifies exactly how much irreversibility occurred.

---

### Part (d) — Lost work

The **lost work** is the useful work that *could* have been extracted by running the same heat transfer reversibly (via a Carnot engine), but which is instead dissipated because the process is irreversible.

A Carnot engine operating between $T_H = 1200$ K and $T_C = 400$ K has efficiency:

$$\eta_\text{Carnot} = 1 - \frac{T_C}{T_H} = 1 - \frac{400}{1200} = \frac{2}{3} \approx 0.667$$

The maximum work extractable from $Q = 48{,}000$ J drawn from the hot reservoir is:

$$W_\text{max} = \eta_\text{Carnot} \times Q = \frac{2}{3} \times 48{,}000 = 32{,}000\;\text{J}$$

In the irreversible process, **no work is extracted at all** — the heat simply flows from H to C without doing anything useful. Therefore:

$$l_w = W_\text{max} - W_\text{actual} = 32{,}000 - 0 = \boxed{32{,}000\;\text{J}}$$

As a fraction of $Q$:

$$\frac{l_w}{Q} = \frac{32{,}000}{48{,}000} = \boxed{\tfrac{2}{3} \approx 66.7\%}$$

**Verification via the entropy relation** $l_w = T_C \cdot \Delta S_\text{universe}$:

$$l_w = T_C \times \Delta S_\text{universe} = 400 \times 80 = 32{,}000\;\text{J}\quad\checkmark$$

This confirms that lost work and entropy generation are linked by $l_w = T_\text{sink}\,\Delta S_\text{universe}$.

---

### Part (e) — Two-step scheme with intermediate reservoir at $T_M = 800$ K

Now the $48{,}000$ J flows in two sequential irreversible steps:

**Step 1:** H (1200 K) $\to$ M (800 K)

$$\Delta S_H^{(1)} = \frac{-48{,}000}{1200} = -40\;\text{J/K}$$

$$\Delta S_M^{\text{receive}} = \frac{+48{,}000}{800} = +60\;\text{J/K}$$

$$\Delta S_\text{universe}^{(1)} = -40 + 60 = +20\;\text{J/K}$$

**Step 2:** M (800 K) $\to$ C (400 K). M now *loses* the same 48,000 J:

$$\Delta S_M^{\text{lose}} = \frac{-48{,}000}{800} = -60\;\text{J/K}$$

$$\Delta S_C^{(2)} = \frac{+48{,}000}{400} = +120\;\text{J/K}$$

$$\Delta S_\text{universe}^{(2)} = -60 + 120 = +60\;\text{J/K}$$

Notice the intermediate reservoir M has zero net entropy change over both steps ($+60 - 60 = 0$), as expected for a reservoir that merely passes heat through.

**Total for the two-step scheme:**

$$\Delta S_\text{universe}^{\text{total}} = 20 + 60 = \boxed{+80\;\text{J/K}}$$

**Conclusion:** The two-step scheme produces the **same** $\Delta S_\text{universe} = +80$ J/K as the single direct step. The intermediate reservoir does **not** reduce the total entropy generation. The irreversibility is determined only by the initial and final temperatures ($T_H$ and $T_C$) and the heat transferred — the path taken between them does not matter, because $\Delta S$ is a **state function**. The only way to reduce $\Delta S_\text{universe}$ toward zero is to approach a *truly reversible* (quasi-static, infinitesimal temperature gradient) process, not to add finite intermediate steps.
L2|hard.final_answer: (a) $\Delta S_H = -40$ J/K; (b) $\Delta S_C = +120$ J/K; (c) $\Delta S_\text{universe} = +80$ J/K (consistent with Second Law); (d) $l_w = 32{,}000$ J, i.e. $\tfrac{2}{3}$ of $Q$; (e) two-step $\Delta S_\text{universe} = +80$ J/K — identical to the single-step result; the intermediate reservoir does not reduce entropy generation.
common_mistakes: Applying $\Delta S = Q/T$ to the irreversible process as a whole rather than evaluating each reservoir separately at its own (constant) temperature. The formula $\mathrm{d}S = \delta Q_\text{rev}/T$ holds for a reversible path; for the universe calculation one must evaluate each sub-system that exchanges heat at a well-defined constant $T$ individually.

Believing that inserting an intermediate reservoir must reduce $\Delta S_\text{universe}$ because the temperature 'jumps' are smaller. Students often confuse reducing the temperature difference at each step with reducing total entropy generation. Since $\Delta S$ is a state function, only the initial state (H at 1200 K) and final state (C at 400 K) determine $\Delta S_\text{universe}$ for the same $Q$; the path is irrelevant.

Forgetting to apply the sign convention correctly: reservoir H loses heat, so its entropy change is negative ($-Q/T_H$), while reservoir C gains heat, giving a positive contribution. Errors often arise when students assign $+Q$ to both reservoirs because 'heat flows'.

L2|hard.title: Entropy Budget for Tempering a Steel Quench
L2|hard.statement:
A materials engineer is tempering a 0.5 kg steel sample. The sample has been quenched to 350 K and must be heated to 820 K in a tube furnace whose interior walls are maintained at a steady 900 K. The furnace atmosphere is inert and the process occurs at constant pressure of 1 atm.

The molar heat capacity of the steel (approximated as $\alpha$-iron) at constant pressure is:
$$C_P = 17.49 + 24.77\times10^{-3}\,T \quad [\text{J\,mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}]$$
Atomic weight of Fe $= 55.85$ g/mol.

**(a)** Calculate the enthalpy change $\Delta H$ of the steel sample during the tempering step.

**(b)** Calculate the entropy change $\Delta S_\text{steel}$ of the steel sample.

**(c)** The furnace walls supply the heat reversibly at the constant furnace temperature of 900 K. Calculate the entropy change of the surroundings $\Delta S_\text{surr}$.

**(d)** Calculate the total entropy change of the universe $\Delta S_\text{univ}$ and confirm that this tempering step is irreversible.

**(e)** A junior engineer proposes running the furnace at exactly 820 K (matching the final steel temperature) instead of 900 K, arguing this will reduce wasted energy. Without recalculating, explain qualitatively what happens to $\Delta S_\text{univ}$ and whether the process becomes reversible in the thermodynamic sense.
L2|hard.solution:
## Step 1 — Number of moles of steel

$$n = \frac{m}{M} = \frac{500\,\text{g}}{55.85\,\text{g/mol}} = 8.953\,\text{mol}$$

---

## Part (a) — Enthalpy change of the steel

At constant pressure, $\mathrm{d}H = C_P\,\mathrm{d}T$, so

$$\Delta H_\text{steel} = n\int_{350}^{820} C_P\,\mathrm{d}T$$

Integrate the polynomial:

$$\int_{350}^{820}\!\left(17.49 + 24.77\times10^{-3}\,T\right)\mathrm{d}T$$
$$= 17.49\,(820-350) + \frac{24.77\times10^{-3}}{2}\,(820^2 - 350^2)$$
$$= 17.49\times470 + 12.385\times10^{-3}\times(672400 - 122500)$$
$$= 8220.3 + 12.385\times10^{-3}\times549900$$
$$= 8220.3 + 6810.6 = 15030.9\,\text{J/mol}$$

Multiply by moles:

$$\Delta H_\text{steel} = 8.953\times15030.9 = 134{,}552\,\text{J} \approx 134.6\,\text{kJ}$$

---

## Part (b) — Entropy change of the steel

At constant pressure, $\mathrm{d}S = C_P\,\mathrm{d}T/T$:

$$\Delta S_\text{steel} = n\int_{350}^{820}\frac{C_P}{T}\,\mathrm{d}T = n\int_{350}^{820}\left(\frac{17.49}{T} + 24.77\times10^{-3}\right)\mathrm{d}T$$

$$= n\left[17.49\ln\frac{820}{350} + 24.77\times10^{-3}\,(820-350)\right]$$

$$\ln\frac{820}{350} = \ln(2.3429) = 0.8513$$

$$= n\left[17.49\times0.8513 + 24.77\times10^{-3}\times470\right]$$
$$= n\left[14.882 + 11.642\right] = n\times26.524\,\text{J\,mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

$$\Delta S_\text{steel} = 8.953\times26.524 = 237.4\,\text{J/K}$$

---

## Part (c) — Entropy change of the surroundings

The furnace walls are at a constant $T_\text{surr} = 900\,\text{K}$. The heat flowing **out** of the surroundings into the steel equals $Q_\text{surr} = -\Delta H_\text{steel}$ (energy conservation; at constant pressure, heat absorbed by steel $= \Delta H_\text{steel}$).

$$\Delta S_\text{surr} = \frac{Q_\text{surr}}{T_\text{surr}} = \frac{-\Delta H_\text{steel}}{T_\text{surr}} = \frac{-134{,}552}{900} = -149.5\,\text{J/K}$$

The surroundings lose entropy because heat flows out of them.

---

## Part (d) — Total entropy change of the universe

$$\Delta S_\text{univ} = \Delta S_\text{steel} + \Delta S_\text{surr} = 237.4 + (-149.5) = +87.9\,\text{J/K}$$

Since $\Delta S_\text{univ} = +87.9\,\text{J/K} > 0$, the process is **irreversible**, consistent with the Second Law. Heat is being transferred across a finite temperature difference (steel at 350–820 K, furnace at 900 K), which is the textbook source of irreversibility.

---

## Part (e) — Qualitative effect of lowering the furnace to 820 K

Lowering the furnace temperature to 820 K reduces the temperature *difference* driving heat into the steel. $\Delta S_\text{steel}$ does not change (it depends only on the initial and final states of the steel, both of which are unchanged). However, $\Delta S_\text{surr}$ becomes $-\Delta H/820$, which is a **larger magnitude** negative number than $-\Delta H/900$. Therefore $\Delta S_\text{univ}$ actually **increases** — the process becomes *more* irreversible, not less.

To approach true thermodynamic reversibility, the furnace temperature would need to match the steel temperature **at every instant** during heating — an infinitely slow, quasi-static process with an infinitely large bank of incrementally different heat reservoirs. A single furnace at any fixed temperature above the initial steel temperature will always produce $\Delta S_\text{univ} > 0$.
L2|hard.final_answer: (a) $\Delta H_\text{steel} \approx +134.6\,\text{kJ}$; (b) $\Delta S_\text{steel} \approx +237.4\,\text{J/K}$; (c) $\Delta S_\text{surr} \approx -149.5\,\text{J/K}$; (d) $\Delta S_\text{univ} \approx +87.9\,\text{J/K} > 0$ (irreversible); (e) $\Delta S_\text{univ}$ increases (process becomes more irreversible) because $|\Delta S_\text{surr}|$ grows as $T_\text{surr}$ decreases while $\Delta S_\text{steel}$ is fixed.
common_mistakes: Forgetting that $\Delta S_\text{steel}$ uses $\int C_P/T\,\mathrm{d}T$ (with the extra $1/T$ factor) while $\Delta H$ uses $\int C_P\,\mathrm{d}T$ — students often compute $\Delta S_\text{steel} = \Delta H / T_\text{average}$ using some average temperature, which is incorrect.

Using the steel's final temperature (820 K) or some intermediate temperature instead of the constant furnace temperature (900 K) when computing $\Delta S_\text{surr} = -Q/T_\text{surr}$ — the surroundings have a single well-defined temperature of 900 K.

Concluding in part (e) that lowering the furnace temperature reduces $\Delta S_\text{univ}$ because it 'wastes less energy' — the opposite is true: a lower fixed furnace temperature means the denominator in $-\Delta H/T_\text{surr}$ is smaller, making $\Delta S_\text{surr}$ more negative and $\Delta S_\text{univ}$ larger.

L2|hard.title: Entropy Budget of a Copper Casting Furnace
L2|hard.statement:
A small copper casting furnace operates continuously at steady state. Each cycle, the furnace draws $Q_H = 85{,}000$ J of heat from its electrical heating elements (which operate at an effective temperature of $T_H = 1450$ K) and rejects $Q_C$ of heat to a cooling-water jacket maintained at $T_C = 320$ K. During the same cycle the furnace delivers $W_\text{net} = 12{,}000$ J of useful shaft work (used to drive a stirring impeller).

**(a)** Using the First Law for a complete cycle, calculate the heat $Q_C$ rejected to the cooling water.

**(b)** Calculate the entropy change of the hot reservoir (heating elements), $\Delta S_H$, and the entropy change of the cold reservoir (cooling water jacket), $\Delta S_C$, per cycle.

**(c)** Calculate the total entropy change of the universe per cycle, $\Delta S_\text{universe}$. Is this process thermodynamically permissible?

**(d)** A design engineer claims that by insulating the furnace more carefully, the heat rejected to the cooling water can be reduced to $Q_C^\prime = 5{,}000$ J per cycle (with the same $Q_H = 85{,}000$ J and the same $W_\text{net} = 12{,}000$ J). Evaluate this claim using the Second Law.

**Given data:**
- $Q_H = 85{,}000$ J per cycle (heat absorbed by furnace from hot reservoir at $T_H = 1450$ K)
- $T_H = 1450$ K
- $T_C = 320$ K
- $W_\text{net} = 12{,}000$ J of useful work delivered per cycle
- $R = 8.314$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$
L2|hard.solution:
## Step-by-step solution

### Sign-convention bookkeeping

We use the course convention $\Delta U = Q + W$, with $Q > 0$ = heat absorbed **by** the system and $W > 0$ = work done **on** the system.

For the furnace as the system:
- Heat absorbed from the hot reservoir: $Q_H = +85{,}000$ J (absorbed by system, positive).
- Heat rejected to the cold reservoir: $Q_C < 0$ (heat leaves the system, negative).
- Shaft work delivered by the furnace: $W_\text{net} = +12{,}000$ J delivered **by** the system, so in our convention work done **on** the system is $W = -12{,}000$ J.

---

### Part (a) — Heat rejected $Q_C$

The furnace runs at steady state and returns to the same macrostate each cycle, so $\Delta U_\text{cycle} = 0$.

Applying the First Law:
$$\Delta U_\text{cycle} = Q_H + Q_C + W = 0$$

where $W = -12{,}000$ J (work done **on** the system is negative because work is actually leaving as shaft output).

$$0 = 85{,}000 + Q_C + (-12{,}000)$$

$$Q_C = 12{,}000 - 85{,}000 = -73{,}000 \text{ J}$$

The furnace rejects $|Q_C| = 73{,}000$ J to the cooling water per cycle.

---

### Part (b) — Entropy changes of the two reservoirs

A reservoir is large enough that heat exchange does not change its temperature. The entropy change of a reservoir exchanging heat $Q$ at constant temperature $T$ is simply $\Delta S = Q/T$ (where $Q$ is the heat absorbed **by** the reservoir).

**Hot reservoir** (heating elements at $T_H = 1450$ K):

The hot reservoir *loses* $85{,}000$ J to the furnace, so heat absorbed by the hot reservoir is $-85{,}000$ J:
