The correct conclusion is that increasing $T$ *opposes* spontaneity here — the reaction is favoured at low $T$ and becomes non-spontaneous above $T^*$.

L3|medium.title: Gibbs Free Energy and Spontaneity for Magnetite Formation
L3|medium.statement:
The formation of magnetite (Fe$_3$O$_4$) from iron and oxygen is a key reaction in corrosion science:

$$4\,\text{Fe(s)} + 3\,\text{O}_2\text{(g)} \longrightarrow 2\,\text{Fe}_3\text{O}_4\text{(s)}$$

Use the thermodynamic data below (all at 298 K, 1 atm) to answer the following:

| Species | $\Delta H_f^\circ$ (kJ/mol) | $S^\circ_{298}$ (J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Fe(s) | 0 | 27.32 |
| O$_2$(g) | 0 | 205.14 |
| Fe$_3$O$_4$(s) | $-1118.4$ | 146.40 |

**(a)** Calculate $\Delta H^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$ and $\Delta S^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$ for the reaction as written.

**(b)** Calculate $\Delta G^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$ at 298 K and state whether the reaction is spontaneous under standard conditions.

**(c)** Estimate the temperature above which the reaction becomes **non-spontaneous** (i.e. find $T^*$ where $\Delta G^\circ = 0$), assuming $\Delta H^\circ$ and $\Delta S^\circ$ are approximately independent of temperature.
L3|medium.solution:
## Step 1 — Calculate $\Delta H^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$

Using Hess's Law (products minus reactants, weighted by stoichiometric coefficients):

$$\Delta H^\circ_{\text{rxn}} = 2\,\Delta H_f^\circ[\text{Fe}_3\text{O}_4] - 4\,\Delta H_f^\circ[\text{Fe}] - 3\,\Delta H_f^\circ[\text{O}_2]$$

$$= 2(-1118.4) - 4(0) - 3(0)$$

$$\boxed{\Delta H^\circ_{\text{rxn}} = -2236.8 \text{ kJ/mol}}$$

The large negative value confirms the reaction is strongly **exothermic** — iron oxidising to magnetite releases substantial heat, consistent with observed corrosion processes.

## Step 2 — Calculate $\Delta S^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$

Using standard molar entropies (products minus reactants):

$$\Delta S^\circ_{\text{rxn}} = 2\,S^\circ[\text{Fe}_3\text{O}_4] - 4\,S^\circ[\text{Fe}] - 3\,S^\circ[\text{O}_2]$$

$$= 2(146.40) - 4(27.32) - 3(205.14)$$

$$= 292.80 - 109.28 - 615.42$$

$$\boxed{\Delta S^\circ_{\text{rxn}} = -431.90 \text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}}$$

**Physical reasoning:** Three moles of O$_2$ gas (high molar entropy, ~205 J mol$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$ each) are consumed to make two moles of a solid oxide. Consuming gases to make solids always decreases entropy strongly. The negative $\Delta S^\circ$ means this reaction is entropically **unfavourable**.

## Step 3 — Calculate $\Delta G^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$ at 298 K

Using the fundamental relation:

$$\Delta G^\circ_{\text{rxn}} = \Delta H^\circ_{\text{rxn}} - T\,\Delta S^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$$

Note: convert $\Delta S^\circ$ to kJ: $-431.90 \text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1} = -0.43190 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$

$$\Delta G^\circ_{298} = -2236.8 - (298)(-0.43190)$$

$$= -2236.8 + 128.71$$

$$\boxed{\Delta G^\circ_{298} = -2108.1 \text{ kJ/mol}}$$

Since $\Delta G^\circ_{298} \ll 0$, the reaction is **strongly spontaneous** at standard conditions (298 K, 1 atm O$_2$). The enthalpy term ($-2236.8$ kJ/mol) completely dominates the unfavourable entropy penalty ($+128.7$ kJ/mol at 298 K).

## Step 4 — Find the crossover temperature $T^*$

At $T^*$, $\Delta G^\circ = 0$, so:

$$0 = \Delta H^\circ - T^*\,\Delta S^\circ$$

$$T^* = \frac{\Delta H^\circ}{\Delta S^\circ} = \frac{-2{,}236{,}800 \text{ J/mol}}{-431.90 \text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}}$$

$$\boxed{T^* \approx 5179 \text{ K}}$$

**Interpretation:** This extraordinarily high crossover temperature (~4906 °C) means magnetite formation remains thermodynamically spontaneous at every practically achievable temperature. Even if you heat iron to its boiling point (~3134 K), $\Delta G^\circ$ is still negative. This is consistent with the well-known observation that iron oxidises at essentially all accessible temperatures — preventing rust requires kinetic barriers (coatings, cathodic protection), not thermodynamic ones.

**Placement in the $\Delta H$–$\Delta S$ matrix (L3 §3.5):** This reaction sits in the lower-left cell — exothermic ($\Delta H < 0$) and entropy-decreasing ($\Delta S < 0$). Such reactions are spontaneous only at **low $T$** (when $|T\Delta S|$ is smaller than $|\Delta H|$). With $T^* \approx 5179$ K, "low $T$" encompasses essentially the entire temperature range of interest.
L3|medium.final_answer: (a) $\Delta H^\circ_{\text{rxn}} = -2236.8$ kJ/mol; $\Delta S^\circ_{\text{rxn}} = -431.90$ J mol$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$. (b) $\Delta G^\circ_{298} = -2108.1$ kJ/mol (strongly spontaneous). (c) $T^* \approx 5179$ K — the reaction remains spontaneous at all practical temperatures.
common_mistakes: **Forgetting to multiply by stoichiometric coefficients.** The reaction produces 2 mol Fe$_3$O$_4$ and consumes 4 mol Fe and 3 mol O$_2$. Students often apply $\Delta H_f^\circ$ and $S^\circ$ for one formula unit without multiplying, giving answers that are exactly half or some other fraction of the correct value.

**Using wrong units when combining $\Delta H$ and $T\Delta S$.** $\Delta H$ is typically in kJ/mol while $S^\circ$ values from tables are in J mol$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$. Failing to convert $\Delta S$ to kJ mol$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$ before computing $T\Delta S$ introduces a factor-of-1000 error in the entropy contribution, making $\Delta G$ appear incorrectly close to $\Delta H$.

**Setting $\Delta H_f^\circ = 0$ for O$_2$ but forgetting $S^\circ[\text{O}_2] \neq 0$.** Standard enthalpy of formation of elements in their standard state is zero, but standard molar entropy is NOT zero for any substance above 0 K (Third Law). Students sometimes omit the O$_2$ entropy contribution entirely when computing $\Delta S^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$, drastically underestimating the entropy decrease.

L3|medium.title: Gibbs Free Energy and Spontaneity of Nickel Oxidation
L3|medium.statement:
Nickel metal can be oxidised according to the reaction:

$$2\,\text{Ni(s)} + \text{O}_2(\text{g}) \rightarrow 2\,\text{NiO(s)}$$

Use the thermodynamic data below (all at 298 K, 1 atm) to answer the following questions.

| Species | $\Delta H_f^\circ$ (kJ mol$^{-1}$) | $S^\circ_{298}$ (J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Ni(s) | 0 | 29.87 |
| O$_2$(g) | 0 | 205.14 |
| NiO(s) | $-$244.35 | 37.99 |

**(a)** Calculate $\Delta H^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$ and $\Delta S^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$ at 298 K.

**(b)** Calculate $\Delta G^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$ at 298 K and state whether oxidation is spontaneous under standard conditions.

**(c)** Estimate the **crossover temperature** $T^*$ above which the oxidation reaction is no longer spontaneous (i.e. where $\Delta G^\circ = 0$), assuming $\Delta H^\circ$ and $\Delta S^\circ$ are approximately independent of temperature.

**(d)** At $T^* + 200\,\text{K}$, determine the sign of $\Delta G^\circ$ and state which direction the reaction is thermodynamically favoured.
L3|medium.solution:
## Step 1 — $\Delta H^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$ at 298 K

Apply Hess's Law (products minus reactants, weighted by stoichiometry):

$$\Delta H^\circ_{\text{rxn}} = 2\,\Delta H_f^\circ[\text{NiO(s)}] - 2\,\Delta H_f^\circ[\text{Ni(s)}] - \Delta H_f^\circ[\text{O}_2(\text{g})]$$

$$= 2(-244.35) - 2(0) - 0 = -488.70\;\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

The reaction is strongly **exothermic**.

---

## Step 2 — $\Delta S^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$ at 298 K

$$\Delta S^\circ_{\text{rxn}} = 2\,S^\circ[\text{NiO(s)}] - 2\,S^\circ[\text{Ni(s)}] - S^\circ[\text{O}_2(\text{g})]$$

$$= 2(37.99) - 2(29.87) - 205.14$$

$$= 75.98 - 59.74 - 205.14 = -188.90\;\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

Negative: a gas (O$_2$) is consumed to form solid NiO, reducing the number of accessible microstates — entropy **decreases**.

---

## Step 3 — $\Delta G^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$ at 298 K (Part b)

Convert $\Delta S^\circ$ to kJ: $-188.90\;\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1} = -0.18890\;\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$.

$$\Delta G^\circ_{\text{rxn}} = \Delta H^\circ - T\,\Delta S^\circ$$

$$= -488.70 - (298)(-0.18890)$$

$$= -488.70 + 56.29 = \boxed{-432.41\;\text{kJ mol}^{-1}}$$

$\Delta G^\circ < 0$ at 298 K: oxidation of Ni is **spontaneous** under standard conditions. Both the large exothermic enthalpy and the entropy penalty combine, with $|\Delta H^\circ|$ dominating at room temperature.

---

## Step 4 — Crossover temperature $T^*$ (Part c)

At $T^*$, $\Delta G^\circ = 0$:

$$\Delta H^\circ - T^*\,\Delta S^\circ = 0$$

$$T^* = \frac{\Delta H^\circ}{\Delta S^\circ} = \frac{-488{,}700\;\text{J mol}^{-1}}{-188.90\;\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}}$$

$$\boxed{T^* \approx 2587\;\text{K}}$$

Note that both numerator and denominator are negative, so $T^*$ is positive — physically sensible.

---

## Step 5 — Sign of $\Delta G^\circ$ above $T^*$ (Part d)

Evaluate at $T = T^* + 200 = 2787\;\text{K}$:

$$\Delta G^\circ = -488.70 - (2787)(-0.18890)$$

$$= -488.70 + 526.65 = +37.95\;\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

$\Delta G^\circ > 0$: at 2787 K the **forward reaction (oxidation) is no longer spontaneous**. The entropy penalty $T|\Delta S^\circ|$ now exceeds the enthalpy release, making the **reverse reaction** (reduction of NiO back to Ni metal) thermodynamically favoured. This is consistent with the temperature-spontaneity matrix in L3: an exothermic, entropy-decreasing reaction sits in the lower-left cell — spontaneous only at low $T$.
L3|medium.final_answer: (a) $\Delta H^\circ = -488.70\;\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$; $\Delta S^\circ = -188.90\;\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$. (b) $\Delta G^\circ_{298} = -432.41\;\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ — spontaneous. (c) $T^* \approx 2587\;\text{K}$. (d) $\Delta G^\circ_{2787} \approx +38\;\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ — reverse reaction favoured above $T^*$.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to apply the stoichiometric coefficient of 2 to both NiO and Ni when computing $\Delta H^\circ$ and $\Delta S^\circ$ — this halves the magnitude of both quantities and gives an incorrect $T^*$.

Mixing units of $\Delta H^\circ$ (kJ) and $\Delta S^\circ$ (J K$^{-1}$) without converting to a common unit before computing $\Delta G^\circ = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ$, leading to an answer off by a factor of 1000.

Concluding that because $\Delta S^\circ < 0$ the reaction cannot be spontaneous at any temperature, overlooking that the large negative $\Delta H^\circ$ dominates at low $T$ and that spontaneity only ceases above the high crossover temperature $T^*$.

L3|medium.title: Gibbs Free Energy of Nitrogen Compression
L3|medium.statement:
Nitrogen gas ($\text{N}_2$) at 298 K is compressed isothermally and reversibly from an initial pressure of $P_1 = 1\text{ atm}$ to a final pressure of $P_2 = 50\text{ atm}$. Treat $\text{N}_2$ as an ideal gas throughout.

(a) Using the appropriate Maxwell relation derived from $\mathrm{d}G = V\,\mathrm{d}P - S\,\mathrm{d}T$, write an expression for $\left(\partial S/\partial P\right)_T$ in terms of measurable quantities.

(b) Calculate the molar entropy change $\Delta S$ (in J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$) for this isothermal compression.

(c) Calculate the molar Gibbs free energy change $\Delta G$ (in J mol$^{-1}$) for this isothermal compression using $\mathrm{d}G = V\,\mathrm{d}P - S\,\mathrm{d}T$ directly.

(d) Verify that your answers to (b) and (c) are consistent with the relation $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$, given that for an isothermal process on an ideal gas $\Delta H = 0$.

Data: $R = 8.314\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$, $T = 298\text{ K}$.
L3|medium.solution:
## Step 1 — Maxwell Relation for $(\partial S/\partial P)_T$

From the fundamental differential of the Gibbs free energy:
$$\mathrm{d}G = V\,\mathrm{d}P - S\,\mathrm{d}T$$

Reading off the partial derivatives:
$$\left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial P}\right)_T = V \qquad \text{and} \qquad \left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial T}\right)_P = -S$$

Since $G$ is a state function, its mixed second partial derivatives must be equal (exact differential test):
$$\frac{\partial^2 G}{\partial T\,\partial P} = \frac{\partial^2 G}{\partial P\,\partial T}$$

This gives the Maxwell relation:
$$\boxed{\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial P}\right)_T = -\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P}$$

## Step 2 — Evaluate $(\partial V/\partial T)_P$ for an Ideal Gas

For one mole of ideal gas: $PV = RT$, so $V = RT/P$.

Differentiating at constant $P$:
$$\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P = \frac{R}{P}$$

Substituting into the Maxwell relation:
$$\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial P}\right)_T = -\frac{R}{P}$$

## Step 3 — Part (b): Molar Entropy Change

Integrating at constant $T$ from $P_1$ to $P_2$:
$$\Delta S = \int_{P_1}^{P_2} \left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial P}\right)_T \mathrm{d}P = \int_{P_1}^{P_2} \left(-\frac{R}{P}\right)\mathrm{d}P = -R\ln\frac{P_2}{P_1}$$

Substituting values:
$$\Delta S = -8.314 \times \ln\!\left(\frac{50}{1}\right) = -8.314 \times \ln(50)$$

$$\ln(50) = \ln(5 \times 10) = \ln 5 + \ln 10 = 1.6094 + 2.3026 = 3.912$$

$$\boxed{\Delta S = -8.314 \times 3.912 = -32.53\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}}$$

**Physical check:** Entropy decreases on isothermal compression — molecules are packed into a smaller volume, reducing the number of accessible microstates. This is consistent with $S = k_B\ln\Omega$. ✓

## Step 4 — Part (c): Molar Gibbs Free Energy Change

At constant $T$, $\mathrm{d}T = 0$, so:
$$\mathrm{d}G = V\,\mathrm{d}P$$

For one mole of ideal gas ($V = RT/P$):
$$\mathrm{d}G = \frac{RT}{P}\,\mathrm{d}P = RT\,\mathrm{d}\ln P$$

Integrating from $P_1$ to $P_2$:
$$\Delta G = RT\ln\frac{P_2}{P_1} = (8.314)(298)\ln(50)$$

$$= 8.314 \times 298 \times 3.912$$

$$= 2477.6 \times 3.912$$

$$\boxed{\Delta G = +9,692\text{ J mol}^{-1} \approx +9.69\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}}$$

**Physical check:** $\Delta G > 0$ is expected — isothermal compression requires external work input and is non-spontaneous. The surroundings must do work on the gas. ✓

## Step 5 — Part (d): Consistency Check via $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$

For an isothermal process on an ideal gas:
$$\left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial P}\right)_T = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \Delta H = 0$$

(This follows from $H = U + PV = U + RT$ for an ideal gas — $H$ depends only on $T$, not $P$; at constant $T$, $\Delta H = 0$.)

Therefore:
$$\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S = 0 - (298)(-32.53)$$

$$= +298 \times 32.53 = +9,694\text{ J mol}^{-1}$$

This agrees with part (c) to within rounding ($9,692$ vs $9,694$ J mol$^{-1}$). ✓

The two routes to $\Delta G$ — integrating $V\,\mathrm{d}P$ and using $\Delta H - T\Delta S$ — give the same answer, confirming that $G$ is a state function.
L3|medium.final_answer: $\Delta S = -32.5\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$; $\Delta G = +9{,}69\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$
common_mistakes: Forgetting the negative sign in the Maxwell relation: students sometimes write $(\partial S/\partial P)_T = +(\partial V/\partial T)_P$ instead of the correct $-(\partial V/\partial T)_P$. The minus sign is essential and comes directly from the signs in $\mathrm{d}G = V\,\mathrm{d}P - S\,\mathrm{d}T$.

Confusing the sign of $\Delta G$: students may expect $\Delta G < 0$ because the gas is being 'compressed into a more ordered state'. In fact, $\Delta G > 0$ because compression at constant $T$ is non-spontaneous and requires external work; the spontaneous direction would be expansion.

Assuming $\Delta H \neq 0$ for the isothermal compression of a real or ideal gas. For an ideal gas specifically, $(\partial H/\partial P)_T = 0$, so $\Delta H = 0$ at constant $T$, and all the Gibbs free energy change comes from the $-T\Delta S$ term. Students unfamiliar with ideal-gas properties may incorrectly include a $PV$-work contribution to $\Delta H$.

L3|medium.title: Gibbs Free Energy of Vaporisation: Finding Equilibrium Temperature
L3|medium.statement:
Liquid zinc evaporates according to the reaction:

$$\text{Zn}(\ell) \rightarrow \text{Zn}(\text{g})$$

Using the thermodynamic data at 298 K and 1 atm given below, determine:

**(a)** $\Delta H^\circ_{298}$, $\Delta S^\circ_{298}$, and $\Delta G^\circ_{298}$ for this vaporisation.

**(b)** The temperature $T^*$ at which liquid and gaseous zinc are in thermodynamic equilibrium at 1 atm (i.e. the normal boiling point of zinc), assuming $\Delta H^\circ$ and $\Delta S^\circ$ are approximately independent of temperature.

**(c)** State whether vaporisation is spontaneous above or below $T^*$, and classify the reaction using the $\Delta H$–$\Delta S$ spontaneity matrix.

**Data (at 298 K, 1 atm):**

| Species | $\Delta H_f^\circ$ (kJ mol$^{-1}$) | $S^\circ_{298}$ (J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Zn($\ell$) | $+7.32$ | $41.6$ |
| Zn(g) | $+130.7$ | $160.9$ |
L3|medium.solution:
## Step 1 — $\Delta H^\circ_{298}$

Apply Hess's Law (products minus reactants, stoichiometric coefficients all 1):

$$\Delta H^\circ_{298} = \Delta H_f^\circ[\text{Zn(g)}] - \Delta H_f^\circ[\text{Zn}(\ell)]$$

$$\Delta H^\circ_{298} = 130.7 - 7.32 = +123.38 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$

The positive sign confirms vaporisation is **endothermic** — heat must be supplied to convert liquid zinc to vapour.

---

## Step 2 — $\Delta S^\circ_{298}$

Apply the entropy analogue of Hess's Law:

$$\Delta S^\circ_{298} = S^\circ_{298}[\text{Zn(g)}] - S^\circ_{298}[\text{Zn}(\ell)]$$

$$\Delta S^\circ_{298} = 160.9 - 41.6 = +119.3 \text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

The positive sign is expected: the gaseous phase has far more accessible microstates than the liquid, so $S_\text{gas} \gg S_\text{liquid}$.

---

## Step 3 — $\Delta G^\circ_{298}$

From the definition $G = H - TS$ applied to the reaction at constant $T = 298$ K:

$$\Delta G^\circ_{298} = \Delta H^\circ_{298} - T\,\Delta S^\circ_{298}$$

Convert $\Delta S^\circ_{298}$ to kJ mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$: $119.3 \text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1} = 0.1193 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$.

$$\Delta G^\circ_{298} = 123.38 - (298)(0.1193)$$

$$\Delta G^\circ_{298} = 123.38 - 35.55 = +87.83 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$

$\Delta G^\circ_{298} > 0$: vaporisation is **non-spontaneous at 298 K** under standard-state conditions (1 atm of Zn vapour), consistent with zinc being a liquid at room temperature.

---

## Step 4 — Equilibrium temperature $T^*$

At the normal boiling point, liquid and gas coexist in equilibrium at 1 atm, meaning $\Delta G = 0$:

$$\Delta G = \Delta H^\circ - T^*\,\Delta S^\circ = 0$$

Solving for $T^*$:

$$T^* = \frac{\Delta H^\circ}{\Delta S^\circ} = \frac{123{,}380 \text{ J mol}^{-1}}{119.3 \text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}}$$

$$\boxed{T^* \approx 1034 \text{ K} \approx 761\,^\circ\text{C}}$$

The experimental normal boiling point of zinc is 1180 K (907 °C). The discrepancy arises because $\Delta H^\circ$ and $\Delta S^\circ$ are not truly temperature-independent over such a large range — the approximation made in part (b) is responsible for the error.

---

## Step 5 — Spontaneity classification

From the $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$ analysis:

- $\Delta H^\circ > 0$ (endothermic)
- $\Delta S^\circ > 0$ (entropy increases)

This falls in the **top-right cell** of the spontaneity matrix: the reaction becomes spontaneous **only above a critical temperature** $T^*$, where the $T\Delta S$ term outweighs $\Delta H$. Below $T^*$, the enthalpy penalty dominates and the process is non-spontaneous.
L3|medium.final_answer: (a) $\Delta H^\circ_{298} = +123.38$ kJ mol$^{-1}$, $\Delta S^\circ_{298} = +119.3$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$, $\Delta G^\circ_{298} = +87.83$ kJ mol$^{-1}$. (b) $T^* \approx 1034$ K ($\approx 761\,^\circ$C). (c) Vaporisation is spontaneous only above $T^*$; classified as endothermic + entropy-increasing → spontaneous at high $T$ only.
common_mistakes: **Unit mismatch between $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$**: $\Delta H$ is in kJ mol$^{-1}$ while $\Delta S$ is in J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$. Students often forget to convert, computing $T^* = 123380/119.3 \approx 1034$ K correctly but sometimes writing $123.38/119.3 \approx 1.03$ K — off by a factor of 1000.

**Applying $\Delta G = 0$ at 298 K instead of at $T^*$**: Some students set $\Delta G^\circ_{298} = 0$ to find the boiling point, not realising that $\Delta G^\circ_{298}$ is the free energy at 298 K. The equilibrium condition requires $\Delta G = \Delta H - T^*\Delta S = 0$, which is satisfied at a *different* temperature $T^*$.

**Confusing standard-state spontaneity with real-world spontaneity**: $\Delta G^\circ_{298} > 0$ means vaporisation is non-spontaneous at 298 K *when the vapour pressure is 1 atm*. Students sometimes conclude zinc cannot evaporate at all at room temperature, ignoring that real evaporation occurs at partial pressures far below 1 atm — the actual equilibrium vapour pressure of zinc at 298 K is extremely small but non-zero.

L3|medium.title: Pressure-Driven Entropy Change in Liquid Copper
L3|medium.statement:
Liquid copper at 1358 K (its melting point) is subjected to an isovolumetric analysis, but an engineer instead wants to know how its molar entropy changes when the pressure is increased **isothermally** from 1 atm to 50 atm at a fixed temperature of 1358 K.

Using the Maxwell relation derived from the Gibbs free energy, calculate the molar entropy change $\Delta S$ of liquid copper under this isothermal compression.

**Given data for liquid copper at 1358 K:**
- Volumetric coefficient of thermal expansion: $\alpha_V = 9.2 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{K}^{-1}$
- Molar mass: $M = 63.55\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$
- Density of liquid Cu: $\rho = 8.00\,\text{g cm}^{-3}$
- $1\,\text{atm} = 1.013 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa}$

State the relevant Maxwell relation, compute the molar volume, and hence evaluate $\Delta S$.
L3|medium.solution:
## Step 1 — Identify the relevant Maxwell relation

From the Gibbs free energy differential $\mathrm{d}G = -S\,\mathrm{d}T + V\,\mathrm{d}P$, the Maxwell relation is:

$$\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial P}\right)_T = -\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P$$

The right-hand side can be written using the definition of the volumetric thermal expansion coefficient:

$$\alpha_V \equiv \frac{1}{V}\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P \implies \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P = V\alpha_V$$

Substituting:

$$\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial P}\right)_T = -V\alpha_V$$

## Step 2 — Compute the molar volume of liquid copper

$$\underline{V} = \frac{M}{\rho} = \frac{63.55\,\text{g mol}^{-1}}{8.00\,\text{g cm}^{-3}} = 7.944\,\text{cm}^3\text{mol}^{-1} = 7.944 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{m}^3\text{mol}^{-1}$$

## Step 3 — Integrate the Maxwell relation at constant $T$

For a condensed phase (liquid), both $V$ and $\alpha_V$ are nearly independent of pressure. Integrating from $P_1 = 1\,\text{atm}$ to $P_2 = 50\,\text{atm}$:

$$\Delta S = \int_{P_1}^{P_2}\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial P}\right)_T \mathrm{d}P = -V\alpha_V\,(P_2 - P_1)$$

## Step 4 — Convert the pressure difference to Pascals

$$\Delta P = (50 - 1)\,\text{atm} = 49\,\text{atm} = 49 \times 1.013 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa} = 4.964 \times 10^{6}\,\text{Pa}$$

## Step 5 — Substitute numerical values

$$\Delta S = -(7.944 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{m}^3\text{mol}^{-1})(9.2 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{K}^{-1})(4.964 \times 10^{6}\,\text{Pa})$$

Carry out the multiplication step by step:

$$7.944 \times 10^{-6} \times 9.2 \times 10^{-5} = 7.309 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{m}^3\text{K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$$

$$7.309 \times 10^{-10} \times 4.964 \times 10^{6} = 3.627 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

$$\boxed{\Delta S = -3.63 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}}$$

## Step 6 — Sanity check

- The negative sign is correct: increasing pressure at constant temperature **reduces** the molar volume accessible to atoms, reducing the number of accessible microstates and therefore entropy.
- The magnitude ($\sim 3.6\,\text{mJ mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$) is tiny — consistent with the fact that liquids and solids are nearly incompressible; their entropy is far less sensitive to pressure than that of gases. Compare: for an ideal gas compressed isothermally from 1 atm to 50 atm, $\Delta S = -R\ln(50) \approx -32\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$ — roughly 10 000 times larger.
- Units check: $[\text{m}^3\text{mol}^{-1}][\text{K}^{-1}][\text{Pa}] = [\text{m}^3\text{mol}^{-1}][\text{K}^{-1}][\text{N m}^{-2}] = [\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}]$. ✓
common_mistakes: **Dropping the negative sign from the Maxwell relation.** The Maxwell relation from $\mathrm{d}G$ gives $(\partial S/\partial P)_T = -(\partial V/\partial T)_P$. Students sometimes write it without the minus sign, getting a positive $\Delta S$ — which would imply compression increases disorder, contradicting physical intuition.

**Forgetting to convert pressure from atm to Pascals before multiplying.** Since $V$ is in m$^3$, the pressure must be in Pa ($\text{N m}^{-2}$) for the product $V \Delta P$ to yield joules. Using atm directly gives an answer wrong by a factor of $1.013 \times 10^5$.

**Confusing the volumetric and linear thermal expansion coefficients.** Tables for metals often list the *linear* coefficient $\alpha_L$; the volumetric coefficient needed here is $\alpha_V = 3\alpha_L$ for isotropic materials. Using $\alpha_L$ in place of $\alpha_V$ underestimates $\Delta S$ by a factor of three.

L3|medium.title: Spontaneity of Iron Carbide Formation at Elevated Temperature
L3|medium.statement:
Iron carbide (cementite, Fe$_3$C) is an important phase in steel microstructures. Consider the following reaction at 1 atm pressure:

$$\text{3 Fe(s)} + \text{C(graphite)} \rightarrow \text{Fe}_3\text{C(s)}$$

The following thermodynamic data are given at 298 K:

| Species | $\Delta H_f^\circ$ (kJ mol$^{-1}$) | $S^\circ_{298}$ (J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Fe(s) | 0 | 27.28 |
| C(graphite) | 0 | 5.74 |
| Fe$_3$C(s) | +25.1 | 104.6 |

Assume $\Delta H^\circ_\text{rxn}$ and $\Delta S^\circ_\text{rxn}$ are approximately independent of temperature over the range of interest.

**(a)** Calculate $\Delta H^\circ_\text{rxn}$ and $\Delta S^\circ_\text{rxn}$ at 298 K using Hess's Law.

**(b)** Calculate $\Delta G^\circ_\text{rxn}$ at 298 K. Is cementite formation spontaneous at standard conditions?

**(c)** Identify the crossover temperature $T^*$ at which $\Delta G^\circ_\text{rxn} = 0$. Above or below $T^*$, is cementite stable?

**(d)** Calculate $\Delta G^\circ_\text{rxn}$ at 1000 K and determine whether cementite is thermodynamically stable relative to iron and graphite at that temperature.
L3|medium.solution:
## Step 1 — Compute $\Delta H^\circ_\text{rxn}$ at 298 K (Hess's Law)

Products minus reactants, each weighted by stoichiometric coefficient:

$$\Delta H^\circ_\text{rxn} = \Delta H_f^\circ(\text{Fe}_3\text{C}) - \left[3\,\Delta H_f^\circ(\text{Fe}) + \Delta H_f^\circ(\text{C})\right]$$

$$= +25.1 - [3(0) + 0] = \boxed{+25.1 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}}$$

The reaction is **endothermic** — energy must be supplied to form cementite from its elements.

---

## Step 2 — Compute $\Delta S^\circ_\text{rxn}$ at 298 K

$$\Delta S^\circ_\text{rxn} = S^\circ_{298}(\text{Fe}_3\text{C}) - \left[3\,S^\circ_{298}(\text{Fe}) + S^\circ_{298}(\text{C})\right]$$

$$= 104.6 - [3(27.28) + 5.74]$$

$$= 104.6 - [81.84 + 5.74]$$

$$= 104.6 - 87.58 = \boxed{+17.02 \text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}}$$

The entropy **increases** upon forming cementite — somewhat surprising for combining solids, but cementite's more complex crystal structure has higher vibrational entropy.

---

## Step 3 (Part b) — Compute $\Delta G^\circ_\text{rxn}$ at 298 K

$$\Delta G^\circ_\text{rxn} = \Delta H^\circ_\text{rxn} - T\,\Delta S^\circ_\text{rxn}$$

Convert $\Delta S^\circ$ to kJ: $+17.02 \text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1} = +0.01702 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$

$$\Delta G^\circ_{298} = +25.1 - (298)(0.01702)$$

$$= +25.1 - 5.07 = \boxed{+20.03 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}}$$

**Interpretation:** $\Delta G^\circ > 0$ at 298 K — cementite formation is **not spontaneous** at standard conditions. Iron and graphite are thermodynamically more stable than Fe$_3$C at room temperature.

---

## Step 4 (Part c) — Find crossover temperature $T^*$

At $T^*$, $\Delta G^\circ = 0$:

$$0 = \Delta H^\circ - T^*\,\Delta S^\circ$$

$$T^* = \frac{\Delta H^\circ}{\Delta S^\circ} = \frac{25{,}100 \text{ J mol}^{-1}}{17.02 \text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}}$$

$$\boxed{T^* \approx 1475 \text{ K} \approx 1202\,^\circ\text{C}}$$

Since $\Delta H^\circ > 0$ and $\Delta S^\circ > 0$ (top-right cell of the $\Delta H$/$\Delta S$ matrix from L3), the reaction is spontaneous **above** $T^*$. Cementite becomes thermodynamically stable only above ~1475 K.

However, note that in real Fe–C systems, cementite is often encountered at lower temperatures as a *metastable* phase — kinetics (diffusion) can trap it. This is the classic thermodynamic vs. kinetic distinction.

---

## Step 5 (Part d) — $\Delta G^\circ$ at 1000 K

Using the same $\Delta H^\circ$ and $\Delta S^\circ$ (approximated as temperature-independent):

$$\Delta G^\circ_{1000} = +25.1 - (1000)(0.01702)$$

$$= +25.1 - 17.02 = \boxed{+8.08 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}}$$

**Interpretation:** Still positive at 1000 K — cementite is **not thermodynamically stable** relative to Fe + graphite at 1000 K. The reaction would need to reach $T > 1475$ K for spontaneous formation. At 1000 K, the system favours reversal (Fe$_3$C → 3 Fe + C graphite). This is consistent with the Fe–C equilibrium phase diagram, where at 1000 K the equilibrium phases are ferrite/austenite plus graphite, not cementite (cementite is a metastable equilibrium phase in practice).
L3|medium.final_answer: (a) $\Delta H^\circ_\text{rxn} = +25.1$ kJ mol$^{-1}$; $\Delta S^\circ_\text{rxn} = +17.02$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$. (b) $\Delta G^\circ_{298} = +20.03$ kJ mol$^{-1}$ — not spontaneous at 298 K. (c) $T^* \approx 1475$ K; cementite is stable only above $T^*$. (d) $\Delta G^\circ_{1000} = +8.08$ kJ mol$^{-1}$ — cementite is thermodynamically unstable relative to Fe + graphite at 1000 K.
common_mistakes: **Forgetting to convert $\Delta S$ from J to kJ** before subtracting from $\Delta H$ in kJ — this gives an answer off by a factor of 1000 (e.g. $\Delta G \approx -17{,}000$ kJ instead of $+8$ kJ at 1000 K).

**Misidentifying the spontaneity direction above $T^*$:** because both $\Delta H > 0$ and $\Delta S > 0$, the reaction only becomes spontaneous at *high* temperature (entropy term wins), not low temperature. Students sometimes assume exothermic reactions are always spontaneous, or confuse which sign of $\Delta H$/$\Delta S$ leads to which temperature dependence.

**Treating the crossover temperature as the melting point or a phase-transition temperature** rather than recognising it as the $T$ where $\Delta G = 0$ — i.e. the thermodynamic stability boundary. Students may also overlook that kinetic factors (metastability) mean cementite can persist in steel well below $T^*$.

L3|hard.title: Entropy Change of Nitrogen Compression via Maxwell Relation
L3|hard.statement:
A materials processing facility uses nitrogen gas (treated as ideal, diatomic) in a sealed rigid heat-treatment chamber. In one stage of the process, the nitrogen is compressed **isothermally** at $T = 450\,\text{K}$ from an initial pressure of $P_1 = 2\,\text{bar}$ to a final pressure of $P_2 = 50\,\text{bar}$. The chamber contains $n = 3.5\,\text{mol}$ of N$_2$.

**(a)** Starting from the Gibbs free energy differential $\mathrm{d}G = V\,\mathrm{d}P - S\,\mathrm{d}T$, derive the Maxwell relation that allows you to compute $(\partial S/\partial P)_T$.

**(b)** Using the Maxwell relation derived in part (a) and the ideal-gas equation of state $PV = nRT$ (with $R = 8.314\,\text{J\,mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$), show that the isothermal entropy change of the nitrogen is:
$$\Delta S = -nR\ln\!\frac{P_2}{P_1}$$

**(c)** Calculate the numerical value of $\Delta S$ for this process.

**(d)** The Helmholtz free energy is defined as $F = U - TS$. Compute $\Delta F$ for the isothermal compression. For an ideal diatomic gas at constant temperature, $\Delta U = 0$. Is $\Delta F$ positive or negative, and what does its sign tell you about the spontaneity of the compression at constant $T$ and $V$?

**(e)** To restore the nitrogen to its original state, the gas is subsequently expanded isothermally and reversibly back to $P_1 = 2\,\text{bar}$ at $T = 450\,\text{K}$. What is the total entropy change of the **universe** for the full compression-then-expansion cycle? Justify your answer using the Second Law.
L3|hard.solution:
## Part (a) — Deriving the Maxwell relation from $\mathrm{d}G$

From the Gibbs free energy differential:
$$\mathrm{d}G = V\,\mathrm{d}P - S\,\mathrm{d}T$$

Reading off the coefficients:
$$\left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial P}\right)_T = V \qquad \text{and} \qquad \left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial T}\right)_P = -S$$

Since $G$ is a state function, its differential is exact, so the mixed second partial derivatives commute:
$$\frac{\partial^2 G}{\partial T\,\partial P} = \frac{\partial^2 G}{\partial P\,\partial T}$$

Applying this to the two first derivatives:
$$\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P = \frac{\partial}{\partial T}\left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial P}\right)_T \qquad \text{and} \qquad -\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial P}\right)_T = \frac{\partial}{\partial P}\left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial T}\right)_P$$

Equating the mixed partials:
$$\boxed{\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial P}\right)_T = -\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P}$$

This is the **Maxwell relation from the Gibbs potential**.

---

## Part (b) — Deriving $\Delta S = -nR\ln(P_2/P_1)$

For $n$ moles of ideal gas: $PV = nRT$, so:
$$V = \frac{nRT}{P}$$

Differentiate with respect to $T$ at constant $P$:
$$\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P = \frac{nR}{P}$$

Substitute into the Maxwell relation:
$$\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial P}\right)_T = -\frac{nR}{P}$$

Integrate at constant $T$ from $P_1$ to $P_2$:
$$\Delta S = \int_{P_1}^{P_2}\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial P}\right)_T \mathrm{d}P = \int_{P_1}^{P_2}\left(-\frac{nR}{P}\right)\mathrm{d}P = -nR\left[\ln P\right]_{P_1}^{P_2}$$

$$\boxed{\Delta S = -nR\ln\frac{P_2}{P_1}}$$

---

## Part (c) — Numerical value of $\Delta S$

Substituting values: $n = 3.5\,\text{mol}$, $R = 8.314\,\text{J\,mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$, $P_1 = 2\,\text{bar}$, $P_2 = 50\,\text{bar}$:

$$\ln\frac{P_2}{P_1} = \ln\frac{50}{2} = \ln 25 = 3.2189$$

$$\Delta S = -(3.5)(8.314)(3.2189)$$

$$\Delta S = -29.099 \times 3.2189$$

$$\boxed{\Delta S \approx -93.7\,\text{J\,K}^{-1}}$$

The entropy of the nitrogen **decreases** during isothermal compression, consistent with physical intuition: the gas is packed into a smaller effective volume of accessible microstates at higher pressure.

---

## Part (d) — Computing $\Delta F$ and interpreting its sign

From the definition $F = U - TS$:
$$\Delta F = \Delta U - \Delta(TS) = \Delta U - T\,\Delta S - S\,\Delta T$$

At **constant temperature** ($\Delta T = 0$):
$$\Delta F = \Delta U - T\,\Delta S$$

For an ideal gas at constant $T$: $\Delta U = 0$ (internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on $T$). Therefore:
$$\Delta F = -T\,\Delta S = -(450\,\text{K})\times(-93.7\,\text{J\,K}^{-1})$$

$$\boxed{\Delta F = +42{,}165\,\text{J} \approx +42.2\,\text{kJ}}$$

**Sign interpretation:** $\Delta F > 0$ at constant $T$ and $V$ means the process is **non-spontaneous** under those constraints — external work must be supplied to compress the gas. The compression does not occur on its own; it requires a piston or compressor to drive it. This is consistent with the Helmholtz criterion: a spontaneous process at constant $T, V$ requires $\Delta F < 0$.

---

## Part (e) — Total entropy change of the universe for the full cycle

The full cycle is: isothermal compression ($P_1 \to P_2$, at $T = 450\,\text{K}$) followed by isothermal **reversible** expansion ($P_2 \to P_1$, at $T = 450\,\text{K}$).

**Entropy is a state function.** After the complete cycle, the nitrogen returns exactly to its initial state $(P_1,\,T)$. Therefore:
$$\Delta S_\text{system, cycle} = 0$$

For the **surroundings**: each leg of the cycle involves heat exchange with the surroundings. During the reversible compression, the surroundings receive heat $|Q_\text{comp}|$; during the reversible expansion, the surroundings give back the same heat $|Q_\text{exp}|$. Since both steps are isothermal and **reversible**, the entropy change of the surroundings is exactly equal and opposite at each stage:
$$\Delta S_\text{surr, comp} = +93.7\,\text{J\,K}^{-1}, \qquad \Delta S_\text{surr, exp} = -93.7\,\text{J\,K}^{-1}$$

So over the full cycle:
$$\Delta S_\text{surr, cycle} = 0$$

By the Second Law, for the **universe**:
$$\Delta S_\text{universe, cycle} = \Delta S_\text{system} + \Delta S_\text{surr} = 0 + 0 = \boxed{0}$$

This confirms that **a fully reversible cycle generates no net entropy** — consistent with $\mathrm{d}S_\text{universe} = 0$ for every reversible step. The cycle neither violates nor exploits the Second Law; it is the theoretical ideal.
L3|hard.final_answer: (a) Maxwell relation: $(\partial S/\partial P)_T = -(\partial V/\partial T)_P$. (b) Derived as shown. (c) $\Delta S \approx -93.7\,\text{J\,K}^{-1}$. (d) $\Delta F \approx +42.2\,\text{kJ}$ (positive; process non-spontaneous at constant $T,V$). (e) $\Delta S_\text{universe, cycle} = 0$ (fully reversible cycle).
common_mistakes: **Forgetting the negative sign in the Maxwell relation.** Students often write $(\partial S/\partial P)_T = +(\partial V/\partial T)_P$ instead of the correct $-(\partial V/\partial T)_P$. The minus sign comes directly from the sign of $-S\,\mathrm{d}T$ in $\mathrm{d}G$, and dropping it reverses the sign of $\Delta S$, leading to a physically wrong result (positive $\Delta S$ for compression).

**Using $\Delta F = \Delta G$ or confusing the Helmholtz and Gibbs spontaneity criteria.** $\Delta F < 0$ governs spontaneity at constant $T$ and $V$, while $\Delta G < 0$ applies at constant $T$ and $P$. Since the compression changes $P$, students must use the Helmholtz criterion here. Applying $\Delta G$ directly to judge spontaneity at constant $V$ is conceptually incorrect.

**Claiming $\Delta S_\text{universe} = \Delta S_\text{system}$ for the cycle.** Some students forget to account for the surroundings and incorrectly conclude the universe entropy is zero simply because the system returns to its start. The correct reasoning is that each individual step is reversible, so $\mathrm{d}S_\text{universe} = 0$ at every instant, and both system and surroundings entropy changes cancel over the full cycle.

L3|hard.title: Gibbs Free Energy and Spontaneity of Iron Oxide Reduction
L3|hard.statement:
The reduction of magnetite by hydrogen gas is an important step in direct reduced iron (DRI) production:

$$\text{Fe}_3\text{O}_4(\text{s}) + 4\,\text{H}_2(\text{g}) \rightarrow 3\,\text{Fe}(\text{s}) + 4\,\text{H}_2\text{O}(\text{g})$$

The following thermodynamic data are given at 298 K and 1 atm:

| Species | $\Delta H_f^\circ$ (kJ mol$^{-1}$) | $S^\circ_{298}$ (J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Fe$_3$O$_4$(s) | $-$1118.4 | 146.4 |
| H$_2$(g) | 0 | 130.7 |
| Fe(s) | 0 | 27.3 |
| H$_2$O(g) | $-$241.8 | 188.7 |

The molar heat capacities (J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$) are:

| Species | $a$ | $b \times 10^{-3}$ (K$^{-1}$) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Fe$_3$O$_4$(s) | 91.6 | 201.6 |
| H$_2$(g) | 29.1 | $-$1.92 |
| Fe(s) | 37.3 | 6.19 |
| H$_2$O(g) | 30.4 | 9.61 |

**(a)** Calculate $\Delta H^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$ and $\Delta S^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$ at 298 K.

**(b)** Calculate $\Delta G^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$ at 298 K and determine whether the reaction is spontaneous under standard conditions.

**(c)** Using Kirchhoff's Law, calculate $\Delta H^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$ and $\Delta S^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$ at 900 K (all species remain in the same phase). Then calculate $\Delta G^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$ at 900 K.

**(d)** At approximately what temperature $T^*$ does the reaction change from non-spontaneous to spontaneous (i.e. $\Delta G^\circ_{\text{rxn}} = 0$)? Use a linearised estimate assuming $\Delta H^\circ$ and $\Delta S^\circ$ are approximately constant at their 298 K values.
L3|hard.solution:
## Part (a) — $\Delta H^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$ and $\Delta S^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$ at 298 K

Apply Hess's Law (products minus reactants, weighted by stoichiometry):

$$\Delta H^\circ_{\text{rxn}} = \left[3\Delta H_f^\circ(\text{Fe}) + 4\Delta H_f^\circ(\text{H}_2\text{O}(\text{g}))\right] - \left[\Delta H_f^\circ(\text{Fe}_3\text{O}_4) + 4\Delta H_f^\circ(\text{H}_2)\right]$$

$$= \left[3(0) + 4(-241.8)\right] - \left[(-1118.4) + 4(0)\right]$$

$$= -967.2 - (-1118.4) = \boxed{+151.2 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}}$$

The reaction is **endothermic** at 298 K.

For the entropy:

$$\Delta S^\circ_{\text{rxn}} = \left[3 S^\circ(\text{Fe}) + 4 S^\circ(\text{H}_2\text{O}(\text{g}))\right] - \left[S^\circ(\text{Fe}_3\text{O}_4) + 4 S^\circ(\text{H}_2)\right]$$

$$= \left[3(27.3) + 4(188.7)\right] - \left[146.4 + 4(130.7)\right]$$

$$= \left[81.9 + 754.8\right] - \left[146.4 + 522.8\right]$$

$$= 836.7 - 669.2 = \boxed{+167.5 \text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}}$$

The entropy **increases** (4 moles of gas consumed, 4 moles of gas produced — but the solid Fe$_3$O$_4$ is replaced by 3 moles of solid Fe releasing structural entropy).

---

## Part (b) — $\Delta G^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$ at 298 K

$$\Delta G^\circ_{\text{rxn}} = \Delta H^\circ_{\text{rxn}} - T\,\Delta S^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$$

$$= 151{,}200 - (298)(167.5)$$

$$= 151{,}200 - 49{,}915 = \boxed{+101{,}285 \text{ J mol}^{-1} \approx +101.3 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}}$$

$\Delta G^\circ > 0$ at 298 K: the reaction is **not spontaneous** under standard conditions at room temperature. The endothermic enthalpy term dominates the favourable entropy term at low temperature.

---

## Part (c) — $\Delta H^\circ$, $\Delta S^\circ$, $\Delta G^\circ$ at 900 K via Kirchhoff's Law

### Step 1: Assemble $\Delta C_P$

$$\Delta C_P = \left[3 C_P(\text{Fe}) + 4 C_P(\text{H}_2\text{O})\right] - \left[C_P(\text{Fe}_3\text{O}_4) + 4 C_P(\text{H}_2)\right]$$

**Constant terms ($a$):**

$$a_{\text{net}} = 3(37.3) + 4(30.4) - 91.6 - 4(29.1)$$
$$= 111.9 + 121.6 - 91.6 - 116.4 = +25.5 \text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$$

**Linear terms ($b \times 10^{-3}$, in K$^{-1}$):**

$$b_{\text{net}} = \left[3(6.19) + 4(9.61) - 201.6 - 4(-1.92)\right] \times 10^{-3}$$
$$= \left[18.57 + 38.44 - 201.6 + 7.68\right] \times 10^{-3}$$
$$= -136.91 \times 10^{-3} \text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-2}$$

So: $\Delta C_P(T) = 25.5 - 0.13691\,T$ (J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$)

### Step 2: Kirchhoff for $\Delta H^\circ$ at 900 K

$$\Delta H^\circ(900) = \Delta H^\circ(298) + \int_{298}^{900} \Delta C_P\,\mathrm{d}T$$

$$= 151{,}200 + \int_{298}^{900}\left(25.5 - 0.13691\,T\right)\mathrm{d}T$$

$$= 151{,}200 + \left[25.5(900 - 298) - \frac{0.13691}{2}(900^2 - 298^2)\right]$$

$$= 151{,}200 + \left[25.5(602) - 0.068455(810{,}000 - 88{,}804)\right]$$

$$= 151{,}200 + \left[15{,}351 - 0.068455 \times 721{,}196\right]$$

$$= 151{,}200 + \left[15{,}351 - 49{,}364\right]$$

$$= 151{,}200 - 34{,}013 = \boxed{+117{,}187 \text{ J mol}^{-1} \approx +117.2 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}}$$

### Step 3: Kirchhoff for $\Delta S^\circ$ at 900 K

$$\Delta S^\circ(900) = \Delta S^\circ(298) + \int_{298}^{900} \frac{\Delta C_P}{T}\,\mathrm{d}T$$

$$= 167.5 + \int_{298}^{900}\left(\frac{25.5}{T} - 0.13691\right)\mathrm{d}T$$

$$= 167.5 + \left[25.5\ln\frac{900}{298} - 0.13691(900 - 298)\right]$$

$$= 167.5 + \left[25.5 \times 1.1054 - 0.13691 \times 602\right]$$

$$= 167.5 + \left[28.19 - 82.42\right]$$

$$= 167.5 - 54.23 = \boxed{+113.3 \text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}}$$

### Step 4: $\Delta G^\circ$ at 900 K

$$\Delta G^\circ(900) = \Delta H^\circ(900) - T\,\Delta S^\circ(900)$$

$$= 117{,}187 - (900)(113.3)$$

$$= 117{,}187 - 101{,}970 = \boxed{+15{,}217 \text{ J mol}^{-1} \approx +15.2 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}}$$

Still positive but **much smaller** than at 298 K — the reaction is approaching spontaneity.

---

## Part (d) — Crossover temperature $T^*$

Using the linearised (298 K) values to estimate when $\Delta G^\circ = 0$:

$$\Delta G^\circ \approx \Delta H^\circ_{298} - T^*\,\Delta S^\circ_{298} = 0$$

$$T^* = \frac{\Delta H^\circ_{298}}{\Delta S^\circ_{298}} = \frac{151{,}200 \text{ J mol}^{-1}}{167.5 \text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}} = \boxed{902 \text{ K} \approx 629\,^\circ\text{C}}$$

The Kirchhoff-corrected values at 900 K gave $\Delta G^\circ \approx +15$ kJ mol$^{-1}$, confirming that the true crossover is slightly above 900 K — consistent with this estimate. The linearised approximation is reliable here because the correction from $\Delta C_P$ partially cancels (both $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ decreased).

**Physical interpretation:** DRI plants operate at 800–1050 °C (1073–1323 K), well above $T^*$. This ensures $\Delta G^\circ < 0$, driving reduction of magnetite to iron. Below ~900 K, hydrogen reduction of Fe$_3$O$_4$ is thermodynamically disfavoured under standard conditions.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to multiply stoichiometric coefficients when computing $\Delta H^\circ$ and $\Delta S^\circ$: e.g. using $S^\circ(\text{H}_2\text{O})$ once instead of $4 \times 188.7$ for the four moles produced.

Using $\Delta G^\circ = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ$ with $\Delta S^\circ$ in J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$ while $\Delta H^\circ$ is in kJ mol$^{-1}$, giving an answer off by a factor of 1000. Always convert to consistent units (both in J or both in kJ) before combining.

When applying Kirchhoff for entropy, using $\int \Delta C_P\,\mathrm{d}T$ (the enthalpy integral) instead of $\int (\Delta C_P / T)\,\mathrm{d}T$ — forgetting the factor of $1/T$ that distinguishes the entropy Kirchhoff from the enthalpy Kirchhoff.

L3|hard.title: Maxwell Relation & Pressure-Dependent Entropy of an Ideal Gas Mixture
L3|hard.statement:
A sealed, rigid furnace atmosphere vessel contains a binary gas mixture of nitrogen (N$_2$) and argon (Ar) behaving as ideal gases. The mole fractions are $X_{\mathrm{N_2}} = 0.70$ and $X_{\mathrm{Ar}} = 0.30$. The vessel initially holds the mixture at $T = 1200\,\mathrm{K}$ and total pressure $P_1 = 2\,\mathrm{atm}$. A high-pressure injection system then isothermally raises the total pressure to $P_2 = 20\,\mathrm{atm}$ at the same temperature.

**(a)** Starting from the Gibbs free energy differential $\mathrm{d}G = V\,\mathrm{d}P - S\,\mathrm{d}T$, derive the Maxwell relation that gives $\left(\partial S/\partial P\right)_T$ in terms of a measurable $P$–$V$–$T$ quantity. State clearly what mathematical property of state functions you invoke.

**(b)** For 3 mol of an ideal gas, show that the molar entropy change under isothermal compression from $P_1$ to $P_2$ is
$$\Delta S = -nR\ln\frac{P_2}{P_1}$$
where $n$ is the number of moles and $R = 8.314\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$.

**(c)** Treating N$_2$ and Ar as an ideal gas mixture, calculate the **total** entropy change $\Delta S_\mathrm{mix}$ when the entire mixture (3 mol total) is compressed isothermally from $P_1 = 2\,\mathrm{atm}$ to $P_2 = 20\,\mathrm{atm}$ at $T = 1200\,\mathrm{K}$.

**(d)** The Helmholtz free energy is defined as $F \equiv U - TS$. At constant temperature, explain — using the differential $\mathrm{d}F = -S\,\mathrm{d}T - P\,\mathrm{d}V$ — why $\Delta F < 0$ is **not** the correct spontaneity criterion for this isothermal compression (which occurs at constant volume in a rigid vessel). State the correct criterion and evaluate $\Delta G^\circ$ for the compression process, given that $\Delta H = 0$ for an ideal gas compressed isothermally.

**Data:** $R = 8.314\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$; $n_\mathrm{total} = 3\,\mathrm{mol}$; ideal gas behaviour throughout.
L3|hard.solution:
## Part (a) — Deriving the Maxwell Relation from $\mathrm{d}G$

**Starting point:**
$$\mathrm{d}G = V\,\mathrm{d}P - S\,\mathrm{d}T$$

This identifies $G$ as a function of its **natural variables** $T$ and $P$, so:
$$\left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial P}\right)_T = V \qquad \text{and} \qquad \left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial T}\right)_P = -S$$

**Mathematical property invoked:** Because $G$ is a **state function**, its differential is **exact**. For an exact differential $\mathrm{d}G = M\,\mathrm{d}P + N\,\mathrm{d}T$, mixed second partial derivatives must be equal (Schwarz/Clairaut's theorem):
$$\frac{\partial^2 G}{\partial T\,\partial P} = \frac{\partial^2 G}{\partial P\,\partial T}$$

Applying this:
$$\frac{\partial}{\partial T}\left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial P}\right)_T = \frac{\partial}{\partial P}\left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial T}\right)_P$$
$$\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P = \left(\frac{\partial(-S)}{\partial P}\right)_T$$
$$\boxed{\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial P}\right)_T = -\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P}$$

This Maxwell relation links the unmeasurable $\left(\partial S/\partial P\right)_T$ to the measurable volumetric thermal expansion $\left(\partial V/\partial T\right)_P$.

---

## Part (b) — Isothermal Entropy Change of an Ideal Gas

From the Maxwell relation derived in (a), at constant $T$:
$$\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial P}\right)_T = -\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P$$

For $n$ moles of an ideal gas, $PV = nRT$, so:
$$V = \frac{nRT}{P} \implies \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P = \frac{nR}{P}$$

Substituting:
$$\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial P}\right)_T = -\frac{nR}{P}$$

Integrating at constant $T$ from $P_1$ to $P_2$:
$$\Delta S = \int_{P_1}^{P_2} \left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial P}\right)_T \mathrm{d}P = \int_{P_1}^{P_2} \left(-\frac{nR}{P}\right)\mathrm{d}P$$
$$\boxed{\Delta S = -nR\ln\frac{P_2}{P_1}}$$

Since $P_2 > P_1$, $\ln(P_2/P_1) > 0$, so $\Delta S < 0$ — compression decreases entropy, consistent with fewer accessible microstates at higher pressure.

---

## Part (c) — Total Entropy Change of the Mixture

For an **ideal gas mixture**, each component behaves independently and responds to its own **partial pressure**. The partial pressure of component $i$ is $p_i = X_i P$, so when total pressure changes from $P_1$ to $P_2$ at constant $T$ and constant composition:
$$p_i^{(1)} = X_i P_1 \qquad \text{and} \qquad p_i^{(2)} = X_i P_2$$
$$\frac{p_i^{(2)}}{p_i^{(1)}} = \frac{X_i P_2}{X_i P_1} = \frac{P_2}{P_1}$$

The mole fractions cancel — the ratio of partial pressures equals the ratio of total pressures. Therefore the entropy change formula applies directly to the full mixture:

**For N$_2$:** $n_{\mathrm{N_2}} = 0.70 \times 3 = 2.10\,\mathrm{mol}$
$$\Delta S_{\mathrm{N_2}} = -n_{\mathrm{N_2}} R \ln\frac{P_2}{P_1} = -(2.10)(8.314)\ln\frac{20}{2}$$
$$= -(2.10)(8.314)(2.3026) = -40.21\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$$

**For Ar:** $n_{\mathrm{Ar}} = 0.30 \times 3 = 0.90\,\mathrm{mol}$
$$\Delta S_{\mathrm{Ar}} = -(0.90)(8.314)\ln\frac{20}{2}$$
$$= -(0.90)(8.314)(2.3026) = -17.23\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$$

**Total entropy change:**
$$\Delta S_\mathrm{mix} = \Delta S_{\mathrm{N_2}} + \Delta S_{\mathrm{Ar}} = -40.21 + (-17.23)$$
$$\boxed{\Delta S_\mathrm{mix} = -57.44\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}}$$

**Verification using total moles directly:**
$$\Delta S = -n_\mathrm{total}\,R\ln\frac{P_2}{P_1} = -(3.00)(8.314)(2.3026) = -57.44\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}} \checkmark$$

---

## Part (d) — Correct Spontaneity Criterion and $\Delta G$

**Why $\Delta F < 0$ is not the correct criterion here:**

From $\mathrm{d}F = -S\,\mathrm{d}T - P\,\mathrm{d}V$, the natural variables of $F$ are **$T$ and $V$**. The criterion $\Delta F < 0$ governs spontaneity only at **constant $T$ and constant $V$** (rigid, isothermal system). 

However, the compression is an externally **driven** process — the injection system does work on the gas, raising pressure at constant $T$. The system does **not** evolve spontaneously; external work is being supplied. Furthermore, identifying the correct spontaneity criterion depends on the constraints:

- Constant $T$, constant $P$: use $\Delta G < 0$ (Gibbs)
- Constant $T$, constant $V$: use $\Delta F < 0$ (Helmholtz)

Since the pressure is changing (not constant), neither $G$ nor $F$ alone serves as a simple spontaneity criterion for the work-driven compression. What matters thermodynamically is $\Delta G$ of the process, which equals the minimum non-$PV$ work required.

**Computing $\Delta G$ for the isothermal compression:**

From $\mathrm{d}G = V\,\mathrm{d}P - S\,\mathrm{d}T$ at constant $T$:
$$\Delta G = \int_{P_1}^{P_2} V\,\mathrm{d}P = \int_{P_1}^{P_2} \frac{nRT}{P}\,\mathrm{d}P = nRT\ln\frac{P_2}{P_1}$$

Alternatively, using $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$. For an ideal gas at constant $T$, $\Delta H = 0$ (internal energy and enthalpy depend only on $T$), so:
$$\Delta G = 0 - T\Delta S = -(1200)(-57.44)$$
$$\boxed{\Delta G = +68{,}928\,\mathrm{J} \approx +68.9\,\mathrm{kJ}}$$

$\Delta G > 0$ confirms that the compression is **non-spontaneous** — it requires external work input from the injection system, which is physically expected. The surroundings must do work on the system to raise its pressure. The minimum reversible work required equals $+\Delta G = 68.9\,\mathrm{kJ}$.
common_mistakes: Forgetting that mole fractions cancel in the partial-pressure ratio — students sometimes try to use $p_i = X_i P$ in the logarithm, computing separate $\ln(X_i P_2 / X_i P_1)$ terms and then getting confused, when in fact the ratio simplifies to $P_2/P_1$ and the whole-mixture formula $\Delta S = -nR\ln(P_2/P_1)$ applies directly.

Applying $\Delta F < 0$ as the spontaneity criterion because the vessel is rigid (constant $V$) and isothermal — students miss that a driven compression is not a spontaneous process, and that the correct question is how much work must be supplied ($\Delta G$), not whether $\Delta F$ is negative.

Using $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$ but forgetting that $\Delta H = 0$ for an ideal gas under isothermal conditions, and instead trying to compute $\Delta H$ from heat capacity data — no temperature change occurs, so $\Delta H = 0$ exactly for an ideal gas.

L3|hard.title: Metastability of Wüstite: Gibbs Free Energy and Maxwell Entropy–Pressure Relation
L3|hard.statement:
Wüstite (FeO, solid) is a nominally metastable iron oxide at room temperature that is important in blast-furnace thermodynamics. In this problem you will (a) decide whether the disproportionation of wüstite is thermodynamically spontaneous at 298 K and 1 atm, and then (b) use a Maxwell relation to estimate how much the molar entropy of solid FeO changes when the pressure in a reactor is raised isothermally from 1 atm to 50 atm at 298 K.

**Thermodynamic data at 298 K, 1 atm:**

| Species | $\Delta H_f^\circ$ (kJ mol$^{-1}$) | $S^\circ_{298}$ (J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$) |
|---|---:|---:|
| FeO(s) | $-272.0$ | $60.75$ |
| Fe(s) | $0$ | $27.28$ |
| Fe$_3$O$_4$(s) | $-1118.4$ | $146.44$ |

**Physical data for solid FeO:**
- Molar mass: $71.85$ g mol$^{-1}$
- Density: $5740$ kg m$^{-3}$
- Linear thermal expansion coefficient: $\alpha_L = 12.0 \times 10^{-6}$ K$^{-1}$

**Part (a):** The disproportionation reaction is
$$4\,\text{FeO(s)} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{Fe(s)} + \text{Fe}_3\text{O}_4\text{(s)}$$
Compute $\Delta H^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$, $\Delta S^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$, and $\Delta G^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$ at 298 K. State whether the reaction is spontaneous and classify the system as being in the exothermic/endothermic and entropy-increase/decrease categories.

**Part (b):** Using the Maxwell relation derived from the Gibbs free energy, calculate the molar entropy change $\Delta S_T$ of solid FeO when the pressure is raised isothermally from $P_1 = 1$ atm to $P_2 = 50$ atm at 298 K. Comment on the physical significance of the result.
L3|hard.solution:
## Part (a) — Spontaneity of FeO Disproportionation

### Step 1 — Standard enthalpy of reaction (Hess's Law)

Products minus reactants, weighted by stoichiometric coefficients:

$$\Delta H^\circ_{\text{rxn}} = \left[\Delta H_f^\circ(\text{Fe}) + \Delta H_f^\circ(\text{Fe}_3\text{O}_4)\right] - \left[4\,\Delta H_f^\circ(\text{FeO})\right]$$

$$= \left[0 + (-1118.4)\right] - \left[4 \times (-272.0)\right]$$

$$= -1118.4 - (-1088.0) = \boxed{-30.4 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}}$$

The reaction is **exothermic** ($\Delta H^\circ < 0$).

### Step 2 — Standard entropy of reaction

$$\Delta S^\circ_{\text{rxn}} = \left[S^\circ(\text{Fe}) + S^\circ(\text{Fe}_3\text{O}_4)\right] - \left[4\,S^\circ(\text{FeO})\right]$$

$$= \left[27.28 + 146.44\right] - \left[4 \times 60.75\right]$$

$$= 173.72 - 243.00 = \boxed{-69.28 \text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}}$$

The reaction **decreases** the system entropy ($\Delta S^\circ < 0$). This is physically reasonable: four formula units of FeO (more atoms, more configurations) condense into one Fe plus one Fe$_3$O$_4$, reducing the number of independent structural units.

### Step 3 — Standard Gibbs free energy at 298 K

$$\Delta G^\circ_{\text{rxn}} = \Delta H^\circ_{\text{rxn}} - T\,\Delta S^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$$

Convert $\Delta S^\circ$ to kJ: $-69.28\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1} = -0.06928\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$.

$$\Delta G^\circ_{298} = -30.4 - (298)(-0.06928)$$

$$= -30.4 + 20.65 = \boxed{-9.75 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}}$$

### Step 4 — Interpretation

$\Delta G^\circ_{298} < 0$: the disproportionation is **thermodynamically spontaneous** at 298 K, 1 atm. This places wüstite in the **exothermic + entropy-decreasing** quadrant of the $\Delta H$–$\Delta S$ matrix (spontaneous only at low enough $T$, because $T\Delta S$ is less negative than $\Delta H$). The cross-over temperature at which $\Delta G = 0$ is

$$T^* = \frac{\Delta H^\circ}{\Delta S^\circ} = \frac{-30{,}400}{-69.28} \approx 439\text{ K}$$

Above ~439 K the entropy penalty wins and the disproportionation becomes non-spontaneous — wüstite is thermodynamically stable above this temperature (consistent with its importance at blast-furnace temperatures of 900–1500 °C). Its persistence at room temperature is a kinetic phenomenon (activation barrier for solid-state diffusion).

---

## Part (b) — Maxwell Relation: Entropy Change with Pressure

### Step 1 — Identify the correct Maxwell relation

From the Gibbs free energy differential:

$$\mathrm{d}G = V\,\mathrm{d}P - S\,\mathrm{d}T$$

Since $G$ is a state function its mixed second partials commute:

$$\frac{\partial^2 G}{\partial T\,\partial P} = \frac{\partial^2 G}{\partial P\,\partial T}$$

which gives the Maxwell relation:

$$\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial P}\right)_T = -\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P$$

### Step 2 — Evaluate $(\partial V/\partial T)_P$ for solid FeO

The volumetric thermal expansion coefficient is $\alpha_V = 3\alpha_L$ for an isotropic solid (since $V \propto L^3$, fractional volume change = 3 × fractional length change):

$$\alpha_V = 3 \times 12.0 \times 10^{-6} = 36.0 \times 10^{-6}\text{ K}^{-1}$$

By definition $\alpha_V = \frac{1}{V}\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P$, so

$$\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P = \alpha_V\,V_m$$

where $V_m$ is the molar volume of FeO:

$$V_m = \frac{M}{\rho} = \frac{71.85 \times 10^{-3}\text{ kg mol}^{-1}}{5740\text{ kg m}^{-3}} = 1.251 \times 10^{-5}\text{ m}^3\text{ mol}^{-1}$$

$$\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P = 36.0 \times 10^{-6} \times 1.251 \times 10^{-5} = 4.504 \times 10^{-10}\text{ m}^3\text{ mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

### Step 3 — Integrate the Maxwell relation at constant T

$$\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial P}\right)_T = -\alpha_V V_m = -4.504 \times 10^{-10}\text{ m}^3\text{ mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

For a solid, $\alpha_V$ and $V_m$ are essentially pressure-independent (solids are nearly incompressible), so the partial derivative is constant and we integrate directly:

$$\Delta S_T = \int_{P_1}^{P_2}\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial P}\right)_T\mathrm{d}P = -\alpha_V V_m\,(P_2 - P_1)$$

Convert the pressure difference to SI: $\Delta P = (50 - 1)\text{ atm} = 49 \times 1.013 \times 10^5\text{ Pa} = 4.964 \times 10^6\text{ Pa}$.

$$\Delta S_T = -(4.504 \times 10^{-10})(4.964 \times 10^6)$$

$$\boxed{\Delta S_T \approx -2.24 \times 10^{-3}\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}}$$

### Step 4 — Physical significance

The molar entropy of solid FeO decreases by only $2.24 \times 10^{-3}$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$ when pressurised from 1 to 50 atm — a reduction of about **0.004%** relative to $S^\circ_{298} = 60.75$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$. This is negligibly small compared to the $\Delta S^\circ_{\text{rxn}} = -69.28$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$ computed in Part (a). The physical reason is that solids have very small molar volumes and very small thermal expansion, so squeezing them changes their entropy far less than compressing a gas (compare: 1 mol of an ideal gas compressed 50× isothermally gives $\Delta S = -R\ln 50 \approx -32$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$, six orders of magnitude larger). In practice, modest pressures of tens of atm have negligible influence on the thermodynamics of solid-state reactions involving only condensed phases.
L3|hard.final_answer: Part (a): $\Delta H^\circ_{\text{rxn}} = -30.4$ kJ mol$^{-1}$; $\Delta S^\circ_{\text{rxn}} = -69.28$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$; $\Delta G^\circ_{298} = -9.75$ kJ mol$^{-1}$ — reaction is spontaneous (exothermic, entropy-decreasing; spontaneous below $T^* \approx 439$ K). Part (b): $\Delta S_T \approx -2.24 \times 10^{-3}$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$ (negligibly small).
common_mistakes: Using $\Delta S^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$ directly in kJ without converting units before computing $T\Delta S$ — multiplying kJ mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ by K correctly requires matching units with $\Delta H$ in kJ, a step students frequently skip, leading to answers off by a factor of 1000.

Applying the Maxwell relation $\left(\partial S/\partial P\right)_T = -\left(\partial V/\partial T\right)_P$ but forgetting to convert $\alpha_L$ to $\alpha_V$ (i.e., omitting the factor of 3 for an isotropic solid), which underestimates the result by a factor of three.

Concluding that because $\Delta G^\circ_{298} < 0$ the reaction proceeds rapidly at room temperature — confusing thermodynamic spontaneity with kinetic feasibility; the disproportionation is thermodynamically allowed but kinetically frozen at room temperature due to the large activation energy for solid-state ionic diffusion.

L3|hard.title: Pressure-Induced Entropy Change in Liquid Copper via Maxwell Relation
L3|hard.statement:
Liquid copper at 1400 K is held in a sealed, thermally insulated crucible. A hydraulic press isothermally increases the external pressure on the melt from $P_1 = 1\,\text{atm}$ to $P_2 = 500\,\text{atm}$ ($1\,\text{atm} = 1.013 \times 10^5\,\text{Pa}$).

The following data for liquid copper at 1400 K are given:
- Molar mass: $M = 63.55\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$
- Density of liquid Cu at 1400 K: $\rho = 7.96\,\text{g cm}^{-3}$
- Linear coefficient of thermal expansion: $\alpha_L = 1.67 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{K}^{-1}$
- Volume coefficient of thermal expansion: $\alpha_V = 3\alpha_L$

**(a)** Starting from the Gibbs free energy differential $\mathrm{d}G = -S\,\mathrm{d}T + V\,\mathrm{d}P$, derive the Maxwell relation that relates $\left(\partial S/\partial P\right)_T$ to a measurable quantity.

**(b)** Calculate the molar volume $\underline{V}$ of liquid copper at 1400 K.

**(c)** Calculate the molar entropy change $\Delta S$ of the liquid copper when the pressure increases isothermally from 1 atm to 500 atm. State whether entropy increases or decreases and explain physically why.

**(d)** For this isothermal pressurisation, compute the corresponding change in molar Gibbs free energy $\Delta G$ using $\mathrm{d}G = V\,\mathrm{d}P$ (at constant $T$). Treat $\underline{V}$ as constant (liquid copper is nearly incompressible). Express your answer in J mol$^{-1}$.
L3|hard.solution:
## Part (a) — Deriving the Maxwell Relation from $\mathrm{d}G$

The fundamental differential of the Gibbs free energy for a closed system is:
$$\mathrm{d}G = -S\,\mathrm{d}T + V\,\mathrm{d}P$$

Because $G$ is a state function, its differential is **exact**. Reading off the partial derivatives:
$$\left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial T}\right)_P = -S \qquad \text{and} \qquad \left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial P}\right)_T = V$$

For an exact differential $\mathrm{d}G = M\,\mathrm{d}T + N\,\mathrm{d}P$, the exactness condition requires:
$$\left(\frac{\partial M}{\partial P}\right)_T = \left(\frac{\partial N}{\partial T}\right)_P$$

Applying this with $M = -S$ and $N = V$:
$$\left(\frac{\partial(-S)}{\partial P}\right)_T = \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P$$

$$\boxed{\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial P}\right)_T = -\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P}$$

The right-hand side is directly related to the volumetric thermal expansion coefficient $\alpha_V \equiv \dfrac{1}{V}\left(\dfrac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P$, so:
$$\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial P}\right)_T = -V\alpha_V$$

This Maxwell relation converts an unmeasurable entropy derivative into a quantity obtainable from thermal expansion measurements.

---

## Part (b) — Molar Volume of Liquid Copper

The molar volume is:
$$\underline{V} = \frac{M}{\rho}$$

Convert density to SI units: $\rho = 7.96\,\text{g cm}^{-3} = 7.96 \times 10^6\,\text{g m}^{-3} = 7960\,\text{kg m}^{-3}$

Convert molar mass: $M = 63.55\,\text{g mol}^{-1} = 63.55 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{kg mol}^{-1}$

$$\underline{V} = \frac{63.55 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{kg mol}^{-1}}{7960\,\text{kg m}^{-3}} = 7.986 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{m}^3\text{ mol}^{-1}$$

$$\boxed{\underline{V} \approx 7.99 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{m}^3\text{ mol}^{-1}}$$

---

## Part (c) — Molar Entropy Change Under Isothermal Pressurisation

From the Maxwell relation derived in Part (a), at constant $T$:
$$\mathrm{d}S = -V\alpha_V\,\mathrm{d}P$$

Integrating from $P_1$ to $P_2$, treating $V$ and $\alpha_V$ as approximately constant (liquid copper is nearly incompressible over this modest pressure range):
$$\Delta S = -V\alpha_V \int_{P_1}^{P_2} \mathrm{d}P = -\underline{V}\,\alpha_V\,(P_2 - P_1)$$

**Calculate $\alpha_V$:**
$$\alpha_V = 3\alpha_L = 3 \times 1.67 \times 10^{-5} = 5.01 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{K}^{-1}$$

**Calculate pressure difference in Pa:**
$$\Delta P = P_2 - P_1 = (500 - 1)\,\text{atm} = 499\,\text{atm} \times 1.013 \times 10^5\,\text{Pa atm}^{-1}$$
$$\Delta P = 5.055 \times 10^7\,\text{Pa}$$

**Substitute:**
$$\Delta S = -(7.986 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{m}^3\text{ mol}^{-1}) \times (5.01 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{K}^{-1}) \times (5.055 \times 10^7\,\text{Pa})$$

$$\Delta S = -(7.986 \times 10^{-6}) \times (5.01 \times 10^{-5}) \times (5.055 \times 10^7)\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

Step by step:
- $7.986 \times 10^{-6} \times 5.01 \times 10^{-5} = 4.001 \times 10^{-10}$
- $4.001 \times 10^{-10} \times 5.055 \times 10^{7} = 2.023 \times 10^{-2}$

$$\boxed{\Delta S \approx -2.02 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}}$$

**Entropy decreases.** Physically: compressing a liquid reduces its volume and forces the atoms into a smaller, more constrained configuration space — there are fewer accessible microstates ($\Omega$ falls), and by $S = k_B \ln \Omega$, entropy must fall. The negative sign in the Maxwell relation ($\partial S/\partial P)_T = -V\alpha_V < 0$ for a normally-expanding material with $\alpha_V > 0$) captures this directly.

---

## Part (d) — Change in Molar Gibbs Free Energy

At constant temperature, the Gibbs differential reduces to:
$$\mathrm{d}G = V\,\mathrm{d}P$$

Integrating with $\underline{V}$ constant:
$$\Delta G = \underline{V}\,(P_2 - P_1) = \underline{V}\,\Delta P$$

$$\Delta G = (7.986 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{m}^3\text{ mol}^{-1}) \times (5.055 \times 10^7\,\text{Pa})$$

$$\Delta G = 7.986 \times 10^{-6} \times 5.055 \times 10^7\,\text{J mol}^{-1}$$

$$\Delta G = 403.7\,\text{J mol}^{-1}$$

$$\boxed{\Delta G \approx +404\,\text{J mol}^{-1}}$$

**Interpretation:** $\Delta G > 0$ — pressurising a liquid at constant temperature raises its Gibbs free energy. This makes sense: the liquid is being pushed to a higher-energy (higher-$\mu$) state. If this pressurised liquid were placed in contact with an unpressurised vapour, the elevated $\mu$ of the liquid would drive evaporation (the Kelvin-equation effect from L4). The increase in $G$ is small (~404 J mol$^{-1}$) relative to typical reaction Gibbs energies (tens of kJ mol$^{-1}$), consistent with the near-incompressibility of liquids.

**Consistency check:** We can verify using $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$. At constant $T$ and nearly constant $V$, the enthalpy change is $\Delta H \approx \Delta U + V\Delta P \approx V\Delta P + V\Delta P\cdot\text{(small correction)} \approx \Delta G + T\Delta S = 404 + 1400\times(-0.0202) = 404 - 28.3 = 375.7\,\text{J mol}^{-1}$, which is $\Delta U + V\Delta P$ as expected. The enthalpy change is slightly less than $\Delta G$ because the entropy term $T\Delta S < 0$ acts to partially offset $G$.
L3|hard.final_answer: (a) $\left(\partial S/\partial P\right)_T = -\left(\partial V/\partial T\right)_P = -V\alpha_V$; (b) $\underline{V} \approx 7.99 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{m}^3\text{ mol}^{-1}$; (c) $\Delta S \approx -2.02 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$ (entropy decreases); (d) $\Delta G \approx +404\,\text{J mol}^{-1}$
common_mistakes: **Using $\alpha_L$ instead of $\alpha_V$** in the Maxwell relation. The relation $\left(\partial S/\partial P\right)_T = -V\alpha_V$ requires the *volumetric* expansion coefficient. Students often substitute $\alpha_L$ directly, underestimating the entropy change by a factor of 3. Always convert: $\alpha_V = 3\alpha_L$ for an isotropic material.

**Forgetting the unit conversion from atm to Pa** before computing $\Delta P$. Substituting $\Delta P = 499\,\text{atm}$ without converting gives an answer in wrong units (appearing ~$10^5$ times too small). Always convert pressure to SI (Pa) when using SI values for $\underline{V}$ in m$^3$ mol$^{-1}$.

**Confusing the sign of $\Delta G$ with spontaneity at constant $T$ and $P$.** Students sometimes see $\Delta G > 0$ and conclude 'the process cannot occur', forgetting that $\Delta G > 0$ simply means external work (from the hydraulic press) must be supplied to drive the pressurisation — it is not a freely spontaneous process. The $\Delta G < 0$ criterion applies only to processes that happen without external mechanical input.

L3|hard.title: Spontaneity Crossover Temperature for MnO Reduction by CO
L3|hard.statement:
The reduction of manganese oxide by carbon monoxide is written as:

$$\text{MnO(s)} + \text{CO(g)} \rightarrow \text{Mn(s)} + \text{CO}_2(\text{g})$$

Use the thermodynamic data below to answer the following:

| Species | $\Delta H_f^\circ$ (kJ/mol) | $S^\circ_{298}$ (J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$) |
|---|---:|---:|
| MnO(s) | $-385.2$ | $59.71$ |
| CO(g) | $-110.5$ | $197.67$ |
| Mn(s) | $0$ | $32.01$ |
| CO$_2$(g) | $-393.5$ | $213.74$ |

**(a)** Compute $\Delta H^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$, $\Delta S^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$, and $\Delta G^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$ at 298 K.

**(b)** Classify the reaction in the $\Delta H$–$\Delta S$ spontaneity matrix and find the **crossover temperature** $T^*$ at which $\Delta G^\circ_{\text{rxn}} = 0$ (i.e. the temperature below which the forward reaction becomes spontaneous, assuming $\Delta H^\circ$ and $\Delta S^\circ$ are approximately independent of temperature).

**(c)** At 900 K, a gas mixture is flowing over MnO pellets. The partial pressures are $P_{\text{CO}} = 0.80\,\text{atm}$ and $P_{\text{CO}_2} = 0.05\,\text{atm}$. Using the value of $\Delta G^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$ extrapolated to 900 K via $\Delta G^\circ(T) \approx \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ$, compute the **reaction quotient** $Q$, then evaluate $\Delta G_{\text{rxn}}$ and determine whether the reaction proceeds forward, backward, or is at equilibrium. ($R = 8.314\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$)
L3|hard.solution:
## Step 1 — Standard enthalpy of reaction (Hess's Law)

Products minus reactants, each weighted by stoichiometric coefficient:

$$\Delta H^\circ_{\text{rxn}} = \left[\Delta H_f^\circ(\text{Mn}) + \Delta H_f^\circ(\text{CO}_2)\right] - \left[\Delta H_f^\circ(\text{MnO}) + \Delta H_f^\circ(\text{CO})\right]$$

$$= \left[0 + (-393.5)\right] - \left[(-385.2) + (-110.5)\right]$$

$$= -393.5 - (-495.7) = \boxed{+102.2\,\text{kJ/mol}}$$

The reaction is **endothermic** at standard state.

---

## Step 2 — Standard entropy of reaction

$$\Delta S^\circ_{\text{rxn}} = \left[S^\circ(\text{Mn}) + S^\circ(\text{CO}_2)\right] - \left[S^\circ(\text{MnO}) + S^\circ(\text{CO})\right]$$

$$= \left[32.01 + 213.74\right] - \left[59.71 + 197.67\right]$$

$$= 245.75 - 257.38 = \boxed{-11.63\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}}$$

The reaction **decreases** entropy of the system. Both gas-phase species are present in equal numbers on each side (1 mol gas in, 1 mol gas out), but CO$_2$ has lower molar entropy than CO at the same temperature, making $\Delta S^\circ < 0$.

---

## Step 3 — Standard Gibbs free energy at 298 K

$$\Delta G^\circ_{298} = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ$$

$$= 102{,}200\,\text{J/mol} - (298)(-11.63\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1})$$

$$= 102{,}200 + 3{,}466 = \boxed{+105{,}666\,\text{J/mol} \approx +105.7\,\text{kJ/mol}}$$

$\Delta G^\circ_{298} > 0$: the forward reaction is **non-spontaneous** at 298 K and standard conditions.

---

## Part (b) — Spontaneity matrix classification and crossover temperature

| | |
|---|---|
| $\Delta H^\circ > 0$ (endothermic) | entropy *decreases* ($\Delta S^\circ < 0$) |

This falls in the **bottom-right cell** of the spontaneity matrix: $\Delta G^\circ = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ > 0$ at **all temperatures** because both terms on the right are positive for all $T > 0$:

$$\Delta G^\circ(T) = \underbrace{+102{,}200}_{>\,0} - T\underbrace{(-11.63)}_{<\,0} = 102{,}200 + 11.63\,T$$

Since the coefficient of $T$ is **positive**, $\Delta G^\circ$ only grows with temperature — there is **no crossover temperature** where $\Delta G^\circ = 0$. Setting $\Delta G^\circ = 0$ gives:

$$T^* = -\frac{\Delta H^\circ}{\Delta S^\circ} = -\frac{102{,}200}{-11.63} \approx 8{,}788\,\text{K}$$

This is a **negative result in physical terms** — the formula gives a mathematically positive $T^*$ only because both $\Delta H^\circ > 0$ and $\Delta S^\circ < 0$ make $-\Delta H^\circ/\Delta S^\circ$ positive, but examining $\Delta G^\circ(T) = 102{,}200 + 11.63T$ reveals it is **always positive and increasing**. There is no temperature at which the forward reaction is thermodynamically spontaneous under standard-state conditions. The reaction is **thermodynamically unfavourable at all temperatures** at standard pressures (the MnO/CO system lies near the top of the Ellingham-type diagram for MnO — Mn is a strongly oxidised metal and is difficult to reduce by CO).

---

## Part (c) — Reaction quotient and $\Delta G_{\text{rxn}}$ at 900 K with real gas mixture

**Step 1 — $\Delta G^\circ$ extrapolated to 900 K:**

$$\Delta G^\circ(900\,\text{K}) = 102{,}200 + 11.63 \times 900 = 102{,}200 + 10{,}467 = 112{,}667\,\text{J/mol}$$

**Step 2 — Reaction quotient $Q$.**

Activity of pure solids (MnO, Mn) = 1. For ideal gases, $a_i = P_i/P^\circ$ with $P^\circ = 1\,\text{atm}$:

$$Q = \frac{a_{\text{Mn}}\cdot a_{\text{CO}_2}}{a_{\text{MnO}}\cdot a_{\text{CO}}} = \frac{1 \times (P_{\text{CO}_2}/1)}{1 \times (P_{\text{CO}}/1)} = \frac{P_{\text{CO}_2}}{P_{\text{CO}}}$$

$$Q = \frac{0.05}{0.80} = 0.0625$$

**Step 3 — $\Delta G_{\text{rxn}}$ at actual conditions:**

$$\Delta G_{\text{rxn}} = \Delta G^\circ(900) + RT\ln Q$$

$$= 112{,}667 + (8.314)(900)\ln(0.0625)$$

$$\ln(0.0625) = \ln(1/16) = -\ln 16 = -2.773$$

$$= 112{,}667 + 7{,}483 \times (-2.773)$$

$$= 112{,}667 - 20{,}754 = \boxed{+91{,}913\,\text{J/mol} \approx +91.9\,\text{kJ/mol}}$$

**Step 4 — Direction of reaction:**

$\Delta G_{\text{rxn}} = +91.9\,\text{kJ/mol} > 0$, so $Q < K$ is **not** satisfied — in fact $\Delta G > 0$ means the **reverse** reaction is spontaneous: CO$_2$ will react with Mn metal to re-form MnO and CO under these conditions. The low CO$_2$ partial pressure reduces $Q$ and shifts $\Delta G$ somewhat (from +112.7 to +91.9 kJ/mol), but the thermodynamic barrier is so large that even a highly CO-rich atmosphere cannot drive the forward reduction at 900 K.
L3|hard.final_answer: (a) $\Delta H^\circ = +102.2$ kJ/mol; $\Delta S^\circ = -11.63$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$; $\Delta G^\circ_{298} = +105.7$ kJ/mol. (b) $\Delta H > 0$, $\Delta S < 0$: reaction is non-spontaneous at all temperatures under standard conditions; no real crossover temperature exists. (c) $Q = 0.0625$; $\Delta G_{\text{rxn}}(900\,\text{K}) = +91.9$ kJ/mol — reaction proceeds in the **reverse** direction (re-oxidation of Mn to MnO).
common_mistakes: Applying $\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K$ to find $K$ and then immediately concluding $K < 1$ means the reaction won't proceed, without checking how the actual $Q$ (which depends on the specific gas-phase conditions) shifts $\Delta G_{\text{rxn}}$ away from $\Delta G^\circ$. The two quantities $\Delta G^\circ$ and $\Delta G_{\text{rxn}}$ are not the same.

Forgetting that pure solids (MnO and Mn) have activity = 1 and should not appear in the expression for $Q$. Students often include mole fractions or masses of the solid phases in the denominator, incorrectly computing $Q$.

Misidentifying the spontaneity-matrix cell: seeing $\Delta S^\circ < 0$ and assuming the reaction might be spontaneous at low temperature. This is only true when $\Delta H^\circ < 0$ (exothermic + entropy-down). Here $\Delta H^\circ > 0$ (endothermic + entropy-down), so $\Delta G^\circ > 0$ at every temperature — the forward reaction is never spontaneous under standard conditions.

L3|hard.title: Spontaneity of Austenite Formation and Equilibrium Carbon Activity
L3|hard.statement:
In steel processing, the transformation from $\alpha$-iron (BCC ferrite) to $\gamma$-iron (FCC austenite) is critical for heat treatment. Consider the following problem involving both free energy calculations and Maxwell relations.

A steel process engineer wants to determine whether carbon redistribution in a partially transformed iron specimen is spontaneous at 950 °C (1223 K) and 1 atm, and to quantify the entropy change when the pressure on the austenite is increased isothermally.

**Part (a) — Spontaneity of the $\alpha \to \gamma$ transformation for pure iron at 950 °C:**

Given the following thermodynamic data for pure iron at 1223 K:

| Phase | $H^\circ_{1223}$ (J/mol, relative to a common reference) | $S^\circ_{1223}$ (J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$) |
|---|---:|---:|
| $\alpha$-Fe (BCC) | 0 | 68.14 |
| $\gamma$-Fe (FCC) | 910 | 69.88 |

Compute $\Delta G^\circ_{1223}$ for the transformation $\alpha\text{-Fe} \to \gamma\text{-Fe}$ and determine whether it is spontaneous.

**Part (b) — Temperature at which $\Delta G = 0$:**

Assuming $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ are approximately constant with temperature (use the 1223 K values), estimate the equilibrium transition temperature $T_\text{eq}$ at which $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ coexist.

**Part (c) — Entropy change on isothermal compression of austenite:**

Using the appropriate Maxwell relation derived from $\mathrm{d}G = V\,\mathrm{d}P - S\,\mathrm{d}T$, calculate the molar entropy change $\Delta S$ of $\gamma$-Fe (austenite) when the pressure is increased isothermally from 1 atm to 500 atm at 1223 K.

Given for $\gamma$-Fe at 1223 K:
- Molar mass: $M = 55.85$ g/mol
- Density: $\rho = 7.26$ g/cm$^3$
- Linear thermal expansion coefficient: $\alpha_L = 23.0 \times 10^{-6}$ K$^{-1}$ (so volumetric $\alpha_V = 3\alpha_L$)
- $1\text{ atm} = 1.013 \times 10^5$ N/m$^2$

**Part (d) — Interpretation:**

Explain whether the sign of $\Delta S$ computed in Part (c) is physically reasonable, and state which Maxwell relation you used and why it follows from $G$ being a state function.
L3|hard.solution:
## Step-by-step solution

### Part (a) — $\Delta G^\circ_{1223}$ for $\alpha \to \gamma$ transformation

**Identify the transformation:**
$$\alpha\text{-Fe}(\text{BCC}) \to \gamma\text{-Fe}(\text{FCC})$$

**Compute $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$:**
$$\Delta H^\circ_{1223} = H^\circ_{\gamma} - H^\circ_{\alpha} = 910 - 0 = +910\;\text{J/mol}$$
