Calculating the excess chemical potential as $RT\ln a_{\text{Ni}}$ instead of $RT\ln\gamma_{\text{Ni}}$, thereby including the ideal logarithmic term and reporting $\mu_{\text{Ni}} - \mu^\circ_{\text{Ni}}$ rather than the true excess quantity.

L5|medium.title: Activity Coefficient from Equilibrium Solubility in a Binary Ag-Pb Alloy
L5|medium.statement:
Lead (Pb) and silver (Ag) form a binary system in which, at 1073 K, the maximum solubility of Ag in liquid Pb is 2.8 wt% Ag and the maximum solubility of Pb in liquid Ag is 1.5 wt% Pb. Assume that no intermediate phases exist in this system at this temperature, and that the two coexisting liquid phases are each dilute enough that Henry's Law applies to the solute in each phase.

**Given data:**
- Molar mass of Ag: $M_\text{Ag} = 107.9$ g/mol
- Molar mass of Pb: $M_\text{Pb} = 207.2$ g/mol
- Temperature: $T = 1073$ K
- $R = 8.314$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$

**(a)** Convert both solubility limits from wt% to mole fraction.

**(b)** At equilibrium between the two liquid phases, the chemical potential of Ag must be equal in both phases: $\mu_\text{Ag}^\alpha = \mu_\text{Ag}^\beta$. Using $\mu_i = \mu_i^\circ + RT\ln a_i$ and the fact that Raoult's Law ($a_i = X_i$, $\gamma_i = 1$) applies to the solvent in each phase, determine the activity coefficient $\gamma_\text{Ag}^{\alpha}$ of Ag (as the solute) in the Pb-rich phase $\alpha$.

**(c)** Calculate the relative chemical potential $\mu_\text{Ag}^\alpha - \mu_\text{Ag}^\circ$ (in kJ/mol) in the Pb-rich phase at the solubility limit.
L5|medium.solution:
## Step-by-Step Solution

### Part (a) — Convert solubility limits to mole fractions

**Pb-rich phase $\alpha$** contains 2.8 wt% Ag. Per 100 g of alloy: 2.8 g Ag and 97.2 g Pb.

$$n_\text{Ag} = \frac{2.8}{107.9} = 0.02595 \text{ mol}, \qquad n_\text{Pb} = \frac{97.2}{207.2} = 0.4691 \text{ mol}$$

$$X_\text{Ag}^{\alpha} = \frac{0.02595}{0.02595 + 0.4691} = \frac{0.02595}{0.4951} = 0.05242$$

**Ag-rich phase $\beta$** contains 1.5 wt% Pb. Per 100 g: 1.5 g Pb and 98.5 g Ag.

$$n_\text{Pb} = \frac{1.5}{207.2} = 0.007238 \text{ mol}, \qquad n_\text{Ag} = \frac{98.5}{107.9} = 0.9129 \text{ mol}$$

$$X_\text{Ag}^{\beta} = \frac{0.9129}{0.9129 + 0.007238} = \frac{0.9129}{0.9201} = 0.9922$$

### Part (b) — Activity coefficient of Ag in the Pb-rich phase

**Equilibrium condition:** at the two-phase boundary both phases coexist, so:

$$\mu_\text{Ag}^{\alpha} = \mu_\text{Ag}^{\beta}$$

Using $\mu_i = \mu_i^\circ + RT\ln a_i$:

$$\mu_\text{Ag}^\circ + RT\ln a_\text{Ag}^{\alpha} = \mu_\text{Ag}^\circ + RT\ln a_\text{Ag}^{\beta}$$

$$a_\text{Ag}^{\alpha} = a_\text{Ag}^{\beta}$$

**Activity in the Ag-rich phase $\beta$:** Ag is the solvent here ($X_\text{Ag}^\beta = 0.9922$), so Raoult's Law applies:

$$a_\text{Ag}^{\beta} = X_\text{Ag}^{\beta} = 0.9922$$

**Activity in the Pb-rich phase $\alpha$:** Ag is the solute, so $a_\text{Ag}^{\alpha} = \gamma_\text{Ag}^{\alpha}\, X_\text{Ag}^{\alpha}$. Setting equal to $a_\text{Ag}^{\beta}$:

$$\gamma_\text{Ag}^{\alpha}\, X_\text{Ag}^{\alpha} = 0.9922$$

$$\gamma_\text{Ag}^{\alpha} = \frac{0.9922}{0.05242} = \boxed{18.93}$$

The large value $\gamma_\text{Ag}^\alpha \gg 1$ reflects positive deviation from ideality: Ag–Ag bonds are strongly preferred over Ag–Pb bonds, so Ag has a much higher escaping tendency in the Pb-rich phase than an ideal solution would predict.

### Part (c) — Relative chemical potential of Ag in phase $\alpha$

The relative chemical potential is $\mu_\text{Ag}^{\alpha} - \mu_\text{Ag}^\circ = RT\ln a_\text{Ag}^{\alpha}$.

From Part (b), $a_\text{Ag}^{\alpha} = 0.9922$, so:

$$\mu_\text{Ag}^{\alpha} - \mu_\text{Ag}^\circ = RT\ln(0.9922)$$

$$= (8.314)(1073)\ln(0.9922)$$

$$= 8920.9 \times (-0.007831)$$

$$= \boxed{-69.9 \text{ J/mol} \approx -0.070 \text{ kJ/mol}}$$

This is nearly zero because the activity of Ag is close to 1 at equilibrium — despite the high activity coefficient, the very low mole fraction in the Pb-rich phase conspires with the equilibrium condition to give $a_\text{Ag}^\alpha \approx 1$.
common_mistakes: Applying Raoult's Law ($\gamma = 1$) to the solute rather than the solvent. Henry's Law governs the solute (low-concentration component); Raoult's Law applies to the solvent (high-concentration component). Confusing which law applies to which component leads to setting $a_\text{Ag}^{\alpha} = X_\text{Ag}^{\alpha}$ directly and obtaining $\gamma = 1$, which is wrong.

Forgetting to convert wt% to mole fraction before using any activity or chemical-potential formula. Activity and chemical potential are defined in terms of mole fractions, not weight fractions; using 0.028 instead of 0.0524 for $X_\text{Ag}^{\alpha}$ gives an activity coefficient about 5 times too large.

Believing a large $\gamma \gg 1$ means the reaction or dissolution cannot proceed. The activity coefficient measures deviation from ideal behaviour; it does not by itself determine spontaneity. Here $\gamma_\text{Ag}^{\alpha} \approx 19$, yet Ag does dissolve up to 2.8 wt% in liquid Pb because the entropic driving force ($\Delta S_\text{mix} > 0$) is sufficient at 1073 K.

L5|hard.title: Activity Coefficient from Gibbs-Duhem Integration in a Cu-Zn Binary Alloy
L5|hard.statement:
A binary Cu-Zn alloy is studied at 1100 K. Experimental vapour-pressure measurements of the solvent (copper) over a range of compositions yield the following activity data for Cu:

| $X_{\text{Zn}}$ | $a_{\text{Cu}}$ |
|:---:|:---:|
| 0.00 | 1.000 |
| 0.10 | 0.915 |
| 0.20 | 0.830 |
| 0.30 | 0.740 |
| 0.40 | 0.642 |
| 0.50 | 0.535 |

Using the **Gibbs-Duhem equation** and a graphical/numerical integration approach, determine:

**(a)** The activity of zinc, $a_{\text{Zn}}$, at $X_{\text{Zn}} = 0.50$, starting from the Henry's Law limit at the dilute end ($X_{\text{Zn}} \to 0$, where $a_{\text{Zn}} \to X_{\text{Zn}}$ as a first approximation — i.e. treat zinc as ideal in the infinitely dilute limit, so $\ln a_{\text{Zn}} \to 0$ as $X_{\text{Zn}} \to 0$).

**(b)** The activity coefficient of zinc, $\gamma_{\text{Zn}}$, at $X_{\text{Zn}} = 0.50$.

**(c)** The molar Gibbs energy of mixing, $\Delta G_{\text{mix}}$, at $X_{\text{Zn}} = 0.50$ and 1100 K.

Useful data: $R = 8.314$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$.
L5|hard.solution:
## Step 1 — Write the Gibbs-Duhem equation in terms of activities

At constant $T$ and $P$, the Gibbs-Duhem equation for a binary is:
$$X_{\text{Cu}}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{\text{Cu}} + X_{\text{Zn}}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{\text{Zn}} = 0$$

Using $\mu_i = \mu_i^\circ + RT\ln a_i$, so $\mathrm{d}\mu_i = RT\,\mathrm{d}\ln a_i$:
$$X_{\text{Cu}}\,\mathrm{d}\ln a_{\text{Cu}} + X_{\text{Zn}}\,\mathrm{d}\ln a_{\text{Zn}} = 0$$

Rearranging for the solute (Zn):
$$\mathrm{d}\ln a_{\text{Zn}} = -\frac{X_{\text{Cu}}}{X_{\text{Zn}}}\,\mathrm{d}\ln a_{\text{Cu}}$$

Integrating from $X_{\text{Zn}} = 0$ (where we set $\ln a_{\text{Zn}} = 0$ by the ideal dilute-limit condition) to $X_{\text{Zn}} = 0.50$:
$$\ln a_{\text{Zn}}\big|_{X_{\text{Zn}}=0.50} = -\int_{X_{\text{Zn}}=0}^{X_{\text{Zn}}=0.50} \frac{X_{\text{Cu}}}{X_{\text{Zn}}}\,\mathrm{d}\ln a_{\text{Cu}}$$

## Step 2 — Compute $\mathrm{d}\ln a_{\text{Cu}}$ across each interval

First, compute $\ln a_{\text{Cu}}$ at each data point:

| $X_{\text{Zn}}$ | $X_{\text{Cu}}$ | $a_{\text{Cu}}$ | $\ln a_{\text{Cu}}$ |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 0.00 | 1.00 | 1.000 | 0.0000 |
| 0.10 | 0.90 | 0.915 | −0.0888 |
| 0.20 | 0.80 | 0.830 | −0.1863 |
| 0.30 | 0.70 | 0.740 | −0.3011 |
| 0.40 | 0.60 | 0.642 | −0.4432 |
| 0.50 | 0.50 | 0.535 | −0.6243 |

Change in $\ln a_{\text{Cu}}$ over each interval $\Delta(\ln a_{\text{Cu}})$:

| Interval | $\Delta\ln a_{\text{Cu}}$ |
|:---:|:---:|
| $X_{\text{Zn}}$: 0.00 → 0.10 | $-0.0888 - 0.0000 = -0.0888$ |
| 0.10 → 0.20 | $-0.1863 - (-0.0888) = -0.0975$ |
| 0.20 → 0.30 | $-0.3011 - (-0.1863) = -0.1148$ |
| 0.30 → 0.40 | $-0.4432 - (-0.3011) = -0.1421$ |
| 0.40 → 0.50 | $-0.6243 - (-0.4432) = -0.1811$ |

## Step 3 — Evaluate the integrand $X_{\text{Cu}}/X_{\text{Zn}}$ at the midpoint of each interval

Use the midpoint of each $X_{\text{Zn}}$ interval for the weighting factor:

| Interval midpoint $X_{\text{Zn}}^{\text{mid}}$ | $X_{\text{Cu}}^{\text{mid}}$ | $X_{\text{Cu}}/X_{\text{Zn}}$ |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 0.05 | 0.95 | 19.0 |
| 0.15 | 0.85 | 5.67 |
| 0.25 | 0.75 | 3.00 |
| 0.35 | 0.65 | 1.857 |
| 0.45 | 0.55 | 1.222 |

## Step 4 — Perform the numerical integration (trapezoidal/midpoint sum)

Each contribution to the integral is $(X_{\text{Cu}}/X_{\text{Zn}})^{\text{mid}} \times \Delta\ln a_{\text{Cu}}$:

| Interval | $(X_{\text{Cu}}/X_{\text{Zn}})^{\text{mid}}$ | $\Delta\ln a_{\text{Cu}}$ | Contribution |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 0.00 → 0.10 | 19.0 | −0.0888 | $19.0 \times (-0.0888) = -1.6872$ |
| 0.10 → 0.20 | 5.67 | −0.0975 | $5.67 \times (-0.0975) = -0.5528$ |
| 0.20 → 0.30 | 3.00 | −0.1148 | $3.00 \times (-0.1148) = -0.3444$ |
| 0.30 → 0.40 | 1.857 | −0.1421 | $1.857 \times (-0.1421) = -0.2639$ |
| 0.40 → 0.50 | 1.222 | −0.1811 | $1.222 \times (-0.1811) = -0.2213$ |

**Sum of contributions:**
$$\int \frac{X_{\text{Cu}}}{X_{\text{Zn}}}\,\mathrm{d}\ln a_{\text{Cu}} \approx -1.6872 - 0.5528 - 0.3444 - 0.2639 - 0.2213 = -3.0696$$

Therefore:
$$\ln a_{\text{Zn}} = -(-3.0696) = +3.0696$$

**Note on the first interval:** The large contribution from the 0.00 → 0.10 interval reflects the singular behaviour of $X_{\text{Cu}}/X_{\text{Zn}}$ as $X_{\text{Zn}} \to 0$. In a more rigorous treatment one would analytically handle this limit using the Raoult/Henry boundary conditions; the midpoint approximation here gives a reasonable estimate.

## Step 5 — Part (a): Activity of Zn at $X_{\text{Zn}} = 0.50$

$$\ln a_{\text{Zn}} \approx +3.07$$
$$\boxed{a_{\text{Zn}} = e^{3.07} \approx 2.16}$$

$a_{\text{Zn}} > 1$ indicates **positive deviation from ideality** — zinc has higher escaping tendency (higher chemical potential) than in an ideal solution at the same composition. This is consistent with Cu-Zn showing $\Delta H_{\text{mix}} > 0$ in Zn-rich regimes (Zn-Zn and Cu-Cu bonds preferred over Zn-Cu bonds).

## Step 6 — Part (b): Activity coefficient of Zn

$$a_{\text{Zn}} = \gamma_{\text{Zn}}\,X_{\text{Zn}}$$
$$\gamma_{\text{Zn}} = \frac{a_{\text{Zn}}}{X_{\text{Zn}}} = \frac{2.16}{0.50} = \boxed{4.32}$$

$\gamma_{\text{Zn}} > 1$ confirms positive deviation — zinc atoms in a copper matrix at $X_{\text{Zn}} = 0.50$ are more active than they would be in an ideal solution.

## Step 7 — Part (c): Molar Gibbs energy of mixing

The general expression for molar Gibbs energy of mixing in a real binary solution is:
$$\Delta G_{\text{mix}} = RT\left(X_{\text{Cu}}\ln a_{\text{Cu}} + X_{\text{Zn}}\ln a_{\text{Zn}}\right)$$

At $X_{\text{Zn}} = 0.50$, $X_{\text{Cu}} = 0.50$:
- $\ln a_{\text{Cu}} = -0.6243$ (from our table)
- $\ln a_{\text{Zn}} = +3.07$

$$\Delta G_{\text{mix}} = (8.314)(1100)\left[0.50(-0.6243) + 0.50(+3.07)\right]$$
$$= 9145.4\left[-0.3122 + 1.535\right]$$
$$= 9145.4 \times 1.2228$$
$$\boxed{\Delta G_{\text{mix}} \approx +11{,}183\;\text{J/mol} \approx +11.2\;\text{kJ/mol}}$$

$\Delta G_{\text{mix}} > 0$ means this mixture is thermodynamically **unfavourable** relative to unmixed components at this temperature and composition — consistent with the positive-deviation character of the system. At 1100 K the system is above a miscibility gap; at lower temperatures the alloy would phase-separate (unmix). This connects directly to the bond-energy parameter: $\varepsilon > 0$ for Cu-Zn in this regime, giving $\Omega > 0$ in the regular-solution model.
common_mistakes: Inverting the Gibbs-Duhem integration sign: writing $\mathrm{d}\ln a_{\text{Zn}} = +(X_{\text{Cu}}/X_{\text{Zn}})\,\mathrm{d}\ln a_{\text{Cu}}$ instead of the correct negative sign, yielding $\ln a_{\text{Zn}} < 0$ and an activity less than 1, contradicting the positive-deviation evidence.

Using mole fractions directly in $\Delta G_{\text{mix}} = RT\sum X_i \ln X_i$ (the ideal-solution formula) rather than the real-solution form $RT\sum X_i \ln a_i$. For a non-ideal solution this gives the wrong answer and misses the entire point of computing activities via Gibbs-Duhem.

Forgetting that $X_{\text{Cu}}/X_{\text{Zn}}$ diverges as $X_{\text{Zn}} \to 0$, and naively applying a uniform trapezoidal rule with equal weight across all intervals — this under-counts the large contribution near the dilute limit and gives a significantly underestimated $\ln a_{\text{Zn}}$.

L5|hard.title: Activity Coefficient from Mutual Solubility in the Cu–Ag Binary
L5|hard.statement:
In the Cu–Ag binary system at 850°C (1123 K), the two terminal solid phases coexist at equilibrium. Phase $\alpha$ (Ag-rich) contains 93.0 at% Ag and 7.0 at% Cu. Phase $\beta$ (Cu-rich) contains 95.5 at% Cu and 4.5 at% Ag. No intermediate phases exist in this binary.

**(a)** Using the mutual solubility limits and the equilibrium condition $\mu_i^\alpha = \mu_i^\beta$, determine the activity coefficients $\gamma_{\text{Cu}}^\alpha$ (Cu in the Ag-rich phase) and $\gamma_{\text{Ag}}^\beta$ (Ag in the Cu-rich phase) at 1123 K, given that Henry's Law applies to each solute in its respective dilute phase and that Raoult's Law applies to each solvent.

**(b)** Calculate the chemical potential difference $\mu_{\text{Cu}}^\alpha - G_{\text{Cu}}^\circ$ (i.e. the relative chemical potential of Cu in the $\alpha$ phase) at 1123 K.

**(c)** Using the Gibbs–Duhem equation at constant $T$ and $P$, verify that your result for $\gamma_{\text{Ag}}^\beta$ is self-consistent by computing $\mathrm{d}\ln a_{\text{Ag}}$ in the $\beta$ phase and checking the sign of $\mathrm{d}\ln a_{\text{Cu}}$ implied by the Gibbs–Duhem relation. State clearly what the sign tells you about the deviation from ideality in the $\beta$ phase.

**Data:** $R = 8.314\;\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$, $T = 1123\;\text{K}$.
L5|hard.solution:
## Step 1 — Write down the mole fractions in each phase

**Phase $\alpha$ (Ag-rich solvent, Cu as solute):**
$$X_{\text{Ag}}^\alpha = 0.930, \quad X_{\text{Cu}}^\alpha = 0.070$$

**Phase $\beta$ (Cu-rich solvent, Ag as solute):**
$$X_{\text{Cu}}^\beta = 0.955, \quad X_{\text{Ag}}^\beta = 0.045$$

## Step 2 — Apply the equilibrium condition for Cu

At equilibrium between phases $\alpha$ and $\beta$:
$$\mu_{\text{Cu}}^\alpha = \mu_{\text{Cu}}^\beta$$

Using $\mu_i = G_i^\circ + RT\ln a_i$:
$$G_{\text{Cu}}^\circ + RT\ln a_{\text{Cu}}^\alpha = G_{\text{Cu}}^\circ + RT\ln a_{\text{Cu}}^\beta$$

This gives:
$$a_{\text{Cu}}^\alpha = a_{\text{Cu}}^\beta$$

## Step 3 — Apply Raoult's Law to the solvent and Henry's Law to the solute

In the Cu-rich phase $\beta$, Cu is the **solvent** and follows Raoult's Law:
$$a_{\text{Cu}}^\beta = \gamma_{\text{Cu}}^\beta \cdot X_{\text{Cu}}^\beta = 1 \times 0.955 = 0.955$$

(Since $X_{\text{Cu}}^\beta \to 1$, Raoult's Law applies and $\gamma_{\text{Cu}}^\beta = 1$.)

In the Ag-rich phase $\alpha$, Cu is the **solute** and follows Henry's Law, so:
$$a_{\text{Cu}}^\alpha = \gamma_{\text{Cu}}^\alpha \cdot X_{\text{Cu}}^\alpha$$

Since $a_{\text{Cu}}^\alpha = a_{\text{Cu}}^\beta = 0.955$:
$$\gamma_{\text{Cu}}^\alpha \cdot 0.070 = 0.955$$

$$\boxed{\gamma_{\text{Cu}}^\alpha = \frac{0.955}{0.070} \approx 13.6}$$

This $\gamma_{\text{Cu}}^\alpha \gg 1$ indicates a strong **positive deviation** from ideality — Cu strongly prefers its own kind over Ag neighbours, consistent with the limited solubility.

## Step 4 — Apply the equilibrium condition for Ag and find $\gamma_{\text{Ag}}^\beta$

Similarly:
$$a_{\text{Ag}}^\alpha = a_{\text{Ag}}^\beta$$

In the Ag-rich phase $\alpha$, Ag is the **solvent** (Raoult's Law, $\gamma_{\text{Ag}}^\alpha = 1$):
$$a_{\text{Ag}}^\alpha = 1 \times X_{\text{Ag}}^\alpha = 0.930$$

In the Cu-rich phase $\beta$, Ag is the **solute** (Henry's Law):
$$a_{\text{Ag}}^\beta = \gamma_{\text{Ag}}^\beta \cdot X_{\text{Ag}}^\beta$$

Setting equal:
$$\gamma_{\text{Ag}}^\beta \cdot 0.045 = 0.930$$

$$\boxed{\gamma_{\text{Ag}}^\beta = \frac{0.930}{0.045} \approx 20.7}$$

Again $\gamma_{\text{Ag}}^\beta \gg 1$: Ag atoms dissolved in the Cu-rich phase also show strong positive deviation — Ag strongly prefers Ag neighbours.

## Part (b) — Relative chemical potential of Cu in the $\alpha$ phase

The relative chemical potential (chemical potential relative to the pure-component standard state) is:
$$\mu_{\text{Cu}}^\alpha - G_{\text{Cu}}^\circ = RT\ln a_{\text{Cu}}^\alpha$$

Using $a_{\text{Cu}}^\alpha = 0.955$:
$$\mu_{\text{Cu}}^\alpha - G_{\text{Cu}}^\circ = (8.314)(1123)\ln(0.955)$$

$$= 9336.7 \times (-0.04602)$$

$$= \boxed{-429.6\;\text{J mol}^{-1} \approx -430\;\text{J/mol}}$$

The small negative value shows that Cu dissolved in the Ag-rich phase has slightly lower chemical potential than pure Cu — it is just barely enthalpically trapped in the dilute solid solution. (The large $\gamma_{\text{Cu}}^\alpha$ raises the activity close to 1 despite the low mole fraction, so the relative chemical potential is nearly zero.)

## Part (c) — Gibbs–Duhem consistency check in the $\beta$ phase

The Gibbs–Duhem equation at constant $T$, $P$ for a binary:
$$X_{\text{Cu}}^\beta\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{\text{Cu}} + X_{\text{Ag}}^\beta\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{\text{Ag}} = 0$$

Rewriting in terms of activities ($\mathrm{d}\mu_i = RT\,\mathrm{d}\ln a_i$):
$$X_{\text{Cu}}^\beta\,\mathrm{d}\ln a_{\text{Cu}} + X_{\text{Ag}}^\beta\,\mathrm{d}\ln a_{\text{Ag}} = 0$$

Therefore:
$$\mathrm{d}\ln a_{\text{Cu}} = -\frac{X_{\text{Ag}}^\beta}{X_{\text{Cu}}^\beta}\,\mathrm{d}\ln a_{\text{Ag}}$$

In the $\beta$ phase, $a_{\text{Ag}}^\beta = \gamma_{\text{Ag}}^\beta X_{\text{Ag}}^\beta$ where $\gamma_{\text{Ag}}^\beta = 20.7 > 1$. As $X_{\text{Ag}}^\beta$ increases (more Ag dissolves into the Cu-rich phase), $a_{\text{Ag}}^\beta$ increases, so:
$$\mathrm{d}\ln a_{\text{Ag}} > 0$$

The Gibbs–Duhem relation then gives:
$$\mathrm{d}\ln a_{\text{Cu}} = -\frac{0.045}{0.955}\underbrace{\mathrm{d}\ln a_{\text{Ag}}}_{>0} < 0$$

As Ag is added to the $\beta$ phase, the activity of Cu **decreases** below its Raoult's Law value. This is physically self-consistent: adding Ag into the Cu lattice dilutes Cu, reducing $a_{\text{Cu}}$. The **positive** $\gamma_{\text{Ag}}^\beta \gg 1$ signals that both components show **positive deviations from ideality** in this system — like-atom bonds (Cu–Cu, Ag–Ag) are energetically preferred over unlike bonds (Cu–Ag), which is precisely why the two metals have limited mutual solubility and a miscibility gap at 850°C.
L5|hard.final_answer: (a) $\gamma_{\text{Cu}}^\alpha \approx 13.6$, $\gamma_{\text{Ag}}^\beta \approx 20.7$; (b) $\mu_{\text{Cu}}^\alpha - G_{\text{Cu}}^\circ \approx -430\;\text{J mol}^{-1}$; (c) Gibbs–Duhem gives $\mathrm{d}\ln a_{\text{Cu}} < 0$ when Ag is added to the $\beta$ phase — consistent with both species showing positive deviation ($\gamma > 1$), indicating Cu–Ag bonds are weaker than like-atom bonds.
common_mistakes: Applying Henry's Law to the solvent instead of the solute — Raoult's Law governs the majority component (solvent) and Henry's Law governs the minority component (solute). Swapping these gives activity coefficients close to 1 rather than the large values expected for a limited-solubility system.

Setting $a_{\text{Cu}}^\alpha = X_{\text{Cu}}^\alpha = 0.070$ (assuming ideal behaviour) instead of using the equilibrium condition $a_{\text{Cu}}^\alpha = a_{\text{Cu}}^\beta$ to find the true activity. This mistake ignores the entire physical content of the equilibrium condition and gives $\gamma = 1$ incorrectly.

Using the Gibbs–Duhem equation with moles $n_i$ instead of mole fractions $X_i$, or forgetting the minus sign in $\mathrm{d}\ln a_{\text{Cu}} = -(X_{\text{Ag}}/X_{\text{Cu}})\,\mathrm{d}\ln a_{\text{Ag}}$, leading to the wrong sign for the deviation from ideality.

L5|hard.title: Gibbs-Duhem Integration: Activity of Carbon in Liquid Iron
L5|hard.statement:
A materials engineer is designing a carbon sensor for liquid iron (Fe-C) at 1600 °C (1873 K). Vapour-pressure measurements of iron above dilute Fe-C melts at 1873 K give the following activity data for iron ($a_{\text{Fe}}$) as a function of carbon mole fraction $X_C$:

| $X_C$ | $a_{\text{Fe}}$ |
|---|---|
| 0.00 | 1.000 |
| 0.02 | 0.980 |
| 0.04 | 0.958 |
| 0.06 | 0.935 |
| 0.08 | 0.910 |
| 0.10 | 0.883 |

**(a)** Using the Gibbs-Duhem equation, derive an expression that relates $d\ln a_C$ to $d\ln a_{\text{Fe}}$ at constant $T$ and $P$.

**(b)** Using the data table and your result from part (a), determine the activity of carbon $a_C$ at $X_C = 0.10$. Assume that in the limit $X_C \to 0$, carbon obeys Henry's Law (i.e. $a_C \to \gamma_C^\infty X_C$ as $X_C \to 0$). Use a numerical integration scheme (trapezoidal rule) over the tabulated data. Note that the Henrian standard state applies: take the lower integration limit condition as $a_C = \gamma_C^\infty X_C$ evaluated at the first non-zero data point $X_C = 0.02$, where you may extract $\gamma_C^\infty$ from the Raoult's Law behaviour of the solvent at infinite dilution.

**(c)** Compute the chemical potential of carbon relative to its standard state, $\mu_C - \mu_C^\circ$, at $X_C = 0.10$ and 1873 K. Express your answer in kJ/mol.

**Given / Constants:** $R = 8.314$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$. For the Fe-C binary, mole fractions satisfy $X_{\text{Fe}} + X_C = 1$. Assume ideal gas behaviour for iron vapour above the melt when interpreting the vapour-pressure measurements (so $a_{\text{Fe}} = P_{\text{Fe}}/P^*_{\text{Fe}}$ directly).
L5|hard.solution:
## Step-by-step solution

### Part (a) — Gibbs-Duhem form

For a binary Fe-C system at constant $T$ and $P$, the Gibbs-Duhem equation is:

$$X_{\text{Fe}}\,d\mu_{\text{Fe}} + X_C\,d\mu_C = 0$$

Using $\mu_i = \mu_i^\circ + RT\ln a_i$, so $d\mu_i = RT\,d\ln a_i$, divide through by $RT$:

$$X_{\text{Fe}}\,d\ln a_{\text{Fe}} + X_C\,d\ln a_C = 0$$

Rearrange:

$$\boxed{d\ln a_C = -\frac{X_{\text{Fe}}}{X_C}\,d\ln a_{\text{Fe}}}$$

This is the working form for Gibbs-Duhem integration: knowing $a_{\text{Fe}}(X_C)$ from vapour-pressure measurements, we can integrate to get $a_C$.

---

### Part (b) — Numerical integration for $a_C$ at $X_C = 0.10$

**Step 1 — Compute the integrand at each tabulated point.**

We need to evaluate $f = -X_{\text{Fe}}/X_C$ and the differential $d\ln a_{\text{Fe}}$ between successive points.

First compute $\ln a_{\text{Fe}}$ at each point:

| $X_C$ | $X_{\text{Fe}}$ | $a_{\text{Fe}}$ | $\ln a_{\text{Fe}}$ | $X_{\text{Fe}}/X_C$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.02 | 0.98 | 0.980 | $-0.02020$ | 49.0 |
| 0.04 | 0.96 | 0.958 | $-0.04289$ | 24.0 |
| 0.06 | 0.94 | 0.935 | $-0.06716$ | 15.667 |
| 0.08 | 0.92 | 0.910 | $-0.09431$ | 11.50 |
| 0.10 | 0.90 | 0.883 | $-0.12462$ | 9.00 |

**Step 2 — Evaluate $\Delta\ln a_{\text{Fe}}$ between consecutive points:**

| Interval | $\Delta\ln a_{\text{Fe}}$ |
|---|---|
| $0.02 \to 0.04$ | $-0.04289 - (-0.02020) = -0.02269$ |
| $0.04 \to 0.06$ | $-0.06716 - (-0.04289) = -0.02427$ |
| $0.06 \to 0.08$ | $-0.09431 - (-0.06716) = -0.02715$ |
| $0.08 \to 0.10$ | $-0.12462 - (-0.09431) = -0.03031$ |

**Step 3 — Apply trapezoidal rule for $\Delta\ln a_C$ over each interval.**

In each interval from $X_C^{(k)}$ to $X_C^{(k+1)}$:

$$\Delta\ln a_C = -\frac{1}{2}\!\left(\frac{X_{\text{Fe}}^{(k)}}{X_C^{(k)}} + \frac{X_{\text{Fe}}^{(k+1)}}{X_C^{(k+1)}}\right)\Delta\ln a_{\text{Fe}}$$

**Interval 1** ($0.02 \to 0.04$):
$$\Delta\ln a_C^{(1)} = -\tfrac{1}{2}(49.0 + 24.0)\times(-0.02269) = -\tfrac{1}{2}(73.0)(-0.02269) = +0.8282$$

**Interval 2** ($0.04 \to 0.06$):
$$\Delta\ln a_C^{(2)} = -\tfrac{1}{2}(24.0 + 15.667)\times(-0.02427) = -\tfrac{1}{2}(39.667)(-0.02427) = +0.4812$$

**Interval 3** ($0.06 \to 0.08$):
$$\Delta\ln a_C^{(3)} = -\tfrac{1}{2}(15.667 + 11.50)\times(-0.02715) = -\tfrac{1}{2}(27.167)(-0.02715) = +0.3687$$

**Interval 4** ($0.08 \to 0.10$):
$$\Delta\ln a_C^{(4)} = -\tfrac{1}{2}(11.50 + 9.00)\times(-0.03031) = -\tfrac{1}{2}(20.50)(-0.03031) = +0.3107$$

**Step 4 — Determine the integration constant (lower limit).**

As $X_C \to 0$, Henry's Law applies: $a_C = \gamma_C^\infty X_C$. At $X_C = 0.02$, we need $\ln a_C(0.02)$.

To find $\gamma_C^\infty$, use the limiting form of Gibbs-Duhem. In the dilute limit ($X_C \to 0$, $X_{\text{Fe}} \to 1$), Raoult's Law governs $a_{\text{Fe}}$:

$$a_{\text{Fe}} \approx X_{\text{Fe}} = 1 - X_C$$

So $\ln a_{\text{Fe}} \approx \ln(1-X_C) \approx -X_C$ for small $X_C$.

Then:
$$d\ln a_C = -\frac{X_{\text{Fe}}}{X_C}d\ln a_{\text{Fe}} \approx -\frac{1}{X_C}\cdot\left(-dX_C\right) = \frac{dX_C}{X_C} = d\ln X_C$$

Integrating from $0$ to $X_C$: $\ln a_C = \ln X_C + \text{const}$, meaning $\gamma_C^\infty$ is constant. Checking with the Raoultian deviation at $X_C = 0.02$:

$$a_{\text{Fe}}(0.02) = 0.980, \quad X_{\text{Fe}} = 0.98$$

The departure from Raoult ($a_{\text{Fe}} = X_{\text{Fe}} = 0.98$) is zero at this point — the data are consistent with Raoult for the solvent at $X_C = 0.02$. Therefore Henry's Law holds at this dilution with:

$$\ln a_C(0.02) = \ln(\gamma_C^\infty \times 0.02)$$

Since the data are consistent with Raoultian solvent at $X_C = 0.02$ (i.e. $a_{\text{Fe}} = X_{\text{Fe}}$ exactly), the activity coefficient $\gamma_C^\infty$ cannot be extracted from the table alone without an additional datum — this is the classical Gibbs-Duhem integration problem. We use the convention that $\gamma_C^\infty$ is determined self-consistently: set $\ln a_C(0.02) = \ln(\gamma_C^\infty \cdot 0.02)$ and accumulate the integral from 0.02 to 0.10.

The **total change** in $\ln a_C$ from $X_C = 0.02$ to $X_C = 0.10$ is:

$$\Delta\ln a_C = 0.8282 + 0.4812 + 0.3687 + 0.3107 = 1.9888$$

So:
$$\ln a_C(0.10) = \ln a_C(0.02) + 1.9888$$

From the Henry's Law lower limit at $X_C = 0.02$ (dilute enough that $\gamma_C^\infty \approx$ const), and using the fact that the Raoultian solvent data give $d\ln a_{\text{Fe}} / dX_{\text{Fe}} = 1$ at the dilute end, we find $\gamma_C^\infty \approx 1$ when referenced to the Raoultian standard. With the **Henrian standard state** (activity coefficient absorbed into the reference), $a_C^H = X_C$ in the dilute limit, so:

$$\ln a_C^H(0.02) = \ln(0.02) = -3.912$$

Therefore:
$$\ln a_C^H(0.10) = -3.912 + 1.989 = -1.923$$

$$\boxed{a_C(0.10) = e^{-1.923} \approx 0.146}$$

The activity coefficient of carbon at $X_C = 0.10$:
$$\gamma_C = \frac{a_C}{X_C} = \frac{0.146}{0.10} = 1.46$$

Carbon shows **positive deviation** from Henry's Law ($\gamma_C > 1$) at 10 mol%, consistent with the C-Fe system where C-C interactions are weaker than C-Fe interactions at this concentration.

---

### Part (c) — Chemical potential relative to standard state

Using $\mu_C - \mu_C^\circ = RT\ln a_C$:

$$\mu_C - \mu_C^\circ = (8.314\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1})(1873\,\text{K})\ln(0.146)$$

$$= (8.314)(1873)(-1.923)$$

$$= 15,572 \times (-1.923)$$

$$= -29,935\,\text{J/mol}$$

$$\boxed{\mu_C - \mu_C^\circ \approx -29.9\,\text{kJ/mol}}$$

The negative value indicates that carbon in the melt at $X_C = 0.10$ has a **lower chemical potential** than in its Henrian standard state — consistent with carbon being in solution rather than as pure solid graphite (which has a different, Raoultian standard state).
common_mistakes: Forgetting the negative sign in the Gibbs-Duhem integrand: the correct form is $d\ln a_C = -(X_{\text{Fe}}/X_C)\,d\ln a_{\text{Fe}}$. Because $a_{\text{Fe}}$ decreases as $X_C$ increases, $d\ln a_{\text{Fe}}$ is negative, so $d\ln a_C$ is positive — $a_C$ increases with $X_C$ as expected. Students who drop the sign get a decreasing $a_C$, which is physically nonsensical.

Confusing the lower integration limit: the integral must start from a known reference state. Using $X_C = 0$ directly is indeterminate (the integrand $X_{\text{Fe}}/X_C \to \infty$). The correct procedure is to anchor the integral at the lowest tabulated $X_C$ where Henry's Law gives a clean reference: $\ln a_C^H = \ln X_C$ in the Henrian convention.

Mixing Raoultian and Henrian standard states for carbon: the Raoultian standard state of C is pure liquid carbon (not relevant here), while the Henrian standard state absorbs $\gamma_C^\infty$ into the reference. If a student uses the Raoultian $\mu_C^\circ$ but the Henrian $a_C$, the chemical potential answer will be off by $RT\ln\gamma_C^\infty$. Always identify which standard state is being used before substituting into $\mu_i = \mu_i^\circ + RT\ln a_i$.

L5|hard.title: Mixing Thermodynamics of a Cu–Zn Brass Alloy
L5|hard.statement:
A brass alloy is prepared by mixing copper (Cu) and zinc (Zn) at 1100 K. The alloy contains 35 at% Zn (i.e., $X_{\mathrm{Zn}} = 0.35$, $X_{\mathrm{Cu}} = 0.65$). Both Cu and Zn share an FCC-like solid-solution phase at this composition and temperature. Treat the alloy as a **regular solution** with an interaction parameter $\Omega = +12{,}000$ J/mol.

(a) Calculate the molar entropy of mixing, $\Delta S_{\mathrm{mix}}$ (J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$).

(b) Calculate the molar enthalpy of mixing, $\Delta H_{\mathrm{mix}}$ (J/mol).

(c) Calculate the molar Gibbs free energy of mixing, $\Delta G_{\mathrm{mix}}$ (J/mol), and determine whether mixing is spontaneous at 1100 K.

(d) The activity coefficient of Zn in this alloy is $\gamma_{\mathrm{Zn}}$. Using the regular-solution model, the activity coefficient is given by
$$\ln \gamma_i = \frac{\Omega}{RT}\,X_j^2$$
where $j$ denotes the other component. Calculate $\gamma_{\mathrm{Zn}}$ and the activity $a_{\mathrm{Zn}}$ at this composition and temperature.

**Data:** $R = 8.314$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$.
L5|hard.solution:
## Step-by-step solution

**Given:**
- $X_{\mathrm{Zn}} = 0.35$, $X_{\mathrm{Cu}} = 0.65$
- $\Omega = +12{,}000$ J/mol
- $T = 1100$ K
- $R = 8.314$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$

---

### Part (a) — Molar entropy of mixing

For any solution (ideal or regular), the configurational entropy of mixing is:
$$\Delta S_{\mathrm{mix}} = -R\sum_i X_i \ln X_i = -R\left(X_{\mathrm{Cu}}\ln X_{\mathrm{Cu}} + X_{\mathrm{Zn}}\ln X_{\mathrm{Zn}}\right)$$

Compute each logarithm:
$$\ln(0.65) = -0.4308, \qquad \ln(0.35) = -1.0498$$

Substitute:
$$\Delta S_{\mathrm{mix}} = -8.314\bigl[(0.65)(-0.4308) + (0.35)(-1.0498)\bigr]$$
$$= -8.314\bigl[-0.2800 - 0.3674\bigr]$$
$$= -8.314 \times (-0.6474)$$
$$\boxed{\Delta S_{\mathrm{mix}} = +5.385 \text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}}$$

---

### Part (b) — Molar enthalpy of mixing

For a regular solution:
$$\Delta H_{\mathrm{mix}} = \Omega\,X_{\mathrm{Cu}}\,X_{\mathrm{Zn}}$$

$$\Delta H_{\mathrm{mix}} = 12{,}000 \times 0.65 \times 0.35 = 12{,}000 \times 0.2275$$

$$\boxed{\Delta H_{\mathrm{mix}} = +2{,}730 \text{ J/mol}}$$

Since $\Omega > 0$, Cu–Cu and Zn–Zn bonds are preferred over Cu–Zn bonds, so mixing is endothermic.

---

### Part (c) — Molar Gibbs free energy of mixing

$$\Delta G_{\mathrm{mix}} = \Delta H_{\mathrm{mix}} - T\,\Delta S_{\mathrm{mix}}$$

$$= 2{,}730 - (1100)(5.385)$$
$$= 2{,}730 - 5{,}924$$

$$\boxed{\Delta G_{\mathrm{mix}} = -3{,}194 \text{ J/mol}}$$

**Spontaneity:** $\Delta G_{\mathrm{mix}} < 0$ — mixing **is spontaneous** at 1100 K at this composition. Although the enthalpy of mixing is positive (unfavourable), the entropy contribution $T\Delta S_{\mathrm{mix}} = 5{,}924$ J/mol is large enough at this elevated temperature to overcome it.

**Physical note:** Since $\Omega > 0$, this system has a miscibility gap at lower temperatures. At high $T$, the $T\Delta S$ term wins and the alloy is a single homogeneous phase. As the alloy cools, there exists a critical temperature $T_c = \Omega/(2R) = 12{,}000/(2\times 8.314) \approx 721$ K below which unmixing would become thermodynamically favourable at $X_{\mathrm{Zn}} = 0.5$. At $X_{\mathrm{Zn}} = 0.35$, the spinodal/binodal boundaries are at different temperatures, but the principle is the same.

---

### Part (d) — Activity coefficient and activity of Zn

Using the regular-solution expression with $j = \mathrm{Cu}$ (the other component, so $X_j = X_{\mathrm{Cu}} = 0.65$):

$$\ln \gamma_{\mathrm{Zn}} = \frac{\Omega}{RT}\,X_{\mathrm{Cu}}^2 = \frac{12{,}000}{8.314 \times 1100}\times (0.65)^2$$

Compute the prefactor:
$$\frac{12{,}000}{9{,}145.4} = 1.3122$$

Multiply by $(0.65)^2 = 0.4225$:
$$\ln \gamma_{\mathrm{Zn}} = 1.3122 \times 0.4225 = 0.5544$$

$$\gamma_{\mathrm{Zn}} = e^{0.5544} = 1.741$$

Since $\gamma_{\mathrm{Zn}} > 1$, Zn shows a **positive deviation** from Raoult's Law — consistent with $\Omega > 0$ (like-atom bonds preferred).

The activity is:
$$a_{\mathrm{Zn}} = \gamma_{\mathrm{Zn}}\,X_{\mathrm{Zn}} = 1.741 \times 0.35$$

$$\boxed{a_{\mathrm{Zn}} = 0.609}$$

For comparison, the ideal value would be $a_{\mathrm{Zn}}^{\mathrm{ideal}} = X_{\mathrm{Zn}} = 0.35$. The actual activity (0.609) is much higher, meaning Zn has a greater tendency to escape the solution than predicted by ideal behaviour — again consistent with the positive $\Omega$.

---

### Summary table

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| $\Delta S_{\mathrm{mix}}$ | $+5.385$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$ |
| $\Delta H_{\mathrm{mix}}$ | $+2{,}730$ J/mol |
| $\Delta G_{\mathrm{mix}}$ | $-3{,}194$ J/mol (spontaneous) |
| $\gamma_{\mathrm{Zn}}$ | $1.741$ |
| $a_{\mathrm{Zn}}$ | $0.609$ |
L5|hard.final_answer: (a) $\Delta S_{\mathrm{mix}} = +5.385$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$; (b) $\Delta H_{\mathrm{mix}} = +2{,}730$ J/mol; (c) $\Delta G_{\mathrm{mix}} = -3{,}194$ J/mol (spontaneous at 1100 K); (d) $\gamma_{\mathrm{Zn}} = 1.741$, $a_{\mathrm{Zn}} = 0.609$
common_mistakes: **Using ideal-solution formula for $\Delta H_{\mathrm{mix}}$:** Students sometimes write $\Delta H_{\mathrm{mix}} = 0$ because they recall the ideal-solution result, forgetting that a regular solution has $\Delta H_{\mathrm{mix}} = \Omega X_A X_B \neq 0$. The ideal-solution model is a special case of the regular-solution model with $\Omega = 0$.

**Confusing which mole fraction enters the activity-coefficient formula:** The expression $\ln\gamma_i = (\Omega/RT)X_j^2$ uses $X_j$, the mole fraction of the *other* component, not $X_i$ of the component whose activity coefficient is being computed. Students frequently square $X_{\mathrm{Zn}}$ instead of $X_{\mathrm{Cu}}$, giving $\ln\gamma_{\mathrm{Zn}} = (\Omega/RT)(0.35)^2$ — an error that changes the result by nearly a factor of four.

**Concluding the reaction is non-spontaneous because $\Delta H_{\mathrm{mix}} > 0$:** A positive enthalpy of mixing does not make mixing non-spontaneous at high temperature. The correct criterion is $\Delta G_{\mathrm{mix}} = \Delta H_{\mathrm{mix}} - T\Delta S_{\mathrm{mix}} < 0$. At 1100 K the large $T\Delta S$ term overwhelms the positive $\Delta H$, so mixing remains spontaneous.

L5|hard.title: Activity Coefficient from Gibbs-Duhem Integration in Ag-Pd
L5|hard.statement:
A binary Ag-Pd alloy at 1300 K is studied by vapour-pressure measurements of the silver component. At this temperature, the following activity data for Ag have been determined experimentally over a range of compositions:

| $X_{\text{Pd}}$ | $a_{\text{Ag}}$ |
|:---:|:---:|
| 0.00 | 1.000 |
| 0.20 | 0.832 |
| 0.40 | 0.650 |
| 0.60 | 0.468 |
| 0.80 | 0.271 |
| 1.00 | 0.000 |

All values satisfy Raoult's Law exactly in the limit $X_{\text{Pd}} \to 0$ (i.e.\ pure Ag) and the system obeys the **regular solution model**, meaning $\ln \gamma_i = \Omega(1-X_i)^2/(RT)$ with the same $\Omega$ for both components.

**(a)** Using the $a_{\text{Ag}}$ data at $X_{\text{Pd}} = 0.40$, determine the activity coefficient $\gamma_{\text{Ag}}$ and hence find the regular-solution interaction parameter $\Omega$ (in J/mol).

**(b)** Using the value of $\Omega$ found in part (a), predict the activity of Pd, $a_{\text{Pd}}$, at $X_{\text{Pd}} = 0.60$.

**(c)** Calculate the molar Gibbs energy of mixing $\Delta G_{\text{mix}}$ (in J/mol) for the alloy at $X_{\text{Pd}} = 0.40$ and $T = 1300$ K, using the activities found in parts (a) and (b) evaluated at $X_{\text{Pd}} = 0.40$.

**(d)** Compare $\Delta G_{\text{mix}}$ from part (c) with the **ideal-solution** value at the same composition. Comment on whether Ag-Pd interactions are energetically favourable or unfavourable, and what this implies for the sign of $\varepsilon$ (the pair-bond interaction energy).
L5|hard.solution:
## Step-by-step solution

### Part (a) — Activity coefficient $\gamma_{\text{Ag}}$ and interaction parameter $\Omega$

**Activity coefficient from data:**

At $X_{\text{Pd}} = 0.40$, we have $X_{\text{Ag}} = 1 - 0.40 = 0.60$ and $a_{\text{Ag}} = 0.650$.

The activity coefficient is defined by $a_i = \gamma_i X_i$, so:

$$\gamma_{\text{Ag}} = \frac{a_{\text{Ag}}}{X_{\text{Ag}}} = \frac{0.650}{0.60} = 1.083$$

**Finding $\Omega$ from the regular-solution model:**

For the regular solution, the activity coefficient obeys:

$$\ln \gamma_i = \frac{\Omega}{RT}\,(1 - X_i)^2$$

For Ag ($i = \text{Ag}$), with $X_{\text{Ag}} = 0.60$ and therefore $(1 - X_{\text{Ag}}) = X_{\text{Pd}} = 0.40$:

$$\ln \gamma_{\text{Ag}} = \frac{\Omega}{RT}\,(X_{\text{Pd}})^2$$

Taking the natural log:

$$\ln(1.083) = 0.07975$$

Substituting $R = 8.314$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$, $T = 1300$ K:

$$0.07975 = \frac{\Omega}{8.314 \times 1300} \times (0.40)^2 = \frac{\Omega}{10808} \times 0.16$$

$$\Omega = \frac{0.07975 \times 10808}{0.16} = \frac{861.9}{0.16} \approx \boxed{+5387 \text{ J/mol}}$$

### Part (b) — Activity of Pd at $X_{\text{Pd}} = 0.60$

In the regular-solution model, both components share the same $\Omega$. For Pd ($i = \text{Pd}$), with $X_{\text{Pd}} = 0.60$ and therefore $(1 - X_{\text{Pd}}) = X_{\text{Ag}} = 0.40$:

$$\ln \gamma_{\text{Pd}} = \frac{\Omega}{RT}\,(X_{\text{Ag}})^2 = \frac{5387}{10808} \times (0.40)^2$$

$$\ln \gamma_{\text{Pd}} = 0.4985 \times 0.16 = 0.07975$$

Note: by symmetry of the regular-solution model at the mirror composition $X_{\text{Pd}} = 0.60$, we get the same $\ln \gamma$ as for Ag at $X_{\text{Pd}} = 0.40$. Therefore:

$$\gamma_{\text{Pd}} = e^{0.07975} \approx 1.083$$

$$\boxed{a_{\text{Pd}} = \gamma_{\text{Pd}}\,X_{\text{Pd}} = 1.083 \times 0.60 = 0.650}$$

### Part (c) — Molar Gibbs energy of mixing at $X_{\text{Pd}} = 0.40$

The general expression for the molar Gibbs energy of mixing in terms of activities is:

$$\Delta G_{\text{mix}} = RT\,(X_{\text{Ag}}\ln a_{\text{Ag}} + X_{\text{Pd}}\ln a_{\text{Pd}})$$

This comes from $\Delta G_{\text{mix}} = \sum_i X_i (\mu_i - \mu_i^\circ) = \sum_i X_i RT \ln a_i$.

At $X_{\text{Pd}} = 0.40$ we have $X_{\text{Ag}} = 0.60$, $a_{\text{Ag}} = 0.650$ (from data), and we need $a_{\text{Pd}}$ **at $X_{\text{Pd}} = 0.40$** (not 0.60 as in part b).

**Calculating $a_{\text{Pd}}$ at $X_{\text{Pd}} = 0.40$:**

With $X_{\text{Ag}} = 0.60$ (the complement), apply the regular-solution formula for Pd:

$$\ln \gamma_{\text{Pd}} = \frac{\Omega}{RT}\,(X_{\text{Ag}})^2 = 0.07975 \times \left(\frac{0.60}{0.40}\right)^2$$

Wait — let us be careful. At $X_{\text{Pd}} = 0.40$: $(1 - X_{\text{Pd}}) = X_{\text{Ag}} = 0.60$, so:

$$\ln \gamma_{\text{Pd}} = \frac{\Omega}{RT}\,(X_{\text{Ag}})^2 = \frac{5387}{10808} \times (0.60)^2 = 0.4985 \times 0.36 = 0.17946$$

$$\gamma_{\text{Pd}} = e^{0.17946} \approx 1.1967$$

$$a_{\text{Pd}} = 1.1967 \times 0.40 = 0.4787$$

**Now compute $\Delta G_{\text{mix}}$:**

$$\Delta G_{\text{mix}} = RT\,(X_{\text{Ag}}\ln a_{\text{Ag}} + X_{\text{Pd}}\ln a_{\text{Pd}})$$

$$= 8.314 \times 1300 \times \bigl[0.60\ln(0.650) + 0.40\ln(0.4787)\bigr]$$

$$= 10808 \times \bigl[0.60 \times (-0.4308) + 0.40 \times (-0.7362)\bigr]$$

$$= 10808 \times \bigl[-0.2585 - 0.2945\bigr]$$

$$= 10808 \times (-0.5530)$$

$$\boxed{\Delta G_{\text{mix}} \approx -5977 \text{ J/mol}}$$

### Part (d) — Comparison with ideal solution

**Ideal-solution $\Delta G_{\text{mix}}$ at $X_{\text{Pd}} = 0.40$:**

$$\Delta G_{\text{mix}}^{\text{ideal}} = RT\,(X_{\text{Ag}}\ln X_{\text{Ag}} + X_{\text{Pd}}\ln X_{\text{Pd}})$$

$$= 10808 \times \bigl[0.60\ln(0.60) + 0.40\ln(0.40)\bigr]$$

$$= 10808 \times \bigl[0.60\times(-0.5108) + 0.40\times(-0.9163)\bigr]$$

$$= 10808 \times \bigl[-0.3065 - 0.3665\bigr]$$

$$= 10808 \times (-0.6730) = -7273 \text{ J/mol}$$

**Comparison:**

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---:|
| $\Delta G_{\text{mix}}$ (real, Ag-Pd) | $-5977$ J/mol |
| $\Delta G_{\text{mix}}^{\text{ideal}}$ | $-7273$ J/mol |
| Difference ($\Delta H_{\text{mix}}$ excess) | $+1296$ J/mol |

The real $\Delta G_{\text{mix}}$ is **less negative** than the ideal value by about 1296 J/mol. The difference is $\Delta H_{\text{mix}} = \Omega X_{\text{Ag}} X_{\text{Pd}} = 5387 \times 0.60 \times 0.40 = +1293$ J/mol (confirming the calculation). Since $\Delta H_{\text{mix}} > 0$, the Ag-Pd interactions at this composition are **energetically unfavourable** — like-atom bonds (Ag-Ag and Pd-Pd) are preferred over unlike bonds (Ag-Pd). By the definition $\varepsilon = E_{AB} - \tfrac{1}{2}(E_{AA}+E_{BB})$, a positive $\Delta H_{\text{mix}}$ corresponds to $\varepsilon > 0$, indicating a tendency toward **clustering** rather than ordering at lower temperatures.
L5|hard.final_answer: (a) $\gamma_{\text{Ag}} = 1.083$, $\Omega = +5387$ J/mol; (b) $a_{\text{Pd}} = 0.650$ at $X_{\text{Pd}}=0.60$; (c) $\Delta G_{\text{mix}} \approx -5977$ J/mol at $X_{\text{Pd}}=0.40$; (d) $\Delta G_{\text{mix}}^{\text{ideal}} = -7273$ J/mol — the real value is less negative by $\approx +1293$ J/mol, reflecting $\Delta H_{\text{mix}} > 0$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ (clustering tendency).
common_mistakes: **Using the wrong composition in the regular-solution exponent.** For component $i$, the exponent is $(1-X_i)^2 = (X_j)^2$, i.e. the mole fraction of the *other* component squared. Students often accidentally square $X_i$ instead, reversing which atom is the 'minority'.

**Evaluating $a_{\text{Pd}}$ at $X_{\text{Pd}}=0.60$ (from part b) instead of at $X_{\text{Pd}}=0.40$ when computing $\Delta G_{\text{mix}}$ in part (c).** The mixing energy must be computed at the single composition of interest; importing a result from a different composition is a conceptual error even though both compositions appear in the problem.

**Forgetting that $\Delta G_{\text{mix}} = RT\sum_i X_i \ln a_i$ (using actual activities), not $RT\sum_i X_i \ln X_i$ (which gives the ideal value).** Students who memo-learn the ideal formula often substitute mole fractions even when the problem has already established non-ideal activity data.

L5|hard.title: Gibbs-Duhem Integration for Solute Activity in Ag-Au
L5|hard.statement:
A researcher measures the chemical potential of gold (Au) in a silver–gold (Ag-Au) liquid alloy at 1400 K over a range of compositions using vapour-pressure methods. The activity of Au relative to pure liquid Au is found to follow:

$$a_\text{Au} = X_\text{Au} \cdot \gamma_\text{Au}$$

where the activity coefficient of Au obeys the **Margules (regular-solution) expression**:

$$\ln \gamma_\text{Au} = \frac{\Omega}{RT}(1 - X_\text{Au})^2$$

with the regular-solution interaction parameter $\Omega = +8{,}500$ J mol$^{-1}$.

The system is binary: components are Ag (1) and Au (2). Use $R = 8.314$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$, $T = 1400$ K.

**(a)** Compute $\ln \gamma_\text{Au}$ and $\gamma_\text{Au}$ at $X_\text{Au} = 0.20$.

**(b)** Compute the activity $a_\text{Au}$ at $X_\text{Au} = 0.20$.

**(c)** Using the **Gibbs-Duhem equation** at constant $T$ and $P$,
$$X_\text{Ag}\,\mathrm{d}\ln a_\text{Ag} + X_\text{Au}\,\mathrm{d}\ln a_\text{Au} = 0$$
derive the regular-solution expression for $\ln \gamma_\text{Ag}$ and hence compute $a_\text{Ag}$ at $X_\text{Au} = 0.20$ (i.e. $X_\text{Ag} = 0.80$).

**(d)** Verify your result in (c) by confirming that both $\ln \gamma_\text{Ag}$ and $\ln \gamma_\text{Au}$ are consistent with the **Gibbs-Duhem constraint** evaluated at $X_\text{Au} = 0.20$. Specifically, check that $X_\text{Ag}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_\text{Ag} + X_\text{Au}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_\text{Au} = 0$ is satisfied by your activity coefficients.
L5|hard.solution:
## Step 1 — Given information

- Binary Ag-Au alloy at $T = 1400$ K
- Regular-solution parameter: $\Omega = +8{,}500$ J mol$^{-1}$
- $R = 8.314$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$
- Composition: $X_\text{Au} = 0.20$, so $X_\text{Ag} = 0.80$
- Regular-solution form: $\ln \gamma_\text{Au} = \dfrac{\Omega}{RT}(1 - X_\text{Au})^2$

Compute the dimensionless parameter first:
$$\frac{\Omega}{RT} = \frac{8{,}500}{8.314 \times 1400} = \frac{8{,}500}{11{,}639.6} = 0.7302$$

---

## Part (a) — $\ln \gamma_\text{Au}$ and $\gamma_\text{Au}$ at $X_\text{Au} = 0.20$

$$\ln \gamma_\text{Au} = \frac{\Omega}{RT}(1 - X_\text{Au})^2 = 0.7302 \times (1 - 0.20)^2 = 0.7302 \times (0.80)^2$$

$$= 0.7302 \times 0.6400 = 0.4673$$

$$\gamma_\text{Au} = e^{0.4673} = 1.596$$

Since $\Omega > 0$, like-atom bonds are preferred, so $\gamma_\text{Au} > 1$ (positive deviation from Raoult's Law). Au in an Ag-rich matrix is less stable than in pure Au — it has a higher escaping tendency.

---

## Part (b) — Activity $a_\text{Au}$ at $X_\text{Au} = 0.20$

$$a_\text{Au} = \gamma_\text{Au} \cdot X_\text{Au} = 1.596 \times 0.20 = 0.3192$$

Note that for an ideal solution, $a_\text{Au}^\text{ideal} = X_\text{Au} = 0.20$. The real activity (0.319) is higher than the ideal value — a consequence of the positive $\Omega$.

---

## Part (c) — Deriving $\ln \gamma_\text{Ag}$ via Gibbs-Duhem and computing $a_\text{Ag}$

### Derivation

The Gibbs-Duhem equation at constant $T$, $P$ for a binary:
$$X_\text{Ag}\,\mathrm{d}\ln a_\text{Ag} + X_\text{Au}\,\mathrm{d}\ln a_\text{Au} = 0$$

Substitute $\ln a_i = \ln X_i + \ln \gamma_i$:
$$X_\text{Ag}\,\mathrm{d}\ln \gamma_\text{Ag} + X_\text{Au}\,\mathrm{d}\ln \gamma_\text{Au} = 0$$

(The $\mathrm{d}\ln X$ terms cancel because $X_\text{Ag} + X_\text{Au} = 1$ forces $\mathrm{d}X_\text{Ag} = -\mathrm{d}X_\text{Au}$, and $X_\text{Ag}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}X_\text{Ag}}{X_\text{Ag}} + X_\text{Au}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}X_\text{Au}}{X_\text{Au}} = \mathrm{d}X_\text{Ag} + \mathrm{d}X_\text{Au} = 0$.)

Let $x \equiv X_\text{Au}$, so $X_\text{Ag} = 1 - x$. From the regular-solution model:
$$\ln \gamma_\text{Au} = \frac{\Omega}{RT}(1 - x)^2$$

Differentiate with respect to $x$:
$$\frac{\mathrm{d}\ln \gamma_\text{Au}}{\mathrm{d}x} = \frac{\Omega}{RT} \cdot 2(1-x)(-1) = -\frac{2\Omega}{RT}(1-x)$$

Gibbs-Duhem rearranged:
$$\frac{\mathrm{d}\ln \gamma_\text{Ag}}{\mathrm{d}x} = -\frac{X_\text{Au}}{X_\text{Ag}}\frac{\mathrm{d}\ln \gamma_\text{Au}}{\mathrm{d}x} = -\frac{x}{1-x}\cdot\left(-\frac{2\Omega}{RT}(1-x)\right) = \frac{2\Omega}{RT}\,x$$

Integrate from $x = 0$ to $x$ (boundary condition: at $X_\text{Au} = 0$, pure Ag, $\gamma_\text{Ag} = 1$ so $\ln \gamma_\text{Ag} = 0$):
$$\ln \gamma_\text{Ag} = \int_0^x \frac{2\Omega}{RT}\,x'\,\mathrm{d}x' = \frac{2\Omega}{RT}\cdot\frac{x^2}{2} = \frac{\Omega}{RT}\,x^2 = \frac{\Omega}{RT}X_\text{Au}^2$$

This is the **symmetric regular-solution result**:
$$\boxed{\ln \gamma_\text{Ag} = \frac{\Omega}{RT}\,X_\text{Au}^2}$$

### Numerical evaluation at $X_\text{Au} = 0.20$

$$\ln \gamma_\text{Ag} = 0.7302 \times (0.20)^2 = 0.7302 \times 0.0400 = 0.02921$$

$$\gamma_\text{Ag} = e^{0.02921} = 1.0296$$

Activity of Ag:
$$a_\text{Ag} = \gamma_\text{Ag} \cdot X_\text{Ag} = 1.0296 \times 0.80 = 0.8237$$

Note that the Ag solvent follows Raoult's Law closely at $X_\text{Ag} = 0.80$ (the ideal value would be 0.80): $a_\text{Ag}^\text{ideal} = 0.80$, and the actual value (0.824) is only 3% higher, consistent with Ag being the majority solvent and $\Omega > 0$.

---

## Part (d) — Gibbs-Duhem consistency check

The Gibbs-Duhem condition requires that at any composition:
$$X_\text{Ag}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}\ln \gamma_\text{Ag}}{\mathrm{d}X_\text{Au}} + X_\text{Au}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}\ln \gamma_\text{Au}}{\mathrm{d}X_\text{Au}} = 0$$

Compute each derivative from the regular-solution expressions:
$$\frac{\mathrm{d}\ln \gamma_\text{Ag}}{\mathrm{d}X_\text{Au}} = \frac{2\Omega}{RT}\,X_\text{Au}$$

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}\ln \gamma_\text{Au}}{\mathrm{d}X_\text{Au}} = -\frac{2\Omega}{RT}(1 - X_\text{Au}) = -\frac{2\Omega}{RT}\,X_\text{Ag}$$

Substitute into the Gibbs-Duhem check:
$$X_\text{Ag}\cdot\frac{2\Omega}{RT}\,X_\text{Au} + X_\text{Au}\cdot\left(-\frac{2\Omega}{RT}\,X_\text{Ag}\right) = \frac{2\Omega}{RT}\,X_\text{Ag}\,X_\text{Au} - \frac{2\Omega}{RT}\,X_\text{Au}\,X_\text{Ag} = 0\;\checkmark$$

Numerically at $X_\text{Au} = 0.20$, $X_\text{Ag} = 0.80$:
- LHS term 1: $0.80 \times 2(0.7302)(0.20) = 0.80 \times 0.2921 = 0.2337$
- LHS term 2: $0.20 \times (-2)(0.7302)(0.80) = 0.20 \times (-1.1683) = -0.2337$
- Sum: $0.2337 - 0.2337 = 0$ ✓

The two activity coefficient expressions are thermodynamically consistent.

---

## Summary of results

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| $\Omega/RT$ | 0.7302 |
| $\ln \gamma_\text{Au}$ at $X_\text{Au}=0.20$ | 0.4673 |
| $\gamma_\text{Au}$ at $X_\text{Au}=0.20$ | 1.596 |
| $a_\text{Au}$ at $X_\text{Au}=0.20$ | 0.319 |
| $\ln \gamma_\text{Ag}$ at $X_\text{Au}=0.20$ | 0.02921 |
| $\gamma_\text{Ag}$ at $X_\text{Au}=0.20$ | 1.030 |
| $a_\text{Ag}$ at $X_\text{Au}=0.20$ | 0.824 |
L5|hard.final_answer: $a_\text{Au} = 0.319$, $a_\text{Ag} = 0.824$ at $X_\text{Au} = 0.20$, $T = 1400$ K. The Gibbs-Duhem equation gives $\ln\gamma_\text{Ag} = (\Omega/RT)X_\text{Au}^2 = 0.02921$.
common_mistakes: Applying the Gibbs-Duhem equation as $X_\text{Ag}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_\text{Ag} + X_\text{Au}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_\text{Au} = 0$ but forgetting that $\mathrm{d}\ln X_i$ terms cancel identically, so only the $\mathrm{d}\ln\gamma_i$ terms survive — students often include a spurious $\mathrm{d}\ln X$ contribution and reach the wrong differential equation for $\gamma_\text{Ag}$.

Confusing which species is solute vs. solvent in the boundary condition: the correct lower limit of integration is $X_\text{Au} \to 0$ (pure Ag), where $\gamma_\text{Ag} \to 1$ and $\ln\gamma_\text{Ag} \to 0$. Using $X_\text{Au} \to 1$ instead gives the wrong sign and a divergent result.

Forgetting that $\gamma > 1$ (positive deviation) corresponds to $\Omega > 0$ (like-atom bonds preferred), not $\Omega < 0$. Students sometimes reason that a positive $\Omega$ means stronger mixing and therefore underestimate activities, when in fact positive $\Omega$ destabilises mixing and raises activities above their ideal (Raoult's Law) values.

L5|hard.title: Activity Coefficient from Gibbs-Duhem Integration in a Pb-Sn Melt
L5|hard.statement:
A binary liquid Pb-Sn alloy is studied at 600 K and 1 atm. Vapour-pressure measurements of the solvent Sn give the following activity data as a function of composition:

| $X_\text{Sn}$ | $a_\text{Sn}$ |
|:---:|:---:|
| 1.00 | 1.000 |
| 0.80 | 0.860 |
| 0.60 | 0.700 |
| 0.40 | 0.520 |
| 0.20 | 0.280 |

The alloy of interest has overall composition $X_\text{Pb} = 0.40$ (i.e. $X_\text{Sn} = 0.60$).

**(a)** Compute the activity coefficient of Sn, $\gamma_\text{Sn}$, at each tabulated composition and confirm that the Sn data obey Raoult's Law in the limit $X_\text{Sn} \to 1$.

**(b)** Using the Gibbs-Duhem equation at constant $T$ and $P$,
$$X_\text{Sn}\,\mathrm{d}\ln a_\text{Sn} + X_\text{Pb}\,\mathrm{d}\ln a_\text{Pb} = 0,$$
perform a **graphical/numerical integration** to obtain $\ln a_\text{Pb}$ at $X_\text{Pb} = 0.40$ (i.e. $X_\text{Sn} = 0.60$). Use the tabulated Sn data directly. Start from the Henry's-Law anchor: as $X_\text{Pb} \to 0$ (i.e. $X_\text{Sn} \to 1$), $\ln a_\text{Pb} \to -\infty$, so instead apply the integration from $X_\text{Sn} = 0.20$ to $X_\text{Sn} = 0.60$, using the boundary condition that at $X_\text{Sn} = 0.20$ ($X_\text{Pb} = 0.80$) the activity of Pb is $a_\text{Pb} = 0.73$ (independently measured).

**(c)** From your result, compute the activity coefficient $\gamma_\text{Pb}$ at $X_\text{Pb} = 0.40$ and state whether the Pb-Sn liquid shows a positive or negative deviation from Raoult's Law for Pb at this composition. Provide a brief physical interpretation in terms of the bond-energy parameter $\varepsilon$.
L5|hard.solution:
## Step-by-step solution

### Part (a) — Activity coefficient of Sn

The activity coefficient is defined as $\gamma_i = a_i / X_i$ (from L5 §5.6). Apply to each row:

| $X_\text{Sn}$ | $a_\text{Sn}$ | $\gamma_\text{Sn} = a_\text{Sn}/X_\text{Sn}$ |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 1.00 | 1.000 | 1.000 |
| 0.80 | 0.860 | 1.075 |
| 0.60 | 0.700 | 1.167 |
| 0.40 | 0.520 | 1.300 |
| 0.20 | 0.280 | 1.400 |

As $X_\text{Sn} \to 1$, $\gamma_\text{Sn} \to 1.000$ — **Raoult's Law is obeyed by the solvent in the dilute-Pb limit**, confirming the expected behaviour (L5 §5.6).

The increasing $\gamma_\text{Sn} > 1$ as $X_\text{Sn}$ decreases signals a **positive deviation** from ideality: Sn atoms in a Pb-rich environment are less stable than in pure Sn.

---

### Part (b) — Gibbs-Duhem integration for $a_\text{Pb}$

**Strategy.** Rearrange the Gibbs-Duhem equation:

$$\mathrm{d}\ln a_\text{Pb} = -\frac{X_\text{Sn}}{X_\text{Pb}}\,\mathrm{d}\ln a_\text{Sn}$$

Integrate from $X_\text{Sn} = 0.20$ (where $a_\text{Pb} = 0.73$ is known) to $X_\text{Sn} = 0.60$ (the target):

$$\ln a_\text{Pb}(X_\text{Sn}=0.60) = \ln a_\text{Pb}(X_\text{Sn}=0.20) - \int_{0.20}^{0.60} \frac{X_\text{Sn}}{X_\text{Pb}}\,\mathrm{d}\ln a_\text{Sn}$$

**Anchor value:**
$$\ln a_\text{Pb}(X_\text{Sn}=0.20) = \ln(0.73) = -0.3147$$

**Build the integrand** $f \equiv \dfrac{X_\text{Sn}}{X_\text{Pb}}\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\ln a_\text{Sn}}{\mathrm{d}X_\text{Sn}}$ using finite differences on $\ln a_\text{Sn}$:

Compute $\ln a_\text{Sn}$ at each composition:

| $X_\text{Sn}$ | $a_\text{Sn}$ | $\ln a_\text{Sn}$ |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 0.20 | 0.280 | $-1.2730$ |
| 0.40 | 0.520 | $-0.6539$ |
| 0.60 | 0.700 | $-0.3567$ |

Estimate $\mathrm{d}\ln a_\text{Sn}/\mathrm{d}X_\text{Sn}$ by central/forward differences:

**Interval $X_\text{Sn} = 0.20 \to 0.40$** (width $\Delta X_\text{Sn} = 0.20$):
$$\frac{\Delta\ln a_\text{Sn}}{\Delta X_\text{Sn}} = \frac{-0.6539 - (-1.2730)}{0.20} = \frac{0.6191}{0.20} = 3.096$$

Mid-point $X_\text{Sn} = 0.30$, $X_\text{Pb} = 0.70$:
$$f_1 = \frac{0.30}{0.70} \times 3.096 = 0.4286 \times 3.096 = 1.327$$

Contribution: $f_1 \times \Delta X_\text{Sn} = 1.327 \times 0.20 = 0.2654$

**Interval $X_\text{Sn} = 0.40 \to 0.60$** (width $\Delta X_\text{Sn} = 0.20$):
$$\frac{\Delta\ln a_\text{Sn}}{\Delta X_\text{Sn}} = \frac{-0.3567 - (-0.6539)}{0.20} = \frac{0.2972}{0.20} = 1.486$$

Mid-point $X_\text{Sn} = 0.50$, $X_\text{Pb} = 0.50$:
$$f_2 = \frac{0.50}{0.50} \times 1.486 = 1.000 \times 1.486 = 1.486$$

Contribution: $f_2 \times \Delta X_\text{Sn} = 1.486 \times 0.20 = 0.2972$

**Total integral:**
$$\int_{0.20}^{0.60} \frac{X_\text{Sn}}{X_\text{Pb}}\,\mathrm{d}\ln a_\text{Sn} \approx 0.2654 + 0.2972 = 0.5626$$

**Apply Gibbs-Duhem result:**
$$\ln a_\text{Pb}(X_\text{Sn}=0.60) = -0.3147 - 0.5626 = -0.8773$$

$$\boxed{a_\text{Pb}(X_\text{Pb}=0.40) = e^{-0.8773} \approx 0.416}$$

---

### Part (c) — Activity coefficient and physical interpretation

$$\gamma_\text{Pb} = \frac{a_\text{Pb}}{X_\text{Pb}} = \frac{0.416}{0.40} = \boxed{1.04}$$

$\gamma_\text{Pb} > 1$ — a **positive deviation from Raoult's Law**.

**Physical interpretation.** In the Pb-Sn system, Pb-Pb and Sn-Sn bonds are energetically preferred over Pb-Sn bonds. This corresponds to a **positive bond-energy parameter** $\varepsilon = E_\text{PbSn} - \tfrac{1}{2}(E_\text{PbPb} + E_\text{SnSn}) > 0$ (L5 §5.7). Pb atoms in a Sn-rich environment are surrounded by less-favoured unlike bonds, raising their chemical potential above the Raoult's-Law baseline — hence $\gamma > 1$. If $\varepsilon$ were large and positive enough, the system would phase-separate at low temperature (a miscibility gap would open). Indeed, Pb-Sn shows a eutectic phase diagram consistent with this positive $\Delta H_\text{mix}$.
L5|hard.final_answer: $a_\text{Pb} \approx 0.416$ and $\gamma_\text{Pb} \approx 1.04$ at $X_\text{Pb} = 0.40$, 600 K — positive deviation from Raoult's Law.
common_mistakes: **Inverting the Gibbs-Duhem integrand sign.** The relation is $\mathrm{d}\ln a_\text{Pb} = -(X_\text{Sn}/X_\text{Pb})\,\mathrm{d}\ln a_\text{Sn}$. Students frequently drop the minus sign, obtaining $\ln a_\text{Pb}$ larger than the anchor rather than smaller, and conclude a non-physical activity greater than 1 for Pb.

**Confusing the integration variable with the mole fraction of the component being found.** The integration is performed over $\mathrm{d}X_\text{Sn}$ (the measured component) from 0.20 to 0.60 even though we seek $a_\text{Pb}$; students sometimes integrate in the wrong direction or use $X_\text{Pb}$ as the variable, which flips both the ratio $X_\text{Sn}/X_\text{Pb}$ and the sign of $\mathrm{d}X$.

**Claiming $\gamma_\text{Sn} \to 1$ proves the *solute* obeys Raoult's Law.** Raoult's Law for the *solvent* ($\gamma \to 1$ as $X \to 1$) is a different limit from Henry's Law for the *solute* ($\gamma \to \gamma^\infty$ as $X \to 0$). Students conflate the two, incorrectly asserting that because $\gamma_\text{Sn}(X_\text{Sn}=1)=1$, Pb also obeys Raoult's Law at low concentrations.

L5|hard.title: Gibbs-Duhem Integration for a Binary Ag-Pb Alloy
L5|hard.statement:
A binary liquid alloy of silver (Ag) and lead (Pb) is studied at 1100 K. Experimental vapour-pressure measurements show that the activity of Ag (component A) follows the expression

$$a_\text{Ag} = X_\text{Ag} \exp\!\left[\,\Omega\,(1 - X_\text{Ag})^2 / RT\,\right]$$

with the regular-solution interaction parameter $\Omega = +18{,}000$ J/mol (positive, indicating Ag-Ag and Pb-Pb bonds are preferred over Ag-Pb bonds), $R = 8.314$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$, $T = 1100$ K.

For a liquid alloy of composition $X_\text{Ag} = 0.30$:

**(a)** Calculate the activity coefficient of Ag, $\gamma_\text{Ag}$, at this composition.

**(b)** Use the **Gibbs-Duhem equation** at constant $T$ and $P$ to derive the activity coefficient of Pb, $\gamma_\text{Pb}$, in the regular-solution model. Show that the result is

$$\ln \gamma_\text{Pb} = \frac{\Omega\, X_\text{Ag}^2}{RT}$$

and evaluate it numerically at $X_\text{Ag} = 0.30$ (i.e. $X_\text{Pb} = 0.70$).

**(c)** Hence calculate the molar Gibbs energy of mixing, $\Delta G_\text{mix}$, for this alloy at $X_\text{Ag} = 0.30$, and compare its magnitude with the ideal-solution value at the same composition. State whether the solution is more or less stable than ideal, and explain physically why.

**Data summary:** $\Omega = +18{,}000$ J/mol, $T = 1100$ K, $R = 8.314$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$, $X_\text{Ag} = 0.30$, $X_\text{Pb} = 0.70$.
L5|hard.solution:
## Part (a) — Activity coefficient of Ag

The activity of Ag in the regular-solution model is

$$a_\text{Ag} = X_\text{Ag}\,\gamma_\text{Ag}$$

From the given expression,

$$a_\text{Ag} = X_\text{Ag}\exp\!\left[\frac{\Omega(1-X_\text{Ag})^2}{RT}\right]$$

Comparing, the activity coefficient is

$$\gamma_\text{Ag} = \exp\!\left[\frac{\Omega(1-X_\text{Ag})^2}{RT}\right]$$

Substitute values at $X_\text{Ag} = 0.30$:

$$\frac{\Omega(1-X_\text{Ag})^2}{RT} = \frac{18{,}000 \times (0.70)^2}{8.314 \times 1100} = \frac{18{,}000 \times 0.49}{9{,}145.4} = \frac{8{,}820}{9{,}145.4} = 0.9644$$

$$\boxed{\gamma_\text{Ag} = e^{0.9644} \approx 2.624}$$

Since $\gamma_\text{Ag} > 1$, Ag has a greater escaping tendency than in an ideal solution — consistent with $\Omega > 0$ (like–like bonds preferred, Ag is less comfortable surrounded by Pb).

---

## Part (b) — Deriving and evaluating $\gamma_\text{Pb}$ via Gibbs-Duhem

### Step 1 — Write down the Gibbs-Duhem equation

At constant $T$ and $P$ for a binary system:

$$X_\text{Ag}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_\text{Ag} + X_\text{Pb}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_\text{Pb} = 0$$

Using $\mu_i = \mu_i^\circ + RT\ln a_i = \mu_i^\circ + RT\ln(\gamma_i X_i)$, differentiate at constant $T$:

$$\mathrm{d}\mu_i = RT\,\mathrm{d}\ln a_i = RT\,\mathrm{d}\ln(\gamma_i X_i)$$

So the Gibbs-Duhem equation becomes:

$$X_\text{Ag}\,\mathrm{d}\ln a_\text{Ag} + X_\text{Pb}\,\mathrm{d}\ln a_\text{Pb} = 0$$

$$\mathrm{d}\ln a_\text{Pb} = -\frac{X_\text{Ag}}{X_\text{Pb}}\,\mathrm{d}\ln a_\text{Ag}$$

### Step 2 — Express $\ln a_\text{Ag}$ and differentiate

From the regular-solution form:

$$\ln a_\text{Ag} = \ln X_\text{Ag} + \frac{\Omega(1-X_\text{Ag})^2}{RT}$$

Let $X \equiv X_\text{Ag}$, so $X_\text{Pb} = 1-X$. Differentiate with respect to $X$:

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}\ln a_\text{Ag}}{\mathrm{d}X} = \frac{1}{X} + \frac{\Omega}{RT}\cdot 2(1-X)(-1) = \frac{1}{X} - \frac{2\Omega(1-X)}{RT}$$

### Step 3 — Substitute into Gibbs-Duhem and integrate

$$\mathrm{d}\ln a_\text{Pb} = -\frac{X}{1-X}\left[\frac{1}{X} - \frac{2\Omega(1-X)}{RT}\right]\mathrm{d}X = -\frac{X}{1-X}\cdot\frac{1}{X}\,\mathrm{d}X + \frac{X}{1-X}\cdot\frac{2\Omega(1-X)}{RT}\,\mathrm{d}X$$

$$= -\frac{1}{1-X}\,\mathrm{d}X + \frac{2\Omega X}{RT}\,\mathrm{d}X$$

Integrate from $X = 0$ (pure Pb, where $a_\text{Pb} = 1$, $\ln a_\text{Pb} = 0$) to general $X$:

$$\ln a_\text{Pb} = \int_0^X \left[-\frac{1}{1-X'} + \frac{2\Omega X'}{RT}\right]\mathrm{d}X'$$

$$= \Big[\ln(1-X')\Big]_0^X + \frac{\Omega X'^2}{RT}\Big|_0^X$$

$$= \ln(1-X) - \ln 1 + \frac{\Omega X^2}{RT}$$

$$= \ln X_\text{Pb} + \frac{\Omega X_\text{Ag}^2}{RT}$$

Since $a_\text{Pb} = X_\text{Pb}\,\gamma_\text{Pb}$, we have $\ln a_\text{Pb} = \ln X_\text{Pb} + \ln\gamma_\text{Pb}$, giving:

$$\boxed{\ln\gamma_\text{Pb} = \frac{\Omega X_\text{Ag}^2}{RT}}$$

This is the standard regular-solution result — the activity coefficient of each component depends on the **square of the opposite component's mole fraction**.

### Step 4 — Evaluate numerically at $X_\text{Ag} = 0.30$

$$\ln\gamma_\text{Pb} = \frac{18{,}000 \times (0.30)^2}{8.314 \times 1100} = \frac{18{,}000 \times 0.09}{9{,}145.4} = \frac{1{,}620}{9{,}145.4} = 0.1772$$

$$\boxed{\gamma_\text{Pb} = e^{0.1772} \approx 1.194}$$

Note: $\gamma_\text{Pb} < \gamma_\text{Ag}$ because Pb is the majority component at $X_\text{Pb} = 0.70$ — it sees mostly Pb neighbours (closer to its Raoult's Law limit), while Ag at $X_\text{Ag} = 0.30$ sees more Pb neighbours and deviates more strongly.

---

## Part (c) — Molar Gibbs energy of mixing

The general expression is:

$$\Delta G_\text{mix} = RT(X_\text{Ag}\ln a_\text{Ag} + X_\text{Pb}\ln a_\text{Pb})$$

Alternatively, split into ideal and excess contributions:

$$\Delta G_\text{mix} = \underbrace{RT(X_\text{Ag}\ln X_\text{Ag} + X_\text{Pb}\ln X_\text{Pb})}_{\Delta G_\text{mix}^\text{ideal}} + \underbrace{RT(X_\text{Ag}\ln\gamma_\text{Ag} + X_\text{Pb}\ln\gamma_\text{Pb})}_{\Delta G_\text{mix}^\text{excess}}$$

### Ideal contribution:

$$\Delta G_\text{mix}^\text{ideal} = RT(0.30\ln 0.30 + 0.70\ln 0.70)$$

$$= 9{,}145.4\times(0.30\times(-1.2040) + 0.70\times(-0.3567))$$

$$= 9{,}145.4\times(-0.3612 - 0.2497)$$

$$= 9{,}145.4\times(-0.6109) = -5{,}587\;\text{J/mol}$$

### Excess (non-ideal) contribution:

In the regular-solution model:

$$\Delta G_\text{mix}^\text{excess} = RT(X_\text{Ag}\ln\gamma_\text{Ag} + X_\text{Pb}\ln\gamma_\text{Pb}) = \Omega X_\text{Ag} X_\text{Pb}$$

$$= 18{,}000 \times 0.30 \times 0.70 = 18{,}000 \times 0.21 = +3{,}780\;\text{J/mol}$$

*(Verification: $RT(0.30\times 0.9644 + 0.70\times 0.1772) = 9{,}145.4\times(0.2893+0.1240) = 9{,}145.4\times 0.4133 = 3{,}781$ J/mol ✓)*

### Total:

$$\boxed{\Delta G_\text{mix} = -5{,}587 + 3{,}780 = -1{,}807\;\text{J/mol}}$$

### Comparison with ideal solution:

The ideal-solution value is $\Delta G_\text{mix}^\text{ideal} = -5{,}587$ J/mol. The real solution has $\Delta G_\text{mix} = -1{,}807$ J/mol, which is **less negative** (less stable) than ideal by $3{,}780$ J/mol.

**Physical interpretation:** With $\Omega > 0$, Ag-Pb bonds are energetically unfavourable relative to Ag-Ag and Pb-Pb bonds ($\Delta H_\text{mix} = +3{,}780$ J/mol > 0). This positive enthalpy of mixing partially offsets the always-favourable entropy of mixing. The alloy still forms spontaneously at 1100 K because $T\Delta S_\text{mix}$ is large enough to overcome $\Delta H_\text{mix}$, but the solution is **less thermodynamically stable than an ideal solution** — and at lower temperatures, the competition could produce a miscibility gap where the alloy phase-separates into Ag-rich and Pb-rich regions.
L5|hard.final_answer: (a) $\gamma_\text{Ag} \approx 2.624$; (b) $\gamma_\text{Pb} \approx 1.194$; (c) $\Delta G_\text{mix} = -1{,}807$ J/mol, which is less negative than the ideal value of $-5{,}587$ J/mol by $+3{,}780$ J/mol.
common_mistakes: Applying the Gibbs-Duhem equation incorrectly by differentiating with respect to $X_\text{Pb}$ instead of $X_\text{Ag}$ (or vice versa) without adjusting the sign, leading to integration bounds or sign errors in $\ln\gamma_\text{Pb}$.

Evaluating $\Delta G_\text{mix}^\text{excess} = RT(X_\text{Ag}\ln\gamma_\text{Ag} + X_\text{Pb}\ln\gamma_\text{Pb})$ by substituting the numerical $\ln\gamma$ values without noticing the shortcut $\Omega X_\text{Ag} X_\text{Pb}$, then making arithmetic errors with the small differences — always verify both routes agree.

Concluding the alloy is 'unstable' because $\Delta G_\text{mix}$ is less negative than ideal. The alloy is still stable against unmixing (total $\Delta G_\text{mix} < 0$) at 1100 K; it is merely less stable than an ideal solution. A miscibility gap only opens when $\Delta G_\text{mix}$ develops a concave region, which occurs below a critical temperature $T_c = \Omega/(2R) \approx 1082$ K for the symmetric regular solution — just below 1100 K, so this system is near-critical.

L5|hard.title: Miscibility Gap and Phase Separation in a Regular Cu–Ag Solution
L5|hard.statement:
The Cu–Ag binary system at low temperatures forms two distinct solid phases (a Cu-rich $\alpha$ phase and an Ag-rich $\beta$ phase) because silver and copper strongly prefer like–like bonds. The system is well described by the **regular solution model**, in which the molar Gibbs energy of mixing is

$$\Delta G_\text{mix} = \Omega\, X_\text{Cu}\, X_\text{Ag} + RT\left(X_\text{Cu}\ln X_\text{Cu} + X_\text{Ag}\ln X_\text{Ag}\right)$$

where $\Omega = +21{,}000\;\text{J mol}^{-1}$ is the regular-solution interaction parameter for Cu–Ag.

**(a)** At $T = 700\;\text{K}$, evaluate $\Delta G_\text{mix}$ (J mol$^{-1}$) at the equimolar composition $X_\text{Cu} = 0.50$. State whether mixing is spontaneous at this composition and temperature.

**(b)** A two-phase miscibility gap opens below a critical temperature $T_c$. For the symmetric regular solution the critical temperature is given by

$$T_c = \frac{\Omega}{2R}$$

Calculate $T_c$ for Cu–Ag.

**(c)** At $T = 900\;\text{K}$ (below the critical temperature you found), the system phase-separates into a Cu-rich phase $\alpha$ and an Ag-rich phase $\beta$. A common-tangent construction gives the equilibrium compositions $X_\text{Cu}^\alpha = 0.85$ and $X_\text{Cu}^\beta = 0.15$.

An overall alloy of composition $X_\text{Cu} = 0.60$ is held at $T = 900\;\text{K}$ until equilibrium is reached. Using the **lever rule**, determine the mole fractions of the $\alpha$ and $\beta$ phases present at equilibrium.

**(d)** Using $\mu_i = \mu_i^\circ + RT\ln a_i$ and the regular-solution result that the activity coefficient of Cu in the $\alpha$ phase at $T = 900\;\text{K}$, $X_\text{Cu}^\alpha = 0.85$ is

$$\ln\gamma_\text{Cu}^\alpha = \frac{\Omega}{RT}\left(1 - X_\text{Cu}^\alpha\right)^2$$

calculate $\gamma_\text{Cu}^\alpha$ and hence the activity $a_\text{Cu}^\alpha$ at this composition. Then verify that the equilibrium condition $a_\text{Cu}^\alpha = a_\text{Cu}^\beta$ is consistent with the $\beta$-phase composition $X_\text{Cu}^\beta = 0.15$ (use the same formula for $\ln\gamma_\text{Cu}^\beta$ with $X_\text{Cu}^\beta = 0.15$).

**Given data:** $R = 8.314\;\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$, $\Omega = 21{,}000\;\text{J mol}^{-1}$.
L5|hard.solution:
## Part (a) — $\Delta G_\text{mix}$ at $X_\text{Cu} = 0.50$, $T = 700\;\text{K}$

**Ideal entropy term:**
$$\Delta G_\text{mix}^\text{ideal} = RT\left(X_\text{Cu}\ln X_\text{Cu} + X_\text{Ag}\ln X_\text{Ag}\right)$$
$$= (8.314)(700)\left(0.5\ln 0.5 + 0.5\ln 0.5\right)$$
$$= 5819.8 \times \left(2 \times 0.5 \times (-0.6931)\right)$$
$$= 5819.8 \times (-0.6931) = -4032\;\text{J mol}^{-1}$$

**Enthalpy (regular solution) term:**
$$\Delta H_\text{mix} = \Omega\, X_\text{Cu}\, X_\text{Ag} = 21{,}000 \times 0.5 \times 0.5 = +5250\;\text{J mol}^{-1}$$

**Total:**
$$\Delta G_\text{mix} = 5250 + (-4032) = \boxed{+1218\;\text{J mol}^{-1}}$$

Since $\Delta G_\text{mix} > 0$ at $X_\text{Cu} = 0.50$ and $T = 700\;\text{K}$, **mixing is NOT spontaneous** at the equimolar composition. The positive interaction parameter dominates the entropy term at this low temperature, meaning the two-phase separated state has lower Gibbs energy than the homogeneous mixture.

---

## Part (b) — Critical temperature $T_c$

$$T_c = \frac{\Omega}{2R} = \frac{21{,}000}{2 \times 8.314} = \frac{21{,}000}{16.628} = \boxed{1263\;\text{K}}$$

This is above both the melting points of pure Cu (1358 K) and pure Ag (1235 K) — which is why in practice the solid-state miscibility gap is cut off by the liquidus. Nevertheless, the thermodynamic miscibility gap would extend to 1263 K for the hypothetical solid solution, and experimentally the solid solubility is indeed very limited at lower temperatures.

**Sanity check:** at $T = 700\;\text{K} < T_c = 1263\;\text{K}$, the system is inside the miscibility gap (consistent with our positive $\Delta G_\text{mix}$ in part (a)).

---

## Part (c) — Lever rule at $T = 900\;\text{K}$

Given:
- $X_\text{Cu}^\alpha = 0.85$ (Cu-rich $\alpha$ phase)
- $X_\text{Cu}^\beta = 0.15$ (Ag-rich $\beta$ phase)
- Overall composition $X_0 = 0.60$

The lever rule gives the mole fraction of each phase:

$$f^\alpha = \frac{X_0 - X_\text{Cu}^\beta}{X_\text{Cu}^\alpha - X_\text{Cu}^\beta} = \frac{0.60 - 0.15}{0.85 - 0.15} = \frac{0.45}{0.70} = \boxed{0.643}$$

$$f^\beta = \frac{X_\text{Cu}^\alpha - X_0}{X_\text{Cu}^\alpha - X_\text{Cu}^\beta} = \frac{0.85 - 0.60}{0.85 - 0.15} = \frac{0.25}{0.70} = \boxed{0.357}$$

**Check:** $f^\alpha + f^\beta = 0.643 + 0.357 = 1.000$ ✓

**Mass balance:** $0.643 \times 0.85 + 0.357 \times 0.15 = 0.547 + 0.054 = 0.601 \approx 0.60$ ✓ (small rounding)

At equilibrium, **64.3 mol% of the alloy is the Cu-rich $\alpha$ phase** and **35.7 mol% is the Ag-rich $\beta$ phase**.

---

## Part (d) — Activity verification of the equilibrium condition

### Activity in the $\alpha$ phase ($X_\text{Cu}^\alpha = 0.85$, $T = 900\;\text{K}$)

$$\ln\gamma_\text{Cu}^\alpha = \frac{\Omega}{RT}\left(1 - X_\text{Cu}^\alpha\right)^2 = \frac{21{,}000}{(8.314)(900)}\times(0.15)^2$$

$$= \frac{21{,}000}{7482.6}\times 0.0225 = 2.806 \times 0.0225 = 0.06313$$

$$\gamma_\text{Cu}^\alpha = e^{0.06313} = \boxed{1.065}$$

$$a_\text{Cu}^\alpha = \gamma_\text{Cu}^\alpha\, X_\text{Cu}^\alpha = 1.065 \times 0.85 = \boxed{0.905}$$

### Activity in the $\beta$ phase ($X_\text{Cu}^\beta = 0.15$, $T = 900\;\text{K}$)

$$\ln\gamma_\text{Cu}^\beta = \frac{\Omega}{RT}\left(1 - X_\text{Cu}^\beta\right)^2 = 2.806 \times (0.85)^2 = 2.806 \times 0.7225 = 2.027$$

$$\gamma_\text{Cu}^\beta = e^{2.027} = 7.593$$

$$a_\text{Cu}^\beta = \gamma_\text{Cu}^\beta\, X_\text{Cu}^\beta = 7.593 \times 0.15 = \boxed{1.139}$$

### Assessment

$$a_\text{Cu}^\alpha = 0.905 \qquad \text{vs} \qquad a_\text{Cu}^\beta = 1.139$$

The two values are **not exactly equal**, which tells us the common-tangent compositions $X_\text{Cu}^\alpha = 0.85$ and $X_\text{Cu}^\beta = 0.15$ given in the problem are **approximate** (the problem stated they come from a graphical construction). The true equilibrium compositions must be found by solving $a_\text{Cu}^\alpha(X) = a_\text{Cu}^\beta(X')$ simultaneously with $a_\text{Ag}^\alpha(X) = a_\text{Ag}^\beta(X')$ — a nonlinear system requiring numerical iteration. The approximate agreement (activities within ~26% of each other) is physically reasonable given that $T = 900\;\text{K}$ is still well inside the miscibility gap ($T_c = 1263\;\text{K}$), and confirms that the direction of the effect is correct: Cu has **higher activity** in the Ag-rich $\beta$ phase than in the Cu-rich $\alpha$ phase (as expected — a minority Cu atom in a mostly-Ag environment has a large positive deviation from Raoult's Law).

**Physical interpretation:** The large $\gamma_\text{Cu}^\beta = 7.6$ in the $\beta$ phase reflects the strong positive $\Omega > 0$ — Cu atoms surrounded predominantly by Ag are energetically unhappy and have a high escaping tendency, consistent with the tendency to phase-separate.
L5|hard.final_answer: (a) $\Delta G_\text{mix} = +1218\;\text{J mol}^{-1}$ — mixing NOT spontaneous at $X_\text{Cu}=0.50$, $T=700\;\text{K}$; (b) $T_c = 1263\;\text{K}$; (c) $f^\alpha = 0.643$, $f^\beta = 0.357$; (d) $\gamma_\text{Cu}^\alpha = 1.065$, $a_\text{Cu}^\alpha = 0.905$; $\gamma_\text{Cu}^\beta = 7.59$, $a_\text{Cu}^\beta = 1.14$ — not exactly equal, confirming the given compositions are approximate.
common_mistakes: **Applying the lever rule with numerator and denominator swapped.** Students often write $f^\alpha = (X^\alpha - X_0)/(X^\alpha - X^\beta)$ instead of $(X_0 - X^\beta)/(X^\alpha - X^\beta)$, yielding $f^\alpha = 0.357$ (the fraction of $\beta$). Always check: the phase *rich* in component B should dominate when the overall composition is shifted toward B.

**Forgetting that $\Delta G_\text{mix} > 0$ does not necessarily mean a reaction is impossible in all contexts** — here it specifically means the *homogeneous* mixed state is unstable relative to phase separation; students sometimes confuse 'positive $\Delta G_\text{mix}$' with 'no reaction occurs at all' rather than recognising it signals phase separation.

**Using $\ln\gamma_i = (\Omega/RT)(1-X_i)^2$ but inserting the wrong $X_i$.** The formula uses $(1 - X_i)^2$, i.e. the mole fraction of the *other* component squared. For Cu in the $\beta$ phase, $(1 - 0.15)^2 = (0.85)^2$, not $(0.15)^2$. Mixing up which mole fraction to subtract from 1 is the most common numerical error in regular-solution activity calculations.

L6|easy.title: Applying the Gibbs Phase Rule to a Binary Alloy
L6|easy.statement:
A binary alloy system consisting of components A and B is held at constant pressure (1 atm). At a certain temperature, three phases are observed to coexist in equilibrium: a liquid phase $L$, an $\alpha$ solid phase, and a $\beta$ solid phase.

(a) State the Gibbs phase rule (at fixed pressure) and identify the number of components $C$ and phases $P$ for this system.

(b) Calculate the number of degrees of freedom $F$.

(c) What does your answer to (b) tell you about the temperature and compositions at which this three-phase equilibrium can exist?
L6|easy.solution:
## Step 1 — State the Gibbs Phase Rule at fixed pressure

When pressure is fixed (held constant at 1 atm), one degree of freedom is consumed, so the phase rule becomes:

$$F = C - P + 1$$

where $C$ is the number of components and $P$ is the number of phases simultaneously in equilibrium.

## Step 2 — Identify $C$ and $P$

The system has **two chemical components**: A and B, so $C = 2$.

Three phases are present simultaneously: liquid $L$, solid $\alpha$, and solid $\beta$, so $P = 3$.

## Step 3 — Calculate $F$

$$F = C - P + 1 = 2 - 3 + 1 = \boxed{0}$$

## Step 4 — Physical interpretation

$F = 0$ means there are **zero degrees of freedom** — the system is **invariant**. This means:

- The temperature at which $L$, $\alpha$, and $\beta$ coexist is **completely fixed** by the thermodynamics of the A–B system. You cannot change it (at fixed pressure).
- The compositions of each of the three phases ($X_A^L$, $X_A^\alpha$, $X_A^\beta$) are also **completely fixed**.

This three-phase point is called the **eutectic point**. It occurs at a unique $(T_E,\, X_E)$ on the binary phase diagram. Any deviation in temperature or overall composition causes one of the three phases to disappear, reducing $P$ and restoring $F > 0$.
L6|easy.final_answer: $F = C - P + 1 = 2 - 3 + 1 = 0$; the system is invariant — temperature and all phase compositions are uniquely fixed (the eutectic point).
common_mistakes: Using the full phase rule $F = C - P + 2$ without accounting for the fixed-pressure condition. At constant pressure one degree of freedom is already consumed, giving $F = C - P + 1$. Using the uncorrected form gives $F = 1$ instead of $0$, leading to the wrong physical conclusion.

Confusing the number of components $C$ with the number of phases $P$. In a binary system $C = 2$ always (two chemical species), regardless of how many phases are present. Students sometimes write $C = 3$ because they count three phases.

Interpreting $F = 0$ as meaning the reaction cannot proceed or the system is 'frozen'. It means only that temperature and phase compositions are uniquely pinned — the system is at a specific invariant point (the eutectic), not that it is kinetically stuck.

L6|easy.title: Applying the Gibbs Phase Rule to a Ternary System
L6|easy.statement: A materials engineer is studying a three-component (ternary) oxide system consisting of CaO, SiO\_2, and Al\_2O\_3 at a fixed pressure of 1 atm. She observes a sample held at a specific temperature where three distinct solid phases are simultaneously present in equilibrium alongside a liquid (slag) phase — giving four phases in total. Using the Gibbs phase rule at constant pressure ($F = C - P + 1$), determine the number of degrees of freedom $F$ available to the system. Based on your result, state whether the temperature and compositions of the phases can be varied independently while maintaining all four phases in equilibrium.
L6|easy.solution:
## Step 1 — Identify the number of components and phases

The system has **three components** ($C = 3$): CaO, SiO$_2$, and Al$_2$O$_3$.

The number of phases simultaneously in equilibrium is **four** ($P = 4$): three solid phases plus one liquid (slag) phase.

## Step 2 — Apply the Gibbs phase rule at fixed pressure

At constant pressure (1 atm), the Gibbs phase rule reduces to:

$$F = C - P + 1$$

Substituting:

$$F = 3 - 4 + 1 = \boxed{0}$$

## Step 3 — Interpret the result

$F = 0$ means the system is **invariant** — there are **zero degrees of freedom**. Every intensive variable (temperature and all phase compositions) is completely fixed by the constraint that all four phases coexist at equilibrium.

The engineer cannot independently vary the temperature or the composition of any phase while keeping all four phases simultaneously present. The four-phase equilibrium exists at one unique temperature and one unique set of phase compositions. This point is analogous to the **eutectic point** in a binary system (where $F = 0$ at fixed $P$) but extended to a ternary — it is called a **ternary invariant point** (or ternary eutectic/peritectic, depending on the reaction type).
L6|easy.final_answer: $F = 0$ (invariant point — temperature and all phase compositions are uniquely fixed; no independent variation is possible)
common_mistakes: Using the full Gibbs phase rule $F = C - P + 2$ instead of the pressure-fixed form $F = C - P + 1$, which would incorrectly give $F = 1$.
Counting only the solid phases and forgetting the liquid phase, giving $P = 3$ and incorrectly obtaining $F = 1$.
Interpreting $F = 0$ as meaning the system is impossible or forbidden, rather than understanding it means the equilibrium exists at one unique fixed state — a perfectly physical invariant point.

L6|easy.title: Degrees of Freedom at the Cu-Ni Liquidus Boundary
L6|easy.statement:
The copper-nickel (Cu-Ni) binary system is a classic isomorphous system with complete solid solubility. At atmospheric pressure ($P = 1$ atm), a Cu-Ni alloy of composition $X_{\text{Ni}} = 0.40$ (mole fraction) is heated until it just reaches the liquidus boundary, where solid and liquid phases coexist in equilibrium.

Using the Gibbs phase rule, determine the number of degrees of freedom $F$ for this two-phase (solid + liquid) equilibrium at fixed pressure. Briefly explain what this value means physically — specifically, how many intensive variables can be independently varied without destroying the two-phase coexistence.
L6|easy.solution:
