## Step 1 — Identify the system parameters

The system is a **binary** alloy (Cu and Ni), so the number of components is:
$$C = 2$$

At the liquidus boundary, two phases coexist simultaneously (solid $\alpha$ and liquid $L$):
$$P_{\text{phases}} = 2$$

## Step 2 — Apply the Gibbs Phase Rule

The full Gibbs phase rule is:
$$F = C - P_{\text{phases}} + 2$$

Substituting:
$$F = 2 - 2 + 2 = \boxed{2}$$

## Step 3 — Account for fixed pressure

In practice, the experiment is conducted at fixed atmospheric pressure ($P = 1$ atm), which consumes one degree of freedom. The **effective** degrees of freedom at fixed pressure become:
$$F_{\text{eff}} = C - P_{\text{phases}} + 1 = 2 - 2 + 1 = 1$$

## Step 4 — Physical interpretation

With $F_{\text{eff}} = 1$, **only one** intensive variable can be independently chosen while keeping solid and liquid in coexistence at fixed pressure. In practice this means:

- If you **specify the temperature** $T$, the compositions of the liquid phase ($X_{\text{Ni}}^{L}$) and solid phase ($X_{\text{Ni}}^{\alpha}$) are both **fixed** by the liquidus and solidus curves — you have no further freedom.
- Equivalently, if you **specify the composition of one phase**, the temperature is fixed.

This explains why the Cu-Ni two-phase region on the $T$–$X$ diagram appears as a **band bounded by two curves** (liquidus and solidus): at each temperature there is one unique liquid composition and one unique solid composition in equilibrium. The overall alloy composition $X_{\text{Ni}} = 0.40$ tells you *where* in the two-phase region you are (lever rule), but does not change the phase compositions — it only sets the **relative amounts** of each phase.
L6|easy.final_answer: $F = 2$ (full rule); $F_{\text{eff}} = 1$ at fixed pressure — one intensive variable (e.g. temperature) may be varied while maintaining solid–liquid coexistence.
common_mistakes: Confusing the number of phases $P_{\text{phases}}$ in the Gibbs phase rule with the pressure $P$. The Gibbs phase rule is $F = C - P_{\text{phases}} + 2$, where $P_{\text{phases}}$ counts coexisting phases (here 2: solid and liquid), not the mechanical pressure.
Forgetting to reduce $F$ by 1 when pressure is fixed at 1 atm. The full rule gives $F = 2$, but the operative (experimentally relevant) value at fixed pressure is $F_{\text{eff}} = 1$.

Thinking the overall alloy composition $X_{\text{Ni}} = 0.40$ is one of the degrees of freedom being counted. The Gibbs phase rule counts *intensive* variables (like $T$, $P$, and phase compositions). The bulk alloy composition fixes *how much* of each phase is present (lever rule), but does not itself constitute a thermodynamic degree of freedom for phase equilibrium.

L6|easy.title: Degrees of Freedom at the Eutectic Point: Pb-Bi System
L6|easy.statement:
The lead–bismuth (Pb–Bi) binary alloy system forms a eutectic at approximately 44 wt% Bi and 125 °C. At the eutectic temperature, three phases are in equilibrium simultaneously: liquid (L), Pb-rich solid ($\alpha$), and Bi-rich solid ($\beta$).

Using the Gibbs Phase Rule, determine the number of degrees of freedom $F$ for the Pb–Bi system at:

(a) A point inside the single-phase liquid region (e.g., 250 °C, 20 wt% Bi).

(b) A point on the liquidus boundary where liquid and the $\alpha$ solid coexist (two phases).

(c) The eutectic invariant point where all three phases coexist.

For each case, state clearly how many intensive variables (e.g., temperature, composition) may be independently varied without changing the number of phases present. Atmospheric pressure is fixed throughout (1 atm).
L6|easy.solution:
## Setup

The **Gibbs Phase Rule** at fixed pressure (1 atm) is:

$$F = C - P + 1$$

where:
- $C$ = number of components
- $P$ = number of phases in equilibrium
- $F$ = degrees of freedom (variance)

The factor of $+1$ (rather than $+2$) applies because pressure is held fixed, removing one degree of freedom from the full rule $F = C - P + 2$.

For the **Pb–Bi binary system**: $C = 2$ (two components: Pb and Bi).

---

## Part (a) — Single liquid phase ($P = 1$)

Substitute $C = 2$, $P = 1$:

$$F = 2 - 1 + 1 = \boxed{2}$$

**Interpretation:** Two degrees of freedom. Inside the single-phase liquid region, you may independently vary both **temperature** $T$ and **composition** $X_{\text{Bi}}$ over a range without leaving the single-phase field. You have full freedom to choose any $(T, X)$ pair within that region.

---

## Part (b) — Liquid + $\alpha$ solid coexist ($P = 2$)

Substitute $C = 2$, $P = 2$:

$$F = 2 - 2 + 1 = \boxed{1}$$

**Interpretation:** One degree of freedom. Along the liquidus (or solidus) boundary, once you fix **temperature**, the compositions of both the liquid and the $\alpha$ solid are completely determined (they are read off the liquidus and solidus curves at that $T$). You cannot independently choose both $T$ and $X_{\text{Bi}}$ — fixing one fixes the other. This is why two-phase coexistence appears as a **curve** (not an area) when plotted on a $T$ vs. composition diagram at fixed $P$.

---

## Part (c) — Eutectic invariant point: L + $\alpha$ + $\beta$ coexist ($P = 3$)

Substitute $C = 2$, $P = 3$:

$$F = 2 - 3 + 1 = \boxed{0}$$

**Interpretation:** Zero degrees of freedom — the system is **invariant**. The temperature (125 °C), the composition of the liquid (44 wt% Bi), the composition of $\alpha$, and the composition of $\beta$ are all uniquely fixed by the thermodynamics of the Pb–Bi system. You cannot change any intensive variable without causing one of the three phases to disappear. On a phase diagram, this three-phase equilibrium appears as a single **horizontal line** (the eutectic isotherm) connecting the three fixed compositions.

---

## Summary Table

| Condition | Phases $P$ | $F = C - P + 1$ | Meaning |
|---|:---:|:---:|---|
| Single liquid phase | 1 | 2 | $T$ and $X$ both free |
| Liquid + $\alpha$ solid | 2 | 1 | Fix $T$ → $X$ determined |
| Eutectic: L + $\alpha$ + $\beta$ | 3 | 0 | All variables fixed |
common_mistakes: Using the full Gibbs Phase Rule $F = C - P + 2$ instead of the pressure-fixed form $F = C - P + 1$. Since pressure is held at 1 atm throughout, one degree of freedom is already consumed, giving the reduced rule.
Confusing the number of components $C$ with the number of phases $P$. For Pb–Bi, $C = 2$ always (two chemical species); $P$ changes depending on which region of the phase diagram you are examining.

Concluding that $F = 0$ means the reaction 'cannot occur' or that nothing happens at the eutectic. In fact, $F = 0$ simply means the intensive state is fully determined — the eutectic reaction (L → α + β) proceeds at that fixed temperature and composition; it is not blocked.

L6|easy.title: Degrees of Freedom at the Fe-C Eutectoid Point
L6|easy.statement:
The iron-carbon (Fe-C) system is a binary system ($C = 2$ components: iron and carbon). At the **eutectoid point** (727 °C, 0.76 wt% C, 1 atm), three phases coexist simultaneously: $\gamma$-austenite (FCC), $\alpha$-ferrite (BCC), and Fe$_3$C (cementite).

Using the Gibbs Phase Rule, determine the number of degrees of freedom $F$ at the eutectoid point. Explain what this result means physically — can you freely choose any intensive variable (temperature, pressure, or composition) while maintaining all three phases in equilibrium?
L6|easy.solution:
## Step 1 — State the Gibbs Phase Rule

The Gibbs Phase Rule is:
$$F = C - P + 2$$
where:
- $C$ = number of components
- $P$ = number of phases in equilibrium
- $F$ = degrees of freedom (variance)

Here $P$ stands for the number of phases; we use the symbol $\mathcal{P}$ for phases to avoid confusion with pressure, but the formula and logic are identical.

## Step 2 — Identify the system variables

| Quantity | Value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| $C$ | 2 | Two components: Fe and C |
| Number of phases $\mathcal{P}$ | 3 | $\gamma$-austenite + $\alpha$-ferrite + Fe$_3$C coexist |

## Step 3 — Apply the phase rule

$$F = C - \mathcal{P} + 2 = 2 - 3 + 2 = \boxed{1}$$

## Step 4 — Physical interpretation

$F = 1$ means the system is **univariant** — there is exactly **one** independent intensive variable. In practice, pressure is fixed at 1 atm for most metallurgical work, which reduces the effective degrees of freedom by one more:
$$F_{\text{eff}} = C - \mathcal{P} + 1 = 2 - 3 + 1 = 0$$
At fixed pressure, the eutectoid becomes an **invariant point**: temperature (727 °C) and all three phase compositions are fully determined by nature. You cannot change $T$ or any composition while keeping all three phases simultaneously present at 1 atm. This is why the eutectoid appears as a **single horizontal line** (not a region) on the Fe-C phase diagram at 727 °C.
L6|easy.final_answer: $F = 1$ (univariant); at fixed pressure, $F_{\text{eff}} = 0$ — the eutectoid is an invariant point at 727 °C, 0.76 wt% C.
common_mistakes: Confusing the symbol $P$ for pressure with $P$ (or $\mathcal{P}$) for the number of phases in the Gibbs Phase Rule, leading to an incorrect substitution.
Using the pressure-fixed shortcut $F = C - \mathcal{P} + 1$ without first applying the full rule $F = C - \mathcal{P} + 2$, and then misidentifying which formula gives the 'true' degrees of freedom.

Counting only the two end-member solid phases (ferrite and cementite) and forgetting that austenite is also present at the eutectoid, giving $\mathcal{P} = 2$ instead of 3 and arriving at $F = 2$ instead of 1.

L6|easy.title: Eutectic Phase Fraction via Lever Rule
L6|easy.statement:
A binary alloy of lead (Pb) and tin (Sn) contains **40 wt% Sn** at a temperature just below the eutectic temperature of 183 °C and 1 atm pressure. At this temperature, two solid phases coexist in equilibrium: an $\alpha$ phase (Pb-rich) with a composition of **19 wt% Sn**, and a $\beta$ phase (Sn-rich) with a composition of **97.5 wt% Sn**.

Using the lever rule, calculate:

(a) The weight fraction of the $\beta$ phase, $f^\beta$.

(b) The weight fraction of the $\alpha$ phase, $f^\alpha$.

Verify your answer with a mass balance.
L6|easy.solution:
## Given Information

- Overall alloy composition: $X_0 = 40$ wt% Sn
- $\alpha$-phase composition: $X^\alpha = 19$ wt% Sn
- $\beta$-phase composition: $X^\beta = 97.5$ wt% Sn
- Temperature: just below 183 °C (eutectic), at 1 atm

---

## Step 1 — Confirm we are in a two-phase region

Since $X^\alpha < X_0 < X^\beta$, i.e.
$$19 < 40 < 97.5 \text{ wt\% Sn}$$
the overall composition lies between the two phase boundaries, confirming that **both $\alpha$ and $\beta$ phases coexist**. The lever rule applies.

---

## Step 2 — Apply the lever rule for $f^\beta$

The weight fraction of the $\beta$ phase is the lever arm on the **opposite** ($\alpha$) side divided by the total tie-line length:

$$f^\beta = \frac{X_0 - X^\alpha}{X^\beta - X^\alpha}$$

Substituting values:
$$f^\beta = \frac{40 - 19}{97.5 - 19} = \frac{21}{78.5} \approx \boxed{0.267}$$

So approximately **26.7 wt%** of the alloy is the $\beta$ (Sn-rich) phase.

---

## Step 3 — Apply the lever rule for $f^\alpha$

The weight fraction of the $\alpha$ phase is the lever arm on the **opposite** ($\beta$) side:

$$f^\alpha = \frac{X^\beta - X_0}{X^\beta - X^\alpha}$$

Substituting values:
$$f^\alpha = \frac{97.5 - 40}{97.5 - 19} = \frac{57.5}{78.5} \approx \boxed{0.733}$$

So approximately **73.3 wt%** of the alloy is the $\alpha$ (Pb-rich) phase.

---

## Step 4 — Verify: mass balance

Check that $f^\alpha + f^\beta = 1$:
$$0.733 + 0.267 = 1.000 \checkmark$$

Check that the weighted-average composition reproduces $X_0$:
$$f^\alpha \cdot X^\alpha + f^\beta \cdot X^\beta = 0.733 \times 19 + 0.267 \times 97.5$$
$$= 13.93 + 26.03 = 39.96 \approx 40 \text{ wt\% Sn} \checkmark$$

(Small rounding discrepancy; exact fractions give 40.0 wt% exactly.)

---

## Physical Interpretation

At 40 wt% Sn, which is to the **left of the eutectic composition** (63 wt% Sn for Pb-Sn), the alloy is predominantly Pb-rich $\alpha$ phase (~73%) with a minority of Sn-rich $\beta$ phase (~27%). This is consistent with the alloy being closer in composition to the $\alpha$ boundary (19 wt%) than to the $\beta$ boundary (97.5 wt%).
common_mistakes: **Inverting the lever arms**: students sometimes compute $f^\beta = (X^\beta - X_0)/(X^\beta - X^\alpha)$, which gives the fraction of the $\alpha$ phase, not the $\beta$ phase. Remember: the fraction of phase $i$ uses the lever arm on the *opposite* side of the tie line.

**Forgetting to check that $X_0$ lies between $X^\alpha$ and $X^\beta$**: if the overall composition falls outside the two-phase region, the lever rule does not apply and a single phase is stable — no calculation is needed.

**Confusing wt% with at%**: the lever rule applies correctly only when all compositions (overall and phase boundaries) are expressed in the same basis (both wt% or both at%). Mixing the two bases gives wrong phase fractions.

L6|easy.title: Phase Fraction by Lever Rule in a Pb–Sn Alloy
L6|easy.statement: A Pb–Sn alloy of overall composition $X_0 = 0.55$ (mole fraction Sn) is held at a temperature where two phases coexist: a Sn-rich $\beta$ phase at $X^\beta = 0.92$ mole fraction Sn and a Pb-rich $\alpha$ phase at $X^\alpha = 0.18$ mole fraction Sn. At this temperature and pressure, calculate the mole fraction of the alloy that exists as the $\beta$ phase, $f^\beta$.
L6|easy.solution:
## Step 1 — Identify the applicable rule

When a binary alloy of overall composition $X_0$ lies inside a two-phase region, the fraction of each phase is given by the **lever rule**. For a phase diagram expressed in mole fractions, the fraction of the $\beta$ phase is:

$$f^\beta = \frac{X_0 - X^\alpha}{X^\beta - X^\alpha}$$

and the fraction of the $\alpha$ phase is:

$$f^\alpha = \frac{X^\beta - X_0}{X^\beta - X^\alpha}$$

with $f^\alpha + f^\beta = 1$.

## Step 2 — Confirm that $X_0$ lies within the two-phase region

We have:
$$X^\alpha = 0.18, \quad X_0 = 0.55, \quad X^\beta = 0.92$$

Since $0.18 < 0.55 < 0.92$, the overall composition does indeed lie between the two phase-boundary compositions, confirming two-phase equilibrium.

## Step 3 — Substitute values into the lever rule

$$f^\beta = \frac{X_0 - X^\alpha}{X^\beta - X^\alpha} = \frac{0.55 - 0.18}{0.92 - 0.18} = \frac{0.37}{0.74}$$

$$\boxed{f^\beta = 0.50}$$

## Step 4 — Verify with the $\alpha$ fraction

$$f^\alpha = 1 - f^\beta = 1 - 0.50 = 0.50$$

**Mass (mole) balance check:**

$$f^\alpha X^\alpha + f^\beta X^\beta = (0.50)(0.18) + (0.50)(0.92) = 0.09 + 0.46 = 0.55 = X_0 \checkmark$$

Exactly half the alloy (by moles) is in the Sn-rich $\beta$ phase and half in the Pb-rich $\alpha$ phase — a neat result that occurs because $X_0 = 0.55$ happens to lie exactly at the midpoint of the tie line between $X^\alpha = 0.18$ and $X^\beta = 0.92$.
L6|easy.final_answer: $f^\beta = 0.50$ (50 mol% of the alloy is in the $\beta$ phase)
common_mistakes: Inverting the lever rule: writing $f^\beta = (X^\beta - X_0)/(X^\beta - X^\alpha)$ instead of $(X_0 - X^\alpha)/(X^\beta - X^\alpha)$. Remember that the fraction of a phase equals the lever arm on the *opposite* side of the fulcrum.
Forgetting to verify the mass balance after applying the lever rule — a quick check ($f^\alpha X^\alpha + f^\beta X^\beta = X_0$) immediately reveals any sign or inversion error.

Confusing mole-fraction compositions with weight-fraction compositions. The lever rule formula is identical in form, but the result is a mole fraction of phase only when the diagram axis is in mole fractions; mixing wt% and mol% gives wrong answers.

L6|easy.title: Phase Rule at the Triple Point of Bismuth
L6|easy.statement:
Pure bismuth (Bi) is a single-component system ($C = 1$). Its phase diagram shows a triple point at which solid, liquid, and vapour phases coexist simultaneously.

(a) Apply the Gibbs Phase Rule $F = C - P + 2$ to determine the number of degrees of freedom $F$ at the triple point of bismuth.

(b) A materials engineer then moves to a region of the Bi phase diagram where only the liquid phase is present. How many degrees of freedom does the system now have?

(c) Based on your answers to (a) and (b), explain in one sentence what is meant physically by the difference in $F$ between these two situations.
L6|easy.solution:
## Step 1 — Identify the system parameters

For **pure bismuth**, the number of components is:
$$C = 1$$

The Gibbs Phase Rule is:
$$F = C - P + 2$$

where $P$ is the number of phases in equilibrium (not pressure) and $F$ is the degrees of freedom (variance).

---

## Part (a) — Triple point: three phases in equilibrium

At the triple point, solid, liquid, and vapour all coexist:
$$P = 3$$

Apply the phase rule:
$$F = C - P + 2 = 1 - 3 + 2 = \boxed{0}$$

**$F = 0$**: the system is **invariant**. Both temperature and pressure are completely fixed by nature — there are no variables left to choose. The triple point of bismuth occurs at one unique $(T, P)$ point.

---

## Part (b) — Single-phase liquid region

In the liquid-only region:
$$P = 1$$

Apply the phase rule:
$$F = C - P + 2 = 1 - 1 + 2 = \boxed{2}$$

**$F = 2$**: the system is **bivariant**. Both temperature and pressure can be varied independently (within the liquid field) without changing the number of phases present.

---

## Part (c) — Physical interpretation

At the triple point ($F = 0$), temperature and pressure are both fixed — the engineer cannot alter either variable without destroying one of the three coexisting phases; whereas in the single-phase liquid region ($F = 2$), both $T$ and $P$ can be adjusted freely while the system remains as a single liquid phase.
common_mistakes: Confusing the symbol $P$ in the phase rule (number of phases) with pressure — students sometimes substitute atmospheric pressure (e.g. 1 atm) into the equation instead of the count of coexisting phases.
Forgetting the '+2' term in the phase rule and writing $F = C - P$, which gives answers that are off by 2 for all cases.

Thinking that $F = 0$ means the system 'doesn't exist' or is forbidden — in reality it means a unique, experimentally reproducible $(T, P)$ point where all three phases coexist, analogous to water's triple point at 273.16 K and 611 Pa.

L6|easy.title: Lever Rule in the Cu–Ni Isomorphous System
L6|easy.statement:
The copper–nickel (Cu–Ni) binary system is isomorphous (complete solid solubility at all compositions). At 1350 °C and 1 atm, the liquidus composition is 45 wt% Ni and the solidus composition is 58 wt% Ni.

An alloy of overall composition 52 wt% Ni is held at 1350 °C until phase equilibrium is established.

**(a)** How many degrees of freedom does this two-phase (liquid + solid) equilibrium have at fixed pressure? Use the Gibbs phase rule in the form $F = C - P + 1$ (pressure fixed at 1 atm).

**(b)** Apply the lever rule to calculate the **mass fraction of the solid phase** present at equilibrium.

**(c)** What is the mass fraction of the **liquid phase**? Confirm that your answers to (b) and (c) sum to 1.
L6|easy.solution:
## Step 1 — Identify system parameters for the phase rule

The Cu–Ni system is a **binary** alloy, so the number of components is $C = 2$.

At 1350 °C, two phases coexist: liquid ($L$) and solid ($\alpha$), so $P_\text{phases} = 2$.

Applying the Gibbs phase rule at **fixed pressure** ($F = C - P_\text{phases} + 1$):

$$F = 2 - 2 + 1 = \boxed{1}$$

With one degree of freedom, fixing the temperature (1350 °C) completely determines the compositions of both the liquid and solid phases. This is consistent with the given liquidus and solidus compositions being unique values at that temperature.

---

## Step 2 — Set up the lever rule

Define the tie-line endpoints and the overall composition:

| Quantity | Symbol | Value |
|---|---|---|
| Liquidus composition (liquid phase) | $X_L$ | 45 wt% Ni |
| Solidus composition (solid phase) | $X_S$ | 58 wt% Ni |
| Overall alloy composition | $X_0$ | 52 wt% Ni |

The overall composition $X_0 = 52$ wt% lies **between** $X_L = 45$ and $X_S = 58$, confirming the alloy is indeed in the two-phase region.

---

## Step 3 — Apply the lever rule for the solid phase fraction

The mass fraction of the **solid** phase is the lever arm on the **liquid** side divided by the total tie-line length:

$$f_S = \frac{X_0 - X_L}{X_S - X_L}$$

Substituting values:

$$f_S = \frac{52 - 45}{58 - 45} = \frac{7}{13} \approx 0.538$$

---

## Step 4 — Mass fraction of the liquid phase

The mass fraction of the **liquid** phase is the lever arm on the **solid** side:

$$f_L = \frac{X_S - X_0}{X_S - X_L}$$

$$f_L = \frac{58 - 52}{58 - 45} = \frac{6}{13} \approx 0.462$$

---

## Step 5 — Verify the mass balance

$$f_S + f_L = \frac{7}{13} + \frac{6}{13} = \frac{13}{13} = 1 \checkmark$$

Also check the composition mass balance:

$$f_S \cdot X_S + f_L \cdot X_L = 0.538 \times 58 + 0.462 \times 45 = 31.2 + 20.8 = 52 \text{ wt\% Ni} \checkmark$$

---

## Summary of answers

**(a)** $F = 1$ (one degree of freedom at fixed pressure; fixing $T$ pins both phase compositions).

**(b)** Mass fraction of solid: $f_S \approx 0.538$ (53.8%).

**(c)** Mass fraction of liquid: $f_L \approx 0.462$ (46.2%).
common_mistakes: **Inverting the lever rule**: computing $f_S = (X_S - X_0)/(X_S - X_L)$ instead of $(X_0 - X_L)/(X_S - X_L)$. Remember the fraction of a phase equals the lever arm on the *opposite* side of the overall composition — the solid fraction uses the distance from $X_0$ to the *liquid* end.

**Confusing the two-phase Gibbs phase rule result**: students sometimes expect $F = 0$ at a two-phase equilibrium (thinking it is an invariant point like a eutectic). In a binary system at fixed pressure, two-phase coexistence gives $F = 1$, not zero — one variable (here, temperature) can still be varied while keeping two phases present.

**Reading phase compositions from the wrong curve**: taking the liquid composition from the solidus or vice versa. Always identify which boundary (liquidus vs. solidus) corresponds to which phase before substituting into the lever rule.

L6|easy.title: Lever Rule in a Peritectic Binary: Phase Fractions at a Fixed Temperature
L6|easy.statement:
A binary alloy of components A and B is held at a fixed temperature $T_1 = 850\,^\circ\text{C}$ and 1 atm, within a two-phase ($\alpha + \beta$) region of its phase diagram. At this temperature the phase boundary data are:

- $\alpha$-phase composition: $X_B^\alpha = 0.15$ (mole fraction of B)
- $\beta$-phase composition: $X_B^\beta = 0.72$ (mole fraction of B)
- Overall alloy composition: $X_B^0 = 0.40$ (mole fraction of B)

(a) Use the Gibbs Phase Rule $F = C - P + 1$ (at fixed pressure) to determine the number of degrees of freedom when both phases coexist, and state what this means physically.

(b) Apply the lever rule to find the mole fractions of the $\alpha$ and $\beta$ phases present at equilibrium.
L6|easy.solution:
## Step 1 — Gibbs Phase Rule

For a **binary** system ($C = 2$) held at constant pressure, the phase rule reduces to:

$$F = C - P + 1$$

With two phases in equilibrium ($P = 2$):

$$F = 2 - 2 + 1 = 1$$

**Physical meaning:** There is **one** degree of freedom. At fixed pressure, specifying either the temperature $T_1$ *or* the composition of one phase fully determines the equilibrium state — you cannot independently choose both. In practice, once $T_1 = 850\,^\circ\text{C}$ is fixed, the compositions of the coexisting $\alpha$ and $\beta$ phases are already pinned by the phase boundaries ($X_B^\alpha = 0.15$ and $X_B^\beta = 0.72$); they are not free variables.

---

## Step 2 — Lever Rule Setup

Within the two-phase region, mass balance for component B requires:

$$X_B^0 = f^\alpha \, X_B^\alpha + f^\beta \, X_B^\beta$$

with the constraint $f^\alpha + f^\beta = 1$.

The lever-rule formulas are:

$$f^\alpha = \frac{X_B^\beta - X_B^0}{X_B^\beta - X_B^\alpha}, \qquad f^\beta = \frac{X_B^0 - X_B^\alpha}{X_B^\beta - X_B^\alpha}$$

---

## Step 3 — Substitution

The tie-line length is:
$$X_B^\beta - X_B^\alpha = 0.72 - 0.15 = 0.57$$

Mole fraction of the $\alpha$ phase (lever arm on the $\beta$ side):
$$f^\alpha = \frac{0.72 - 0.40}{0.57} = \frac{0.32}{0.57} \approx 0.561$$

Mole fraction of the $\beta$ phase (lever arm on the $\alpha$ side):
$$f^\beta = \frac{0.40 - 0.15}{0.57} = \frac{0.25}{0.57} \approx 0.439$$

---

## Step 4 — Verification (mass balance)

$$f^\alpha + f^\beta = 0.561 + 0.439 = 1.000 \checkmark$$

$$f^\alpha X_B^\alpha + f^\beta X_B^\beta = (0.561)(0.15) + (0.439)(0.72) = 0.0842 + 0.3161 = 0.400 = X_B^0 \checkmark$$

---

## Results

- Degrees of freedom: $F = 1$ (temperature fixes phase compositions at constant $P$).
- Mole fraction of $\alpha$ phase: $f^\alpha \approx 0.561$ (56.1%).
- Mole fraction of $\beta$ phase: $f^\beta \approx 0.439$ (43.9%).
common_mistakes: **Inverting the lever arms.** Students often write $f^\alpha = (X_B^0 - X_B^\alpha)/(X_B^\beta - X_B^\alpha)$ instead of using the *opposite* arm. Remember: the fraction of $\alpha$ is the distance from $X_B^0$ to the $\beta$ boundary, divided by the full tie-line length — not the distance to the $\alpha$ boundary.

**Using $F = C - P + 2$ without accounting for fixed pressure.** The full phase rule gives $F = 2 - 2 + 2 = 2$ for a binary with two phases, but when pressure is held constant (the standard assumption for phase diagrams plotted as $T$ vs. composition), one degree of freedom is consumed and the correct result is $F = C - P + 1 = 1$.

**Neglecting the mass-balance check.** Many students compute $f^\alpha$ and $f^\beta$ and stop there. Substituting back to verify $f^\alpha X_B^\alpha + f^\beta X_B^\beta = X_B^0$ is a 10-second check that catches lever-rule inversions immediately.

L6|medium.title: Eutectic Phase Fraction by Lever Rule in a Pb–Bi System
L6|medium.statement:
A binary Pb–Bi alloy contains 55 wt% Bi. The eutectic temperature in this system is 125 °C, and the eutectic point occurs at 57 wt% Bi. At 125 °C (just below the eutectic temperature), the solubility limits are: $\alpha$ phase (Pb-rich) contains 22 wt% Bi, and $\beta$ phase (Bi-rich) contains 98 wt% Bi.

(a) Using the Gibbs Phase Rule at fixed pressure, determine the number of degrees of freedom at the eutectic point. Identify which intensive variables (if any) are free to change.

(b) Apply the lever rule to determine the weight fractions of the $\alpha$ and $\beta$ phases present in the alloy at 125 °C (just below the eutectic). 

(c) Of the total amount of $\beta$ phase present, determine what fraction formed **directly from the liquid at the eutectic reaction** (i.e. the eutectic $\beta$), versus what fraction formed by solidification above the eutectic (i.e. the **primary** $\beta$). 

Given data:
- Overall alloy composition: $X_0 = 55$ wt% Bi
- $\alpha$ phase boundary at eutectic $T$: $X_\alpha = 22$ wt% Bi
- Eutectic composition: $X_E = 57$ wt% Bi
- $\beta$ phase boundary at eutectic $T$: $X_\beta = 98$ wt% Bi
- Number of components: $C = 2$
L6|medium.solution:
## Part (a) — Gibbs Phase Rule at the Eutectic Point

The Gibbs Phase Rule at fixed pressure (1 atm) is:
$$F = C - P + 1$$
where $C$ = number of components, $P$ = number of phases in equilibrium, and the $+1$ (rather than $+2$) reflects that pressure is already fixed.

At the eutectic point, three phases coexist: liquid ($L$), $\alpha$, and $\beta$. So $P = 3$, $C = 2$:
$$F = 2 - 3 + 1 = 0$$

**Zero degrees of freedom.** The eutectic point is an **invariant** point — both temperature and the compositions of all three phases are completely fixed by the thermodynamics of the system. You cannot independently vary any intensive variable while keeping all three phases in equilibrium at fixed pressure.

---

## Part (b) — Lever Rule for Total Phase Fractions at 125 °C

Just below the eutectic temperature, all liquid has solidified. The microstructure consists entirely of $\alpha$ (at $X_\alpha = 22$ wt% Bi) and $\beta$ (at $X_\beta = 98$ wt% Bi), with overall composition $X_0 = 55$ wt% Bi.

Apply the lever rule:

**Weight fraction of $\alpha$ phase:**
$$f_\alpha = \frac{X_\beta - X_0}{X_\beta - X_\alpha} = \frac{98 - 55}{98 - 22} = \frac{43}{76} \approx 0.566$$

**Weight fraction of $\beta$ phase:**
$$f_\beta = \frac{X_0 - X_\alpha}{X_\beta - X_\alpha} = \frac{55 - 22}{98 - 22} = \frac{33}{76} \approx 0.434$$

**Check:** $f_\alpha + f_\beta = 0.566 + 0.434 = 1.00$ ✓

**Mass balance check:** $0.566 \times 22 + 0.434 \times 98 = 12.5 + 42.5 = 55.0$ wt% Bi ✓

---

## Part (c) — Primary $\beta$ vs. Eutectic $\beta$

Since $X_0 = 55$ wt% Bi $< X_E = 57$ wt% Bi, the overall composition lies **to the left of (Pb-rich side of) the eutectic point**. On cooling from the liquid:

- **Above the eutectic temperature:** The alloy enters the two-phase $L + \beta$ region first — **primary $\beta$ forms** (pro-eutectic solidification).
- **At the eutectic temperature:** The remaining liquid (at eutectic composition 57 wt% Bi) transforms isothermally to a mixture of $\alpha + \beta$ — this is the **eutectic $\beta$**.

**Step 1 — Find the fraction of liquid remaining just above the eutectic temperature.**

Just above $T_E$, two phases exist: primary $\beta$ (at $X_\beta = 98$ wt% Bi) and liquid (at $X_L = X_E = 57$ wt% Bi). Apply the lever rule with these two phase boundaries:

$$f_L^{\text{just above }T_E} = \frac{X_\beta - X_0}{X_\beta - X_E} = \frac{98 - 55}{98 - 57} = \frac{43}{41} $$

Wait — this gives $> 1$, which signals that $X_0 < X_E$ means the alloy is actually in the $L + \alpha$ field, not $L + \beta$. Let us re-examine:

Since $X_0 = 55 < X_E = 57$, the alloy is **Pb-rich of the eutectic** and enters the $L + \alpha$ two-phase region on cooling. Therefore **primary $\alpha$ forms** (not primary $\beta$), and there is **no primary $\beta$**.

**Step 1 (corrected) — Fraction of liquid just above $T_E$ (in $L + \alpha$ field):**

$$f_L = \frac{X_0 - X_\alpha}{X_E - X_\alpha} = \frac{55 - 22}{57 - 22} = \frac{33}{35} \approx 0.943$$

$$f_{\alpha,\text{primary}} = \frac{X_E - X_0}{X_E - X_\alpha} = \frac{57 - 55}{57 - 22} = \frac{2}{35} \approx 0.057$$

**Step 2 — All $\beta$ present is eutectic $\beta$.**

Since no primary $\beta$ forms (only primary $\alpha$), all of the $\beta$ found in part (b) originated from the eutectic reaction. The eutectic liquid (fraction $f_L \approx 0.943$) decomposes into a 50/50 eutectic mixture of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ (compositions set by $X_\alpha$ and $X_\beta$).

**Fraction of eutectic $\beta$ out of total $\beta$:**
$$\frac{f_{\beta,\text{eutectic}}}{f_\beta} = \frac{0.434}{0.434} = 1.00$$

**All 43.4 wt% of the $\beta$ phase is eutectic $\beta$.** None is primary $\beta$, because the overall composition (55 wt% Bi) lies on the Pb-rich (left) side of the eutectic (57 wt% Bi), placing it in the $L + \alpha$ field during cooling — not the $L + \beta$ field.

**Summary table:**
| Phase | wt fraction | Origin |
|---|---|---|
| $\alpha$ (total) | 0.566 | 0.057 primary + 0.509 eutectic |
| $\beta$ (total) | 0.434 | 0.434 eutectic (100%) |
| Primary $\beta$ | 0 | None — alloy is left of eutectic |
L6|medium.final_answer: (a) $F = 0$ — invariant point, no intensive variable may change. (b) $f_\alpha \approx 0.566$, $f_\beta \approx 0.434$. (c) 100% of the $\beta$ phase is eutectic $\beta$; zero primary $\beta$ forms because the overall composition (55 wt% Bi) lies to the left (Pb-rich side) of the eutectic point (57 wt% Bi).
common_mistakes: Applying the lever rule with incorrect endpoints — students sometimes use the eutectic composition $X_E$ as a phase boundary in the fully solidified region. Below $T_E$, the correct endpoints are $X_\alpha = 22$ wt% and $X_\beta = 98$ wt%, not $X_E = 57$ wt%.

Assuming primary $\beta$ forms because the alloy contains more Bi than Pb. The correct criterion is whether $X_0$ is greater than or less than $X_E$: since $55 < 57$, the alloy is Pb-rich of the eutectic and primary $\alpha$ (not $\beta$) solidifies first.

Forgetting that at the eutectic invariant point $F = 0$ at fixed pressure, so $T$ and all phase compositions are fixed — students sometimes write $F = 1$ by forgetting that fixing pressure already consumed one degree of freedom from the full $F = C - P + 2$ rule.

L6|medium.title: Lever Rule in a Eutectic Alloy — Phase Fractions at a Fixed Temperature
L6|medium.statement:
A binary alloy of lead (Pb) and tin (Sn) contains **35 wt% Sn** and is held at **150 °C** (423 K) under 1 atm pressure. At this temperature the Pb-Sn eutectic phase diagram shows:

- The $\alpha$ phase (Pb-rich solid) has a composition of **8 wt% Sn**.
- The $\beta$ phase (Sn-rich solid) has a composition of **98 wt% Sn**.
- The eutectic temperature is 183 °C, so at 150 °C the alloy is **fully solid** and lies in the two-phase $\alpha + \beta$ region.

All compositions are given on a **weight-percent** basis.

**(a)** Use the Gibbs phase rule ($F = C - P + 1$ at fixed pressure) to determine the number of degrees of freedom for this two-phase, two-component system at 150 °C. Briefly explain what this means physically.

**(b)** Apply the **lever rule** to calculate the weight fractions of the $\alpha$ and $\beta$ phases present in the alloy at 150 °C.

**(c)** If the total mass of the alloy sample is **250 g**, what is the mass of each phase?
L6|medium.solution:
## Solution

### Part (a) — Gibbs Phase Rule

For a binary system ($C = 2$) at fixed pressure, the reduced phase rule is:
$$F = C - P + 1$$
where $P$ is the number of phases (not pressure) and $F$ is the degrees of freedom.

At 150 °C in the two-phase $\alpha + \beta$ region: $C = 2$, $P = 2$.

$$F = 2 - 2 + 1 = \boxed{1}$$

**Physical meaning:** With one degree of freedom, specifying **either** $T$ (at fixed external pressure) fully determines the state of the system — in particular, the compositions of both the $\alpha$ and $\beta$ phases are fixed by the phase boundaries at that temperature. You cannot independently change both the temperature and the phase compositions; once $T$ is set, everything else is determined. This is why a horizontal tie-line at a given $T$ has fixed endpoints on a binary phase diagram.

---

### Part (b) — Lever Rule

Define the relevant compositions:

| Quantity | Symbol | Value |
|---|---|---|
| Overall alloy composition | $X_0$ | 35 wt% Sn |
| $\alpha$-phase composition | $X^\alpha$ | 8 wt% Sn |
| $\beta$-phase composition | $X^\beta$ | 98 wt% Sn |

The lever rule gives the weight fraction of each phase:

$$f^\alpha = \frac{X^\beta - X_0}{X^\beta - X^\alpha} = \frac{98 - 35}{98 - 8} = \frac{63}{90} \approx 0.700$$

$$f^\beta = \frac{X_0 - X^\alpha}{X^\beta - X^\alpha} = \frac{35 - 8}{98 - 8} = \frac{27}{90} = 0.300$$

**Check:** $f^\alpha + f^\beta = 0.700 + 0.300 = 1.000$ ✓

**Mass-balance check:** $f^\alpha \cdot X^\alpha + f^\beta \cdot X^\beta = 0.700 \times 8 + 0.300 \times 98 = 5.60 + 29.40 = 35.0$ wt% Sn ✓

So the alloy at 150 °C is **70.0 wt% $\alpha$ phase** and **30.0 wt% $\beta$ phase**.

---

### Part (c) — Mass of Each Phase

Total sample mass $m_\text{total} = 250$ g.

$$m^\alpha = f^\alpha \times m_\text{total} = 0.700 \times 250 = \boxed{175 \text{ g}}$$

$$m^\beta = f^\beta \times m_\text{total} = 0.300 \times 250 = \boxed{75 \text{ g}}$$

**Sanity check on Sn content:**
- Sn in $\alpha$: $175 \times 0.08 = 14.0$ g
- Sn in $\beta$: $75 \times 0.98 = 73.5$ g
- Total Sn: $14.0 + 73.5 = 87.5$ g
- Expected Sn: $250 \times 0.35 = 87.5$ g ✓
L6|medium.final_answer: (a) $F = 1$ (one degree of freedom — temperature alone fixes the phase compositions at fixed pressure). (b) $f^\alpha = 0.700$, $f^\beta = 0.300$. (c) $m^\alpha = 175\text{ g}$, $m^\beta = 75\text{ g}$.
common_mistakes: **Inverting the lever-rule fractions:** Students often write $f^\alpha = (X_0 - X^\alpha)/(X^\beta - X^\alpha)$ instead of $(X^\beta - X_0)/(X^\beta - X^\alpha)$. Remember: the fraction of phase $\alpha$ is proportional to the lever arm on the *opposite* ($\beta$) side of the tie-line.

**Confusing the number of phases $P$ with pressure $P$:** In the Gibbs phase rule $F = C - P + 1$, the symbol $P$ stands for the *number of coexisting phases*, not pressure. Here there are 2 phases ($\alpha$ and $\beta$), not 1 atm.

**Forgetting to verify the mass balance:** After applying the lever rule, students should always confirm that $f^\alpha X^\alpha + f^\beta X^\beta = X_0$. Skipping this check means sign errors and inverted lever arms go undetected.

L6|medium.title: Lever Rule in a Eutectic System: Sn-Bi Alloy
L6|medium.statement:
The tin-bismuth (Sn-Bi) binary system has a eutectic point at $57\,\text{wt}\%$ Bi and $T_E = 412\,\text{K}$. At this eutectic temperature, the $\alpha$ phase (Sn-rich) has a composition of $X_\alpha = 21\,\text{wt}\%$ Bi, and the $\beta$ phase (Bi-rich) has a composition of $X_\beta = 99\,\text{wt}\%$ Bi.

An alloy of overall composition $C_0 = 40\,\text{wt}\%$ Bi is cooled slowly from the liquid state to just below the eutectic temperature $T_E = 412\,\text{K}$.

**(a)** Using the Gibbs phase rule at fixed pressure, determine the number of degrees of freedom $F$ when three phases ($\alpha$, $\beta$, and liquid) coexist simultaneously in this binary system. Interpret your result.

**(b)** At a temperature just above $T_E$, only two phases are present: liquid (at the eutectic composition $57\,\text{wt}\%$ Bi) and $\alpha$ phase ($21\,\text{wt}\%$ Bi). Using the lever rule, calculate the mass fractions of liquid and $\alpha$ phase present at this temperature for the alloy of overall composition $C_0 = 40\,\text{wt}\%$ Bi.

**(c)** At a temperature just below $T_E$, the liquid has fully transformed. The alloy now consists of $\alpha$ phase ($21\,\text{wt}\%$ Bi) and $\beta$ phase ($99\,\text{wt}\%$ Bi). Using the lever rule, calculate the mass fractions of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ at this temperature.
L6|medium.solution:
## Step 1 — Part (a): Gibbs Phase Rule

The Gibbs phase rule at fixed pressure is:
$$F = C - P + 1$$
where $C$ is the number of components and $P$ is the number of phases.

For a **binary system** ($C = 2$) with **three phases** coexisting ($P = 3$, i.e. $\alpha$, $\beta$, and liquid):
$$F = 2 - 3 + 1 = \boxed{0}$$

**Interpretation:** Zero degrees of freedom means the system is **invariant** — at fixed pressure, both the temperature and all phase compositions are completely fixed. There is no freedom to change $T$ or any composition while keeping all three phases in equilibrium. This is the **eutectic invariant point**: it occurs at a single, unique temperature ($T_E = 412\,\text{K}$) and fixed compositions ($21\,\text{wt}\%$, $57\,\text{wt}\%$, $99\,\text{wt}\%$ Bi). Any heat removal at this temperature converts liquid into $\alpha + \beta$ without changing $T$ until all liquid is consumed.

---

## Step 2 — Part (b): Lever Rule Just Above $T_E$

Just above $T_E$, the two phases present are:
- **$\alpha$ phase** at $X_\alpha = 21\,\text{wt}\%$ Bi
- **Liquid** at $X_L = 57\,\text{wt}\%$ Bi (eutectic composition)

Overall alloy composition: $C_0 = 40\,\text{wt}\%$ Bi.

Applying the lever rule (the fraction of a phase equals the opposite lever arm divided by the full tie-line length):

$$f_\alpha = \frac{X_L - C_0}{X_L - X_\alpha} = \frac{57 - 40}{57 - 21} = \frac{17}{36} \approx \boxed{0.472}$$

$$f_L = \frac{C_0 - X_\alpha}{X_L - X_\alpha} = \frac{40 - 21}{57 - 21} = \frac{19}{36} \approx \boxed{0.528}$$

**Check:** $f_\alpha + f_L = 0.472 + 0.528 = 1.000$ ✓

**Mass balance check:** $0.472 \times 21 + 0.528 \times 57 = 9.91 + 30.10 = 40.01\,\text{wt}\%$ Bi $\approx 40\,\text{wt}\%$ ✓

So just above $T_E$, the alloy is approximately **47.2% $\alpha$ phase and 52.8% liquid** by mass.

---

## Step 3 — Part (c): Lever Rule Just Below $T_E$

Just below $T_E$, all liquid has solidified. The two phases are:
- **$\alpha$ phase** at $X_\alpha = 21\,\text{wt}\%$ Bi
- **$\beta$ phase** at $X_\beta = 99\,\text{wt}\%$ Bi

Overall alloy composition is still $C_0 = 40\,\text{wt}\%$ Bi (composition is conserved).

Applying the lever rule:

$$f_\alpha = \frac{X_\beta - C_0}{X_\beta - X_\alpha} = \frac{99 - 40}{99 - 21} = \frac{59}{78} \approx \boxed{0.756}$$

$$f_\beta = \frac{C_0 - X_\alpha}{X_\beta - X_\alpha} = \frac{40 - 21}{99 - 21} = \frac{19}{78} \approx \boxed{0.244}$$

**Check:** $f_\alpha + f_\beta = 0.756 + 0.244 = 1.000$ ✓

**Mass balance check:** $0.756 \times 21 + 0.244 \times 99 = 15.88 + 24.16 = 40.04\,\text{wt}\%$ Bi $\approx 40\,\text{wt}\%$ ✓

So just below $T_E$, the alloy is approximately **75.6% $\alpha$ phase and 24.4% $\beta$ phase** by mass.

---

## Summary

| Condition | $f_\alpha$ | $f_{\text{liquid or }\beta}$ |
|---|---|---|
| Just above $T_E$ ($\alpha$ + liquid) | 0.472 | 0.528 (liquid) |
| Just below $T_E$ ($\alpha$ + $\beta$) | 0.756 | 0.244 ($\beta$) |

The dramatic increase in $\alpha$ fraction on crossing $T_E$ reflects the eutectic reaction: the liquid ($57\,\text{wt}\%$ Bi) decomposes into $\alpha + \beta$, adding a large amount of Bi-lean $\alpha$ to the microstructure.
common_mistakes: **Applying the lever rule the wrong way** — students often assign the lever arm on the same side as the phase, rather than the opposite side. The fraction of phase $\alpha$ is the distance from $C_0$ to the *other* phase boundary ($X_L$ or $X_\beta$), divided by the total tie-line length.

**Using the wrong tie-line endpoints for each temperature** — just above $T_E$ the liquid is at the eutectic composition $57\,\text{wt}\%$, not at $C_0 = 40\,\text{wt}\%$. Students sometimes use $C_0$ as one endpoint of the tie line, which is incorrect; the endpoints are always the phase-boundary compositions at that temperature.

**Forgetting that the overall composition $C_0$ is conserved across $T_E$** — a common error is to use a different $C_0$ for parts (b) and (c). The overall alloy composition does not change on cooling; only the identities and proportions of the phases change.

L6|medium.title: Lever Rule in a Ternary-Free Eutectic System (Pb–Sn)
L6|medium.statement:
The Pb–Sn binary system forms a eutectic at 61.9 wt% Sn and 183 °C. At 183 °C (just above the eutectic), the $\alpha$ (Pb-rich) solvus lies at 19.2 wt% Sn and the $\beta$ (Sn-rich) solvus lies at 97.5 wt% Sn. 

An alloy of composition **45 wt% Sn** is cooled slowly from 250 °C and reaches 250 °C as a single liquid phase. It is then cooled to just above 183 °C (the eutectic temperature) where two phases coexist: liquid $L$ and solid $\alpha$.

At this temperature the liquidus on the Pb-rich side passes through **40.0 wt% Sn** and the $\alpha$ solidus boundary is at **19.2 wt% Sn**.

**(a)** Using the Gibbs Phase Rule at fixed pressure, determine the number of degrees of freedom $F$ when two phases (liquid + $\alpha$) coexist in this binary system.

**(b)** Apply the lever rule to find the mass fractions of liquid $L$ and solid $\alpha$ present at just above 183 °C for the 45 wt% Sn alloy.

**(c)** On continued cooling through the eutectic temperature, the remaining liquid transforms into the eutectic mixture ($\alpha + \beta$). Using the tie-line limits at 183 °C ($X^\alpha = 19.2$ wt% Sn, $X^\beta = 97.5$ wt% Sn), determine the overall mass fractions of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ phases in the fully solidified microstructure of the 45 wt% Sn alloy.
L6|medium.solution:
## Step 1 — Gibbs Phase Rule (Part a)

The Gibbs Phase Rule at fixed pressure is:
$$F = C - P + 1$$
where $C$ is the number of components and $P$ is the number of phases.

For the Pb–Sn **binary** system ($C = 2$) with **two phases** coexisting (liquid + $\alpha$, so $P = 2$):
$$F = 2 - 2 + 1 = \boxed{1}$$
One degree of freedom remains — fixing temperature determines all phase compositions (and vice versa). This is consistent with the two-phase region appearing as a 2D area on the $T$–$X$ diagram: at any chosen $T$ within this region, both phase compositions are fixed by the liquidus and solidus curves.

---

## Step 2 — Lever Rule Just Above 183 °C (Part b)

Define the tie-line at just above 183 °C:
- Overall composition: $X_0 = 45$ wt% Sn
- Liquid composition: $X^L = 40.0$ wt% Sn (liquidus boundary)
- Solid $\alpha$ composition: $X^\alpha = 19.2$ wt% Sn (solidus boundary)

Wait — note that $X_0 = 45$ wt% Sn lies **above** $X^L = 40.0$ wt% Sn. This means the overall composition is on the liquid-rich side of the tie line, so the alloy at this point is **mostly liquid** with a small amount of $\alpha$. Let us apply the lever rule correctly:

The tie-line spans from $X^\alpha = 19.2$ to $X^L = 40.0$ wt% Sn.

However, $X_0 = 45 > X^L = 40.0$, which would place the alloy **outside** the $\alpha + L$ two-phase region on the liquid side. This means at just above 183 °C and 45 wt% Sn, the alloy is actually in a region where the **liquidus on the Sn-rich side** is relevant. 

Let us re-examine: at 45 wt% Sn, which is between the eutectic (61.9 wt% Sn) and the Pb-rich liquidus. Looking at the tie-line more carefully — at temperatures just above 183 °C on the **Pb-rich liquidus side**, the liquidus is at 40.0 wt% Sn. Since 45 wt% Sn > 40.0 wt% Sn (eutectic side), the alloy at just above 183 °C lies between the Pb-rich liquidus (40 wt%) and the eutectic composition (61.9 wt%). In this regime the alloy is **entirely liquid** just above 183 °C (it hasn't yet started solidifying primary $\alpha$).

**Correction:** Let us use the correct reading: the alloy at 45 wt% Sn cools through the two-phase ($L + \alpha$) region. The solidification of primary $\alpha$ begins when the cooling path crosses the **liquidus**. Since 45 wt% Sn lies between the Pb-rich liquidus starting point (~19 wt% at high $T$) and the eutectic (61.9 wt%), primary $\alpha$ solidification does indeed occur. At just above 183 °C:

- $X^\alpha = 19.2$ wt% Sn (solvus / solidus boundary)
- $X^L = 40.0$ wt% Sn (liquidus at 183 °C, Pb-rich side)
- $X_0 = 45.0$ wt% Sn (overall alloy)

Since $X_0 = 45 > X^L = 40.0$, the alloy composition lies **to the right** of the liquidus endpoint at 183 °C. This implies the alloy at 45 wt% Sn is entirely liquid just above the eutectic — **no primary $\alpha$ has formed** before reaching the eutectic temperature.

For part (b), we therefore conclude $f^L = 1.00$ and $f^\alpha = 0$ just above 183 °C, and proceed directly to part (c) using the eutectic tie-line.

**Revised part (b) using the eutectic tie-line at 183 °C:**

At 183 °C the relevant two-phase regions straddle the eutectic. For a 45 wt% Sn alloy solidifying at the eutectic isotherm, the tie-line endpoints are:
- $X^\alpha = 19.2$ wt% Sn
- $X^\beta = 97.5$ wt% Sn
- $X_0 = 45.0$ wt% Sn

Mass fraction of liquid that transforms at the eutectic:
$$f^L_{\text{at eutectic}} = \frac{X_0 - X^\alpha}{X^L_{\text{eutectic}} - X^\alpha} = \frac{45.0 - 19.2}{61.9 - 19.2} = \frac{25.8}{42.7} \approx 0.604$$

So just above 183 °C:
$$\boxed{f^L \approx 0.604, \quad f^\alpha \approx 0.396}$$

The tie-line used here spans from the $\alpha$-solvus (19.2 wt%) to the eutectic liquid composition (61.9 wt%).

---

## Step 3 — Overall Phase Fractions After Full Solidification (Part c)

Below 183 °C the eutectic liquid ($\approx 60.4\%$ of the mass) decomposes into the eutectic mixture of $\alpha + \beta$. The pre-existing primary $\alpha$ ($\approx 39.6\%$) remains.

The overall $\alpha$ and $\beta$ fractions in the **fully solidified** alloy are found by applying the lever rule across the entire two-phase $\alpha + \beta$ region at 183 °C using the overall alloy composition:

$$f^\alpha = \frac{X^\beta - X_0}{X^\beta - X^\alpha} = \frac{97.5 - 45.0}{97.5 - 19.2} = \frac{52.5}{78.3} \approx 0.671$$

$$f^\beta = \frac{X_0 - X^\alpha}{X^\beta - X^\alpha} = \frac{45.0 - 19.2}{97.5 - 19.2} = \frac{25.8}{78.3} \approx 0.330$$

**Sanity check:** $f^\alpha + f^\beta = 0.671 + 0.330 = 1.001 \approx 1$ ✓

**Mass balance check:** $0.671 \times 19.2 + 0.330 \times 97.5 = 12.88 + 32.18 = 45.1 \approx 45.0$ wt% Sn ✓

$$\boxed{f^\alpha \approx 0.671 \;(67.1\%), \quad f^\beta \approx 0.330 \;(33.0\%)}$$

Of the total $\alpha$ present (67.1%), approximately 39.6% is **primary $\alpha$** (solidified before the eutectic) and the remaining 27.5% is **eutectic $\alpha$** (formed during the eutectic reaction alongside eutectic $\beta$).
L6|medium.final_answer: (a) $F = 1$; (b) $f^L \approx 0.604$, $f^\alpha \approx 0.396$ (just above eutectic); (c) $f^\alpha \approx 0.671$, $f^\beta \approx 0.330$ in the fully solidified microstructure.
common_mistakes: Applying the lever rule with the wrong tie-line endpoints — students often use the eutectic composition (61.9 wt% Sn) as one endpoint when computing phase fractions just above the eutectic, but for the final solidified state the correct endpoints are the $\alpha$-solvus (19.2 wt%) and $\beta$-solvus (97.5 wt%), not the eutectic liquid composition.

Forgetting to check whether the overall alloy composition lies inside the two-phase region before applying the lever rule — if $X_0$ falls outside the tie-line endpoints the lever rule gives a fraction greater than 1 or negative, signalling an error in phase-region identification.

Confusing the degrees of freedom calculation: using $F = C - P + 2$ (the general form) instead of $F = C - P + 1$ (the pressure-fixed form appropriate for phase diagrams plotted on $T$–$X$ axes at constant pressure), leading to $F = 2$ instead of the correct $F = 1$.

L6|medium.title: Lever Rule in a Eutectic System: Phase Fractions at Two Temperatures
L6|medium.statement:
The Pb–Bi binary system forms a eutectic at 44.0 wt% Bi and 125 °C (398 K). At 150 °C (423 K), the solid solubility limits are: the $\alpha$ phase (Pb-rich) can dissolve up to 20.0 wt% Bi, and the $\beta$ phase (Bi-rich) can dissolve up to 5.0 wt% Pb (i.e. the $\beta$ phase contains 95.0 wt% Bi).

An alloy of overall composition $X_0 = 60.0$ wt% Bi is cooled slowly from the fully liquid state.

**(a)** Apply the Gibbs Phase Rule ($F = C - P + 1$ at fixed pressure) to determine the number of degrees of freedom in the two-phase liquid + $\alpha$ region for this binary system.

**(b)** At $T = 150$ °C (423 K), the alloy is in the two-phase $\alpha + \beta$ region. Using the lever rule, calculate the weight fractions $f^{\alpha}$ and $f^{\beta}$ of each phase present.

**(c)** Just below the eutectic temperature (398 K), the liquid has completely solidified. The $\alpha$ phase at the eutectic now has composition 20.0 wt% Bi and the $\beta$ phase has composition 95.0 wt% Bi. Re-apply the lever rule at this temperature to find the new weight fractions $f^{\alpha}$ and $f^{\beta}$. Comment on how and why the phase fractions changed between 423 K and 398 K.
L6|medium.solution:
## Step 1 — Identify the system parameters

Binary system: $C = 2$ (Pb and Bi). Pressure is fixed at 1 atm throughout.

## Part (a) — Gibbs Phase Rule in the two-phase liquid + $\alpha$ region

At fixed pressure the phase rule reduces to:
$$F = C - P + 1$$

In the liquid + $\alpha$ two-phase region: $P = 2$ phases (using $P$ for number of phases).

$$F = 2 - 2 + 1 = \boxed{1}$$

There is **one degree of freedom** — fixing the temperature completely determines the compositions of both the liquid and the $\alpha$ phase (they are locked onto the liquidus and solidus curves respectively). Equivalently, the overall composition $X_0$ does *not* add a degree of freedom because the system is already constrained to the two-phase field; only $T$ (or equivalently one phase composition) can be independently varied.

## Part (b) — Lever rule at 423 K in the $\alpha + \beta$ region

At 150 °C the tie-line connects:
$$X^{\alpha} = 20.0 \text{ wt\% Bi}, \qquad X^{\beta} = 95.0 \text{ wt\% Bi}$$

Overall alloy composition: $X_0 = 60.0$ wt% Bi.

The lever rule gives:
$$f^{\alpha} = \frac{X^{\beta} - X_0}{X^{\beta} - X^{\alpha}} = \frac{95.0 - 60.0}{95.0 - 20.0} = \frac{35.0}{75.0} = \boxed{0.467}$$

$$f^{\beta} = \frac{X_0 - X^{\alpha}}{X^{\beta} - X^{\alpha}} = \frac{60.0 - 20.0}{95.0 - 20.0} = \frac{40.0}{75.0} = \boxed{0.533}$$

**Check (mass balance):** $f^{\alpha} + f^{\beta} = 0.467 + 0.533 = 1.000$ ✓

Composition check: $0.467 \times 20.0 + 0.533 \times 95.0 = 9.34 + 50.6 = 59.9 \approx 60.0$ wt% Bi ✓ (small rounding difference).

## Part (c) — Lever rule just below the eutectic at 398 K

Just below the eutectic, the entire alloy is solid. The two solid phases are:
$$X^{\alpha} = 20.0 \text{ wt\% Bi}, \qquad X^{\beta} = 95.0 \text{ wt\% Bi}$$

The tie-line endpoints are the same as at 423 K in this simplified problem (the solubility limits are given as identical at both temperatures). Therefore:

$$f^{\alpha} = \frac{95.0 - 60.0}{95.0 - 20.0} = \frac{35.0}{75.0} = \boxed{0.467}$$

$$f^{\beta} = \frac{60.0 - 20.0}{95.0 - 20.0} = \frac{40.0}{75.0} = \boxed{0.533}$$

**Comment on the change between 423 K and 398 K:**

In this idealised case the $\alpha$ and $\beta$ solubility limits are assumed constant with temperature, so the tie-line endpoints do not shift, and the lever-rule fractions are unchanged. In a real Pb–Bi system the solubility limits do shift slightly with temperature, which would cause a small change in phase fractions. More importantly, *at* the eutectic temperature (398 K) a **third phase** (liquid) is transiently present: $F = C - P + 1 = 2 - 3 + 1 = 0$ — an invariant point, with the liquid at 44.0 wt% Bi solidifying completely at constant temperature into the $\alpha + \beta$ mixture. The fraction of eutectic microstructure formed from that liquid is:
$$f_{\text{eutectic liquid}} = \frac{X_0 - X^{\alpha}}{X_{\text{eutectic}} - X^{\alpha}} = \frac{60.0 - 20.0}{44.0 - 20.0} = \frac{40.0}{24.0} \approx 1.67$$
This value exceeds 1, which signals that our alloy at 60.0 wt% Bi lies **to the right of the eutectic composition**. The primary solidification product before the eutectic reaction is $\beta$ phase (Bi-rich), not $\alpha$. The $\alpha$ present in the final structure comes entirely from the eutectic decomposition of the liquid.
L6|medium.final_answer: (a) $F = 1$; (b) $f^{\alpha} = 0.467$, $f^{\beta} = 0.533$; (c) $f^{\alpha} = 0.467$, $f^{\beta} = 0.533$ (fractions unchanged because solubility limits are given as constant; the eutectic reaction converts all remaining liquid at 398 K without altering the overall solid phase fractions).
common_mistakes: **Inverting the lever-rule formula**: writing $f^{\alpha} = (X_0 - X^{\alpha})/(X^{\beta} - X^{\alpha})$ instead of $(X^{\beta} - X_0)/(X^{\beta} - X^{\alpha})$. Remember the fraction of phase $\alpha$ uses the lever arm on the *opposite* ($\beta$) side: $(X^{\beta} - X_0)$ divided by the full tie-line length.

**Confusing number of phases $P$ with pressure $P$ in the phase rule**: in $F = C - P + 1$, the symbol $P$ counts phases in equilibrium (here $P = 2$ for a two-phase field), not the thermodynamic pressure. Writing $P = 1$ atm into the formula gives a nonsensical result.

**Applying a single lever rule across the eutectic without splitting the calculation**: for compositions near or at the eutectic, students sometimes apply the lever rule using only the $\alpha$ and $\beta$ endpoints and forget that just *at* the eutectic temperature three phases coexist (invariant point, $F = 0$), and the liquid contributes additional $\beta$ (or $\alpha$) upon solidification. Always check whether your overall composition lies to the left or right of the eutectic before setting up the lever rule.

L6|medium.title: Lever Rule in a Eutectic Alloy System
L6|medium.statement:
A binary alloy of elements P and Q exhibits a eutectic phase diagram at 1 atm. The eutectic point occurs at 40 wt% Q and 580 °C. At 650 °C, the liquidus on the P-rich side passes through 20 wt% Q and the liquidus on the Q-rich side passes through 65 wt% Q. The solidus on the P-rich side is at 8 wt% Q (giving the $\alpha$ solid phase) and the solidus on the Q-rich side is at 78 wt% Q (giving the $\beta$ solid phase), both also at 650 °C.

An alloy containing **50 wt% Q** is slowly cooled from 750 °C to 620 °C (which is just above the eutectic temperature of 580 °C).

**(a)** Apply the Gibbs phase rule $F = C - P_{\text{ph}} + 1$ (pressure fixed at 1 atm) to determine the number of degrees of freedom at 650 °C for this alloy in the two-phase liquid + $\beta$ region. Identify what the remaining free variable(s) are.

**(b)** At 650 °C, identify which two phases are present for the 50 wt% Q alloy (use the phase boundary data above), state their compositions, and calculate their mass fractions using the lever rule.

**(c)** Just above the eutectic temperature (620 °C), the tie-line endpoints are: $\alpha$ at 8 wt% Q and $\beta$ at 78 wt% Q, with any remaining liquid at 40 wt% Q (the eutectic composition). For the 50 wt% Q alloy at 620 °C, determine all phases present, their compositions, and their mass fractions.

Given data summary:
- Eutectic point: 40 wt% Q, 580 °C
- At 650 °C: $\alpha$-solidus = 8 wt% Q, liquid P-rich liquidus = 20 wt% Q, liquid Q-rich liquidus = 65 wt% Q, $\beta$-solidus = 78 wt% Q
- At 620 °C (just above eutectic): $\alpha$ = 8 wt% Q, liquid = 40 wt% Q, $\beta$ = 78 wt% Q
- Overall alloy composition: $X_0 = 50$ wt% Q
L6|medium.solution:
## Step-by-step solution

### Part (a) — Gibbs phase rule at 650 °C in the liquid + $\beta$ region

At fixed pressure, the Gibbs phase rule is:
$$F = C - P_{\text{ph}} + 1$$

For this binary alloy: $C = 2$ (components P and Q).

In the liquid + $\beta$ two-phase region: $P_{\text{ph}} = 2$.

$$F = 2 - 2 + 1 = \boxed{1}$$

**One degree of freedom remains.** Physically, once you fix the temperature (one variable), the compositions of both the liquid phase and the $\beta$ phase are completely determined by the phase boundaries — you cannot independently choose both temperature and phase composition. The remaining free variable is **temperature** (or equivalently, once $T$ is set, the tie-line endpoints are fixed and the only remaining adjustable quantity is *how much* of each phase is present — but that is not a thermodynamic degree of freedom, it is set by the overall alloy composition via the lever rule).

---

### Part (b) — Phases and lever rule at 650 °C

**Identify the two-phase region.** The overall composition is $X_0 = 50$ wt% Q. At 650 °C:
- Q-rich liquidus: 65 wt% Q
- $\beta$-solidus: 78 wt% Q

Since $65 < 50$ is false — checking: 50 wt% Q lies between the Q-rich liquidus (65 wt% Q) and the eutectic composition (40 wt% Q)... Let us re-examine both sides of the diagram.

At 650 °C the four boundaries are:
- P-rich liquidus: 20 wt% Q (left liquidus)
- $\alpha$-solidus: 8 wt% Q (left solidus, defines $\alpha$)
- Q-rich liquidus: 65 wt% Q (right liquidus)
- $\beta$-solidus: 78 wt% Q (right solidus, defines $\beta$)

The alloy at 50 wt% Q lies between the Q-rich liquidus (65 wt% Q) and the eutectic composition. More precisely, 50 wt% Q sits to the **right of the P-rich liquidus (20 wt%)** and to the **left of the Q-rich liquidus (65 wt%)**. This region between the two liquidus curves is entirely **liquid** — wait, that would be the case only if 50 wt% is within the lens. Let us reason carefully:

- Below the left liquidus (20 wt%) and above the $\alpha$-solidus (8 wt%): liquid + $\alpha$ two-phase region.
- Below the right liquidus (65 wt%) and above the $\beta$-solidus (78 wt%): liquid + $\beta$ two-phase region.
- Between 20 wt% and 65 wt% at 650 °C: **single-phase liquid**.

Since $20 < 50 < 65$, the 50 wt% Q alloy at 650 °C is in the **single-phase liquid region**.

$$\boxed{\text{At 650 °C: one phase — liquid at 50 wt% Q}}$$

$F = C - P_{\text{ph}} + 1 = 2 - 1 + 1 = 2$: two degrees of freedom (temperature and composition both free), consistent with a single-phase field.

*Correction to part (a):* The question asked about the liquid + $\beta$ region specifically. For a point that **is** in liquid + $\beta$ (e.g., a composition of 70 wt% Q at 650 °C, which lies between 65 and 78 wt%), the phase rule gives $F = 1$ as derived. The 50 wt% alloy itself is single-phase liquid at 650 °C.

---

### Part (b) revised — phases at 620 °C (just above eutectic)

We now use the data for 620 °C where the tie-line gives: $\alpha$ at 8 wt% Q, liquid at 40 wt% Q, $\beta$ at 78 wt% Q.

At 620 °C (just above 580 °C), three phases are potentially present: $\alpha$, liquid, and $\beta$. By Gibbs phase rule at fixed $P$:
$$F = 2 - 3 + 1 = 0 \quad \text{(invariant)}$$

This is the **eutectic isotherm** — three phases coexist at a single temperature. But at 620 °C we are *above* the eutectic (580 °C), so the liquid has not yet fully decomposed. However, the problem states the tie-line endpoints at 620 °C are $\alpha$ (8 wt%), liquid (40 wt%), and $\beta$ (78 wt%), implying we are at or very near the three-phase equilibrium line.

For overall composition $X_0 = 50$ wt% Q, which lies between 40 (liquid) and 78 ($\beta$), the alloy is in the **liquid + $\beta$** two-phase field at 620 °C.

**Lever rule for liquid + $\beta$ at 620 °C:**

Tie-line: liquid at $X_L = 40$ wt% Q, $\beta$ at $X_\beta = 78$ wt% Q, overall $X_0 = 50$ wt% Q.

$$f_\beta = \frac{X_0 - X_L}{X_\beta - X_L} = \frac{50 - 40}{78 - 40} = \frac{10}{38} \approx 0.263$$

$$f_L = \frac{X_\beta - X_0}{X_\beta - X_L} = \frac{78 - 50}{78 - 40} = \frac{28}{38} \approx 0.737$$

**Mass balance check:** $0.737 \times 40 + 0.263 \times 78 = 29.47 + 20.53 = 50.00$ wt% Q. $\checkmark$

### Summary table

| Temperature | Phases present | Phase compositions | Mass fractions |
|---|---|---|---|
| 650 °C | Liquid only | 50 wt% Q | $f_L = 1.00$ |
| 620 °C | Liquid + $\beta$ | $L$: 40 wt% Q; $\beta$: 78 wt% Q | $f_L \approx 0.737$; $f_\beta \approx 0.263$ |
L6|medium.final_answer: At 650 °C: single-phase liquid ($F = 2$). At 620 °C (liquid + $\beta$ region, $F = 1$): liquid (40 wt% Q) with mass fraction $f_L \approx 0.737$ and $\beta$ phase (78 wt% Q) with mass fraction $f_\beta \approx 0.263$.
common_mistakes: Incorrectly assuming the 50 wt% Q alloy is in a two-phase region at 650 °C without checking whether the composition falls between the two liquidus boundaries (20 and 65 wt% Q). Any composition between those two liquidus lines is single-phase liquid at 650 °C.

Applying the lever rule with the wrong tie-line endpoints — for example, using the solidus values (8 and 78 wt%) instead of the correct liquidus/solidus pair that brackets the actual two-phase region at the temperature of interest.

Confusing the Gibbs phase rule count by including pressure as a variable (using $F = C - P_{\text{ph}} + 2$) instead of the fixed-pressure form $F = C - P_{\text{ph}} + 1$, leading to answers that are one degree of freedom too high.

L6|medium.title: Lever Rule in a Peritectic System: Phase Fractions at a Fixed Temperature
L6|medium.statement:
A binary alloy system A–B has the phase diagram shown schematically below. At a temperature of $T = 950\,\text{K}$ (which lies in a two-phase $\alpha + \beta$ region at fixed pressure of 1 atm), experiments show that the $\alpha$ phase boundary is at $X_B = 0.12$ and the $\beta$ phase boundary is at $X_B = 0.68$.

An alloy is prepared with overall composition $X_B = 0.40$ (mole fraction of B).

**(a)** State how many degrees of freedom $F$ the system has at $T = 950\,\text{K}$ and $P = 1\,\text{atm}$, using the Gibbs phase rule. Identify what the degrees of freedom correspond to physically.

**(b)** Using the lever rule, calculate the mole fraction of each phase present at $T = 950\,\text{K}$.

**(c)** The alloy is then cooled to $T = 800\,\text{K}$, where the $\alpha$ phase boundary shifts to $X_B = 0.08$ and the $\beta$ phase boundary shifts to $X_B = 0.74$. Determine the new mole fractions of each phase. Comment on the direction of change and give a brief thermodynamic explanation in terms of $\Delta H_\text{mix}$ and $\Delta G$.

**Given data:**
- Binary system A–B, two components ($C = 2$)
- Pressure fixed at 1 atm throughout
- $T = 950\,\text{K}$: $X_B^\alpha = 0.12$, $X_B^\beta = 0.68$, overall $X_B^0 = 0.40$
- $T = 800\,\text{K}$: $X_B^\alpha = 0.08$, $X_B^\beta = 0.74$, overall $X_B^0 = 0.40$
L6|medium.solution:
## Part (a) — Gibbs Phase Rule

The Gibbs phase rule (at fixed pressure, so one degree of freedom is already consumed):

$$F = C - P_\text{phases} + 1$$

where $C = 2$ (components A and B) and $P_\text{phases} = 2$ (two phases $\alpha$ and $\beta$ coexist in the two-phase region).

$$F = 2 - 2 + 1 = \boxed{1}$$

**Physical interpretation:** With one degree of freedom, specifying the temperature $T$ completely fixes the compositions of both coexisting phases — i.e. $X_B^\alpha$ and $X_B^\beta$ are both determined once $T$ is chosen. The fraction of each phase is then set by the lever rule from the overall composition. You cannot independently vary both $T$ and the phase compositions; only one of these is free.

---

## Part (b) — Lever Rule at $T = 950\,\text{K}$

The lever rule for a two-phase region with a tie line from $X_B^\alpha = 0.12$ to $X_B^\beta = 0.68$, and overall composition $X_B^0 = 0.40$:

$$f^\alpha = \frac{X_B^\beta - X_B^0}{X_B^\beta - X_B^\alpha}$$

$$f^\alpha = \frac{0.68 - 0.40}{0.68 - 0.12} = \frac{0.28}{0.56} = 0.50$$

$$f^\beta = \frac{X_B^0 - X_B^\alpha}{X_B^\beta - X_B^\alpha}$$

$$f^\beta = \frac{0.40 - 0.12}{0.68 - 0.12} = \frac{0.28}{0.56} = 0.50$$

**Check (mass balance):**
$$f^\alpha X_B^\alpha + f^\beta X_B^\beta = (0.50)(0.12) + (0.50)(0.68) = 0.06 + 0.34 = 0.40 \checkmark$$

At $T = 950\,\text{K}$, the alloy is exactly **50 mol% $\alpha$ phase and 50 mol% $\beta$ phase**. The overall composition happens to sit precisely at the midpoint of the tie line.

---

## Part (c) — Lever Rule at $T = 800\,\text{K}$ and Thermodynamic Explanation

New tie-line endpoints: $X_B^\alpha = 0.08$, $X_B^\beta = 0.74$, overall composition unchanged at $X_B^0 = 0.40$.

$$f^\alpha = \frac{X_B^\beta - X_B^0}{X_B^\beta - X_B^\alpha} = \frac{0.74 - 0.40}{0.74 - 0.08} = \frac{0.34}{0.66} \approx 0.515$$

$$f^\beta = \frac{X_B^0 - X_B^\alpha}{X_B^\beta - X_B^\alpha} = \frac{0.40 - 0.08}{0.74 - 0.08} = \frac{0.32}{0.66} \approx 0.485$$

**Check (mass balance):**
$$0.515 \times 0.08 + 0.485 \times 0.74 = 0.0412 + 0.3589 = 0.400 \checkmark$$

### Direction of change

Cooling from 950 K to 800 K shifts $f^\alpha$ from 0.500 to 0.515 — a slight **increase in the $\alpha$ fraction** and corresponding decrease in $\beta$. The tie line has also widened (from $\Delta X = 0.56$ to $\Delta X = 0.66$), meaning the two phases become more compositionally distinct.

### Thermodynamic explanation

This behaviour is characteristic of a system with $\Delta H_\text{mix} > 0$ (A–A and B–B bonds preferred over A–B bonds). At high $T$, the entropy term $T\Delta S_\text{mix}$ is large enough to keep the two-phase region relatively narrow — the system tolerates more mixing disorder. As $T$ decreases, $|T\Delta S_\text{mix}|$ shrinks while $\Delta H_\text{mix}$ remains approximately constant, so $\Delta G_\text{mix} = \Delta H_\text{mix} - T\Delta S_\text{mix}$ becomes less negative (or more positive) at intermediate compositions. The common tangent construction on the $G$–$X$ curves at 800 K touches the two phase-parabola minima at more extreme compositions, giving a wider miscibility gap. In terms of the lever rule, a wider tie line means that for the same overall $X_B^0$, the lever arm lengths change — here shifting slightly more material into the $\alpha$ phase.
L6|medium.final_answer: (a) $F = 1$; (b) $f^\alpha = 0.50$, $f^\beta = 0.50$; (c) $f^\alpha \approx 0.515$, $f^\beta \approx 0.485$ — the $\alpha$ fraction increases slightly and the tie line widens on cooling, consistent with a positive $\Delta H_\text{mix}$ driving greater phase separation at lower $T$.
common_mistakes: Inverting the lever rule: computing $f^\alpha = (X_B^0 - X_B^\alpha)/(X_B^\beta - X_B^\alpha)$ instead of using the opposite arm. Students should remember that the fraction of a phase equals the lever arm on the **opposite** side of the overall composition divided by the full tie-line length.

Applying $F = C - P + 2$ (the full Gibbs phase rule) without accounting for the fixed pressure constraint. Since $P$ is fixed at 1 atm, the correct reduced form is $F = C - P_\text{phases} + 1$, giving $F = 1$ rather than $F = 2$.

Failing to perform the mass-balance check after applying the lever rule. A quick verification $f^\alpha X_B^\alpha + f^\beta X_B^\beta = X_B^0$ catches arithmetic errors immediately and should always be done.

L6|medium.title: Eutectic Alloy Composition from Phase Fraction Data
L6|medium.statement:
A binary alloy of elements A and B (with negligible mutual solid solubility — treat the pure solids as having essentially zero solute content) has a eutectic temperature of 520 K at 1 atm. At the eutectic temperature, the following equilibrium phase compositions apply:

| Phase | Composition |
|---|---|
| Liquid (eutectic) | $X_B^L = 0.38$ |
| Solid $\alpha$ (A-rich) | $X_B^\alpha \approx 0$ |
| Solid $\beta$ (B-rich) | $X_B^\beta \approx 1$ |

A technician has a crucible containing 2.5 mol of a binary A–B alloy at exactly 520 K and 1 atm. She observes under the microscope that the alloy is **two-thirds liquid and one-third solid** by mole fraction at this temperature (i.e. $f_L = 2/3$, $f_\text{solid} = 1/3$).

**(a)** Using the Gibbs Phase Rule (at fixed pressure), determine the number of degrees of freedom when three phases coexist in a binary system. What does this imply about the temperature and phase compositions in the crucible?

**(b)** Using the lever rule, determine the **overall mole-fraction composition** $X_B^0$ of the alloy in the crucible.

**(c)** Using your result from (b), calculate the **number of moles of liquid** and the **number of moles of each solid phase** ($\alpha$ and $\beta$) present at 520 K.

Additional data: total moles $n_\text{total} = 2.5$ mol.
L6|medium.solution:
## Step-by-step solution

### Part (a) — Gibbs Phase Rule at fixed pressure

The Gibbs Phase Rule at fixed pressure is:
$$F = C - P + 1$$
where $C$ = number of components, $P$ = number of phases.

Here $C = 2$ (binary system) and $P = 3$ (liquid + $\alpha$ solid + $\beta$ solid):
$$F = 2 - 3 + 1 = 0$$

**Zero degrees of freedom** — the system is **invariant**. At the eutectic point, *both* the temperature and the composition of every phase are completely fixed by nature. The technician cannot independently adjust $T$ or any phase composition while keeping all three phases in equilibrium. This is why the eutectic is a single point $(T_E, X_B^L)$ on the phase diagram, not a region.

---

### Part (b) — Overall composition from the lever rule

At the eutectic temperature the system contains **liquid** at $X_B^L = 0.38$ and **total solid** (a mixture of $\alpha$ and $\beta$). Because $\alpha$ is pure A ($X_B^\alpha \approx 0$) and $\beta$ is pure B ($X_B^\beta \approx 1$), we can treat the combined solid as occupying one end of the eutectic tie-line.

However, the most direct approach is to apply the lever rule between the **liquid phase** and the **total solid** on the overall composition axis.

For a two-region lever rule at the eutectic line (liquid coexisting with the aggregate solid), the two tie-line endpoints on the $X_B$ axis are:
- Liquid end: $X_B^L = 0.38$
- Solid aggregate end: since $\alpha \approx 0$ and $\beta \approx 1$ and they appear in proportion, the aggregate solid tracks toward pure A side or pure B side depending on $X_B^0$ relative to the eutectic.

Actually, the cleanest approach is a **global mass balance**. The overall system has mole fractions $f_L = 2/3$ and $f_\text{solid} = 1/3$. The liquid has $X_B^L = 0.38$; the total solid is a mixture of $\alpha$ ($X_B^\alpha = 0$) and $\beta$ ($X_B^\beta = 1$). We do not yet know the composition of the combined solid, but we can still use the lever rule between liquid and the entire solid field:

$$X_B^0 = f_L \cdot X_B^L + f_\text{solid} \cdot X_B^\text{solid,avg}$$

But we need $X_B^\text{solid,avg}$ first. Instead, apply the lever rule directly between the **two known pure-phase limits** — treating the eutectic point as the fulcrum:

Alternatively and most cleanly: use the lever rule between the **liquid composition** ($X_B^L = 0.38$) and the **overall composition**, noting the phase fractions:

$$f_L = \frac{X_B^\beta - X_B^0}{X_B^\beta - X_B^L} = \frac{1 - X_B^0}{1 - 0.38}$$

Set $f_L = 2/3$:
$$\frac{2}{3} = \frac{1 - X_B^0}{0.62}$$

$$1 - X_B^0 = \frac{2}{3} \times 0.62 = 0.4133$$

$$\boxed{X_B^0 = 1 - 0.4133 = 0.587}$$

Alternative check using the $\alpha$-end lever:
$$f_L = \frac{X_B^0 - X_B^\alpha}{X_B^L - X_B^\alpha} \quad\text{does not apply here because }X_B^0 > X_B^L$$

Since $X_B^0 = 0.587 > X_B^L = 0.38$, the overall composition lies to the **right** (B-rich side) of the eutectic liquid. The correct lever arm runs from $X_B^L$ to $X_B^\beta = 1$:

$$f_L = \frac{X_B^\beta - X_B^0}{X_B^\beta - X_B^L} = \frac{1 - 0.587}{1 - 0.38} = \frac{0.413}{0.620} = 0.667 \approx \frac{2}{3} \checkmark$$

The overall mole-fraction composition is $X_B^0 \approx 0.587$.

---

### Part (c) — Moles of each phase

**Total moles of liquid:**
$$n_L = f_L \times n_\text{total} = \frac{2}{3} \times 2.5 = 1.667 \text{ mol}$$

**Total moles of solid:**
$$n_\text{solid} = \frac{1}{3} \times 2.5 = 0.833 \text{ mol}$$

Now split the solid between $\alpha$ and $\beta$. The solid itself obeys a lever rule between $X_B^\alpha = 0$ and $X_B^\beta = 1$. The average $X_B$ of the combined solid is found from mass balance on B:

$$n_\text{total} \cdot X_B^0 = n_L \cdot X_B^L + n_\text{solid} \cdot X_B^\text{solid,avg}$$

$$2.5 \times 0.587 = 1.667 \times 0.38 + 0.833 \times X_B^\text{solid,avg}$$

$$1.4675 = 0.6335 + 0.833 \cdot X_B^\text{solid,avg}$$

$$X_B^\text{solid,avg} = \frac{1.4675 - 0.6335}{0.833} = \frac{0.834}{0.833} \approx 1.001 \approx 1.0$$

This tells us the combined solid is essentially **pure $\beta$** (pure B), with essentially no $\alpha$ phase present. This makes physical sense: because $X_B^0 = 0.587$ is **above** the eutectic composition $X_B^L = 0.38$, the alloy is **B-hyper-eutectic** — on cooling from the melt, primary $\beta$ solidifies first, leaving a residual liquid that becomes more enriched toward the eutectic composition. At the eutectic temperature, the remaining liquid ($X_B^L = 0.38$) solidifies as eutectic microstructure, but here at $f_L = 2/3$ we have not yet fully solidified — most B-rich material is in the liquid and the solid is $\beta$.

Therefore:
$$n_\beta = n_\text{solid} \approx 0.833 \text{ mol}, \qquad n_\alpha \approx 0 \text{ mol}$$

**Summary:**
| Phase | Moles |
|---|---|
| Liquid ($X_B^L = 0.38$) | **1.667 mol** |
| $\beta$ solid ($X_B^\beta \approx 1$) | **0.833 mol** |
| $\alpha$ solid ($X_B^\alpha \approx 0$) | **0 mol** |

This is consistent with the alloy being hyper-eutectic (B-rich relative to the eutectic point): primary $\beta$ precipitates before the eutectic reaction begins, and at this snapshot the system sits at the eutectic temperature with $2/3$ liquid yet to transform.
L6|medium.final_answer: (a) $F = 0$: zero degrees of freedom — temperature and all phase compositions are fixed. (b) $X_B^0 \approx 0.587$. (c) $n_L = 1.667$ mol liquid; $n_\beta \approx 0.833$ mol solid $\beta$; $n_\alpha \approx 0$ mol solid $\alpha$.
common_mistakes: Applying the lever rule between $X_B^\alpha$ and $X_B^L$ instead of between $X_B^L$ and $X_B^\beta$. Because the overall composition $X_B^0 = 0.587$ lies to the right of the eutectic liquid composition $X_B^L = 0.38$, the correct tie-line endpoints for liquid vs. total solid are $X_B^L$ and $X_B^\beta = 1$, not $X_B^\alpha = 0$ and $X_B^L$.

Forgetting that $F = 0$ at the eutectic means all phase compositions are fixed — students sometimes try to vary the liquid composition away from $X_B^L = 0.38$ to satisfy the lever rule constraint, which is not permitted at the invariant point.

Assuming the solid must be a mixture of both $\alpha$ and $\beta$ in all cases. For a hyper-eutectic alloy ($X_B^0 > X_B^L$), the solid present at the eutectic temperature (before the eutectic reaction completes) is primary $\beta$ only; the $\alpha + \beta$ eutectic microstructure forms only once the remaining liquid transforms.

L6|medium.title: Lever Rule on a Peritectic Tie-Line in the Cu–Zn System
L6|medium.statement:
A binary Cu–Zn alloy at constant pressure contains **38 wt% Zn** and is held at a temperature where it sits in a two-phase ($\alpha + \beta$) region on the phase diagram. At this temperature, the equilibrium phase compositions are:

- $\alpha$ phase: **28 wt% Zn**
- $\beta$ phase: **52 wt% Zn**

**(a)** State how many degrees of freedom $F$ the system has at this temperature and pressure, using the Gibbs phase rule. Explain what that means physically.

**(b)** Apply the lever rule to determine the mass fractions $f^{\alpha}$ and $f^{\beta}$ of the two phases present.

**(c)** A second alloy of the **same Cu–Zn system** but with overall composition **45 wt% Zn** is cooled from the fully liquid state to the same temperature. State, with reasoning, whether the $\beta$ phase fraction in this second alloy is higher or lower than in the first alloy, and calculate it.

**(d)** At a lower temperature, three phases ($\alpha$, $\beta$, and liquid $L$) coexist simultaneously in the Cu–Zn binary at fixed pressure. How many degrees of freedom does the system now have? What is the geometric representation of this three-phase equilibrium on a $T$–composition phase diagram?
L6|medium.solution:
## Step 1 — Gibbs Phase Rule (Part a)

The Gibbs phase rule at fixed pressure is:
$$F = C - P + 1$$
where $C$ is the number of components and $P$ is the number of phases.

For the Cu–Zn binary at the temperature in question:
- $C = 2$ (Cu and Zn)
- $P = 2$ (the $\alpha$ and $\beta$ phases coexist)

$$F = 2 - 2 + 1 = \boxed{1}$$

**Physical meaning:** With one degree of freedom, only *one* intensive variable can be varied independently while keeping both phases present. At fixed pressure, that one variable is temperature — but choosing $T$ then fixes the compositions of *both* phases (they lie on the phase-boundary curves). The overall composition $X_0$ determines only the *proportions* of the two phases via the lever rule, not a new independent variable.

---

## Step 2 — Lever Rule for Alloy 1: $X_0 = 38$ wt% Zn (Part b)

Label the tie-line endpoints:
$$X^{\alpha} = 28 \text{ wt\% Zn}, \quad X^{\beta} = 52 \text{ wt\% Zn}, \quad X_0 = 38 \text{ wt\% Zn}$$

Mass fraction of $\beta$ phase (lever arm on the $\alpha$ side, divided by total tie-line length):
$$f^{\beta} = \frac{X_0 - X^{\alpha}}{X^{\beta} - X^{\alpha}} = \frac{38 - 28}{52 - 28} = \frac{10}{24} \approx \boxed{0.417}$$

Mass fraction of $\alpha$ phase:
$$f^{\alpha} = \frac{X^{\beta} - X_0}{X^{\beta} - X^{\alpha}} = \frac{52 - 38}{52 - 28} = \frac{14}{24} \approx \boxed{0.583}$$

**Verification (mass balance):**
$$f^{\alpha} + f^{\beta} = 0.583 + 0.417 = 1.000 \checkmark$$
$$f^{\alpha}\,X^{\alpha} + f^{\beta}\,X^{\beta} = 0.583 \times 28 + 0.417 \times 52 = 16.3 + 21.7 = 38.0 \text{ wt\%} \checkmark$$

---

## Step 3 — Lever Rule for Alloy 2: $X_0 = 45$ wt% Zn (Part c)

The phase boundary compositions at the **same temperature** are unchanged:
$$X^{\alpha} = 28 \text{ wt\% Zn}, \quad X^{\beta} = 52 \text{ wt\% Zn}$$

$$f^{\beta} = \frac{X_0 - X^{\alpha}}{X^{\beta} - X^{\alpha}} = \frac{45 - 28}{52 - 28} = \frac{17}{24} \approx \boxed{0.708}$$

$$f^{\alpha} = 1 - 0.708 = 0.292$$

**Reasoning:** Alloy 2 has an overall composition (45 wt% Zn) that is closer to $X^{\beta}$ (52 wt%) than Alloy 1 (38 wt%) is. The lever rule fulcrum shifts toward the $\beta$ boundary, so the $\beta$ lever arm lengthens relative to the total tie-line and $f^{\beta}$ increases. The $\beta$ fraction in Alloy 2 (0.708) is **higher** than in Alloy 1 (0.417).

---

## Step 4 — Three-Phase Coexistence (Part d)

With $C = 2$, $P = 3$ at fixed pressure:
$$F = C - P + 1 = 2 - 3 + 1 = \boxed{0}$$

**Zero degrees of freedom** — the system is **invariant**.
